### The wait-queue ping-pong and the timer queue under host load (`wait::prove_ping_pong`, `wait::run_ping_pong`, `prove_timers`, `timers::Firing`, `timers::Verdict`, `timers::judge`, `runqueue::judge_round_trips`, `runqueue::RoundTrips`, `runqueue::ROUND_TRIP_LIMIT_MICROS`, `runqueue::DISTURBED_PER_MILLE`, `sched::yield_until_away`; CLAUDE.md §26, §30, §68, §72; task WAIT-TIMERS-LOAD; 2026-11-08)

- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08, task WAIT-TIMERS-LOAD, on `claude/priceless-einstein-d6f3b9` from `118834b` (the weighted-share proof, `claude/elegant-thompson-48edc8`). Original code. The ping-pong's first rule (`05deb69`) was replaced after review, in the commit that follows it; see "The first two designs" below.
- **Merged:** into `claude/interesting-carson-ae7c83` on 2026-11-09, on the owner's word (`31c3d39`; `framekernel/src/main.rs`, also changed by the early console, merged automatically). On that tree `cargo xtask check` passes (827 tests, 0 failures, 6 ignored) and `cargo xtask boot-matrix` passes on a quiet host: all 15 ping-pongs passed at their first run (41 to 56 µs on two or more processors, 5 µs on one) and all 15 `prove_timers` runs decided at their first run (worst lateness 0 µs in 14, 38 µs in one).
- **Why.** The two boot proofs still failing on a loaded host, seen at double load (two `yes` per logical core, about 20 processes on this 10-core M1 Max) by the session before this one: the wake-up ping-pong in `wait::prove` (1000 round trips between two processors, each woken by the other; a round trip must average under 2000 µs) failed in 3 boots of 5 of that session's probe kernels (2003, 2045 and 2084 µs), and `prove_timers` (a timer at most 2 ms late) failed in 2 boots of 30 of its A/B (worst lateness 3300 and 6979 µs), each after six runs.
- **The cause, measured.** A probe kernel (not committed) added, to each boot, 20 more ping-pongs timing every round trip and 600 more runs of the timer loop recording the polls around every firing. Each row below is the boots named, one at a time, with the named number of `yes` per logical core and, as in the earlier sections, whatever else other sessions ran on the machine (1-minute load averages from about 5, quiet, to over 250). The 3× and 4× rows go beyond the requested load to show where each mean finally gives way.

  The timer proof, per run of three firings (a run is "undecided" if a firing's poll was 2 ms or more after its deadline with the previous poll before it: `timers::Verdict::Undecided`; the probe runs back to back, so a budget of *n* runs is measured on *n* consecutive runs, over every starting point; the old rule itself, replayed on the same logs, gives the same failure rates to within 0.1 of a percentage point):

  | Load | Runs (boots) | Firings on time / decisively late (`Verdict::Late`) / undecided | Runs undecided | Longest streak of undecided runs | Budget of 6 runs ran out (the old budget) | 12 runs | 24 runs |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | quiet | 1200 (2) | 3600 / 0 / 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
  | 1× | 3600 (6) | 10314 / 0 / 486 | 11.0 % | 7 | 0.14 % | 0 | 0 |
  | 2× | 3600 (6) | 7678 / 0 / 3122 | 55.0 % | 12 | 4.4 % | 0.08 % | 0 |
  | 3× | 2400 (4) | 4248 / 0 / 2952 | 75.0 % | 22 | 20.8 % | 3.6 % | 0 |
  | 4× | 1200 (2) | 1966 / 0 / 1634 | 81.6 % | 21 | 29.6 % | 6.1 % | 0 |

  In all 36 000 firings, none was decisively late. In the 27 609 firings of the runs whose polls were logged (every run with a firing at least 200 µs late or a poll gap of at least 500 µs), none had its deadline already passed at the poll before the one that fired it, and the other 8 391 firings came within 200 µs of their deadlines: the queue did not hold a due timer. Every lateness the proof reported was a late look. (The queue is polled, and on this host the polling loop's vCPU is simply away for milliseconds; a stall across a deadline makes the poll that follows report the stall's length.)

  The ping-pong, per run of 1000 round trips (microseconds; "slow" means a round trip of at least 2 ms; the boot flow's away time is the sum of its spin loop's steps of at least 3 ms, as a share of the run; the 4× row's 60 runs are 3 boots, the fourth stopped at another proof):

  | Load | Runs (boots) | Mean round trip: average of the runs (range) | Runs ≥ 2000 µs | Median round trip: average (worst run) | Slow round trips per 1000: average (worst) | Boot flow's processor away, per mille of the run: average (lowest) | Far CPU's reschedule IPIs per run: lowest, median |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | quiet | 40 (2) | 38 (28–46) | 0 | 27 (33) | 1 (1) | 0 (0) | 908, 948 |
  | 1× | 120 (6) | 258 (68–519) | 0 | 102 (184) | 23 (65) | 119 (0) | 824, 904 |
  | 2× | 120 (6) | 583 (145–1713) | 0 | 170 (638) | 66 (220) | 284 (0) | 852, 918 |
  | 3× | 80 (4) | 861 (486–1387) | 0 | 208 (343) | 108 (186) | 433 (268) | 887, 918 |
  | 4× | 60 (3) | 1255 (738–2563) | 4 | 276 (758) | 155 (312) | 561 (399) | 894, 922 |

  The mean is the host's tail, not the kernel: at 2× the slowest tenth of the round trips carries 60 % of the time, and the mean of a run varies from 145 to 1713 µs while the worst run's median is 638 µs and the median across runs is about a third of the mean. Quiet, the median round trip is 27 µs; loading the host does not change what the kernel does for a round trip, only when the host lets it happen. At 4× the mean finally crosses the bound (2563, 2474, 2044 and 2005 µs in 4 runs of 60, medians 578, 758, 514 and 507 µs); in those four runs the boot flow's processor was away for at least 65 % of the run, and the far CPU took at least 900 reschedule IPIs. (In every run at every load, the far CPU took at least 824; in the 72 runs whose mean was at least 1 ms, the boot flow's processor was away for at least 34 % of the run.) The 75th percentile, by contrast, would have failed 6 of the 60 runs at 4× (up to 312 slow round trips per 1000), so a percentile higher than the median does not survive this host.
- **What changed (kernel binary).**
  - `prove_timers` (`main.rs`): every firing's lateness is an interval from the polls around it, and a run decides only if the whole interval of every firing is inside or outside the 2 ms limit (`timers::judge`). A firing whose previous poll is already past the deadline by the limit means the queue held a due timer (`Late`): a stall cannot make that happen, and it fails at once, as does a firing in the wrong order (a stall cannot reorder a queue or fire a cancelled timer). A stall across a deadline leaves the firing `Undecided`, and the whole run is measured again, up to 64 runs; each run is about 15 ms and only an undecided run leads to another, so an undisturbed boot pays for one run, as before. The boot line is unchanged except that `(after a stalled run)` now means any undecided run came first.
  - `wait::prove` (`wait.rs`): the ping-pong moves into `prove_ping_pong` and `run_ping_pong`. **The bound did not change, and only the bound can pass a run: its mean round trip must be under 2000 µs** (`runqueue::judge_round_trips`). The boot flow, which spins in `yield_until_away` while it waits, adds up the steps of its own loop of at least 3 ms (the same 3 ms the weighted-share proof uses). A run over the bound during which that came to at least a tenth of the run (`runqueue::DISTURBED_PER_MILLE`) says nothing either way and is measured again, at most 8 runs in all, each against the same bound. A run over the bound without that reading fails at once, as before. The reading is only a hint: a thread under test on the boot flow's processor can produce it just by running, which is why it can earn a repeat and never a pass. A run on one processor never earns a repeat: there the boot flow takes turns with the two threads, so the reading is about 80 % on a quiet boot and says nothing about the host. The boot line reports the reading and the run number, `… 1000 round trips, N us each, woken by IPI (boot flow away for A per mille of the run, run R of 8)`, ending in `(after a stalled run)` when a run was repeated, and on one processor `… N us each (one processor)`; the `boot-test` markers still match.
  - `sched::yield_until_away`: `yield_until`'s loop, returning the sum of its steps of at least `RUNNING_STEP_MICROS` (3 ms). `yield_until` calls it and discards the result; the cost is one more `rdtsc` a turn. A step that long means the virtual CPU was descheduled or that another thread on that processor ran for that long, and the loop cannot tell which, as its comment now says: its result may earn a repeat of a measurement, never a more lenient verdict.
- **What changed (library, host-tested).** `timers::Firing` (the polls around a firing, with `latest`, `earliest` and `verdict`), `timers::Verdict` and `timers::judge`, with hand cases at the limit's edges, undecided, on-time, late, a timer that never fired, a closely polled run deciding exactly, and a seeded property test (4000 cases of random stalls) that a correct queue is never judged `Late` and a queue holding timers past the limit is never `OnTime`. `runqueue::judge_round_trips` and `RoundTrips`, with a test that a disturbance earns a repeat and never a pass: the bound's edges, the tenth, and, over a grid of inputs, that only a mean under the bound passes.
- **Why these rules, and not others.**
  - *The timer proof:* the two polls around a firing bound its lateness, so the verdict needs no assumption about the host: the interval either fits inside the 2 ms or does not, and a stall can only widen it. A run decides only when every firing is decided (three deadlines in one run, as before; the whole-run rule rather than accumulating per deadline, because 24 runs were never exhausted at any load measured and the code is simpler), and the budget of 64 is cheap: an undisturbed boot still pays one 15 ms run. The bound (2 ms) did not change: a queue that is late with the poller looking fails at once, as the controls show.
  - *The ping-pong:* every run that passes has met the old bound. What changed is only what happens to a run over it. On a quiet host such a run fails at once, as it always did. On a loaded host the mean of a run can be carried by stalls of the host (the table above: at 4× the mean reached 2563 µs with medians under 760 µs), and such a run says nothing about the kernel, so it is measured again, against the same bound: the method of the clock proofs and the weighted-share proof, where evidence of a disturbance buys a repeat and nothing else. How far that carries is in the boot-level table below. The budget is 8 runs because a repeat costs nothing unless it is used: an undisturbed boot pays for one run, two of the boots measured at 4× below passed only at their fifth and eighth runs, and a genuinely slow kernel still fails, later rather than sooner (at most 8 runs of at most 5 s). The price of the rule is that a kernel which is too slow in only some of its runs, and keeps the boot flow away while it is, can pass on a repeat; the first two designs below show what it costs to try to do better.
  - A percentile or a trimmed mean instead of the mean, used always, was rejected: the 75th percentile fails at 4× (the slow share reaches 31 %), and either statistic would throw away part of what the old bound was sensitive to on a quiet host.
- **The first two designs, and why they were not shipped.** `05deb69`, the first version of this rule, judged a run by its median and by the share of its round trips that came by reschedule IPI, instead of its mean, whenever the boot flow was away for at least a tenth of the run. That was wrong, and its record's statement that the bound was unchanged did not hold for such a run: the pinger runs on the boot flow's processor, so a step of 3 ms there can be the pinger running, and false evidence bought a looser verdict, not only a repeat. Two reviewing sessions found it (the reviewer's control is below: with the pinger spinning 10 ms on every fourth round trip and no host load, `05deb69` passed both boots, 2555 and 2554 µs, medians 55 and 56 µs, away for 893 and 891 per mille, where `118834b` failed both). A second design was built and not shipped: keep the looser verdict, on evidence neither thread can produce on the other's processor, both processors losing at least 3 timer ticks (`prove_weights`' threshold). It fired on all four runs over the bound at 4× (at least 18 ticks lost on one processor and 9 on the other) and never on a quiet or 1× run. But a kernel holding interrupts off on both processors produces it too: with both threads spinning 25 ms with interrupts off on every twentieth round trip and no host load, it passed (`2553 us each (median 55 us, 916 reschedule IPIs, 73 and 80 ticks lost, …)`). And it is weakest where a repeat is enough: on the eight longest runs at 2×, the far processor lost under 3 ticks in five. Hence the shipped rule: a disturbance earns a repeat, and only the bound earns a pass (CLAUDE.md P0: a ping-pong that can still fail under heavy load is better than one that passes a slow kernel).
- **Measured at boot level.** `cargo xtask boot-test`, the parent kernel `118834b` and the final rule alternating boot by boot, each boot's first failure. The load in the first column is the range and median of the 1-minute load average when each boot ended.

  | Experiment (alternating boot by boot) | Kernel | Boots | Pass | First failure: ping-pong | First failure: timers | First failure: another proof | Failure rate | Ping-pong mean in the boot lines (range, µs) | Timer proof repeated a run | Mean boot time |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 1×, 10 pairs (load 21 to 32, median 25) | original (`118834b`) | 10 | 10 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 % | 89–1030 | 2 of 10 | 30 s |
  | | **final rule** | 10 | 9 | **0** | **0** | 1 (`clock`) | 10 % | 64–1014 | 1 of 9 | 29 s |
  | 2×, 15 pairs (load 27 to 34, median 30) | original (`118834b`) | 15 | 13 | 0 | 1 | 1 (the timed wait, 81 ms, bound 80) | 13 % | 1389–1722 | 5 of 14 | 41 s |
  | | **final rule** | 15 | 14 | **0** | **0** | 1 (`scheduler`) | 7 % | 1287–1683 | 7 of 14 | 42 s |
  | 4×, 20 pairs (load 33 to 58, median 53) | original (`118834b`) | 20 | 0 | 5 | 0 | 15 (`clock` 9, APIC timer 6) | 100 % | 2823–3408 (5 boots reached it) | none reached it | 21 s |
  | | **final rule** | 20 | 2 | **4** | 0 | 14 (APIC timer 8, `clock` 5, `scheduler` 1) | 90 % | 391–2982 (6 boots reached it) | 1 of 2 | 30 s |

  The host was not the one of the earlier measurements in this section: other sessions had gone idle, and the same kernel `118834b` took about 2.5 times as long per round trip (the median of its boot-line means was 796 µs at 1×, 1540 at 2× and 3110 at 4×, against 314, 559 and 1356 earlier the same day). A count of `yes` does not by itself fix the stress.

  At 2×, the load this task is for, no boot of either kernel failed the ping-pong: the final rule's 14 boots all passed at the first run, with means of 1287 to 1683 µs, not far under the bound. Its timer proof passed all 14, seven of them after a stalled run, where the old kernel's failed 1 of 14 (`worst lateness 3111 us (after a stalled run): timers failed`, the failure this task started from). At 1× neither kernel failed either proof.

  At 4× the host's ordinary round trip in this batch is over the bound (means of 2761 to 3408 µs), and repeats cannot change that. The final rule passed 2 of the 6 boots that reached the proof, at runs 5 and 8, and failed 4 after all 8 runs (for example `2761 us each, woken by IPI (boot flow away for 703 per mille of the run, run 8 of 8) (after a stalled run): wait queues failed`); the old kernel failed all 5 it reached. That is the cost of refusing a looser verdict: at that load the proof measures the host, and says so by failing. Most boots at 4× stopped earlier in both kernels, at the APIC timer proof (`50 interrupts in 756124 us, expected 50 in 500000 us`; 6 and 8 boots) and the clock proofs (the RTC rule and the cross-CPU check's 100 handoffs; 9 and 5): other proofs, not touched.

  The `scheduler` failures in the final arm are the two-worker fairness check of `sched::prove` (iterations within a factor of 2: `counted 549175 and 253257` at 2×, `133233 and 359113` at 4×), already recorded as sensitive to load. The only change on its path is one more `rdtsc` per turn of `yield_until`. Over every batch of this section it failed 0 of 105 boots of the old kernel and 2 of 105 of the new; over the last batch the ratios match (median 1.11 to 1.22, 90th percentile 1.27 to 1.70, in both arms), so the sample cannot tell a change from chance, and it is reported here rather than explained away. The RTC failure at 1× in the final arm (`too uncertain to confirm within 1 %`) is the clock proof's, unrelated and not touched.
- **Negative and positive controls** (each a temporary edit on a scratch copy of the final tree, booted with `cargo xtask boot-test`; positive controls in italics; quiet host unless noted):
  - timer queue: a timer genuinely 3 ms late with the poller running → `worst lateness 3000 us: timers failed`, at the first run; the cancelled timer fires → `fired in order [10, 20, 99, 30], … : timers failed`; a queue that never fires → `fired in order [], … : timers failed`;
  - *a 9 ms stall across a deadline in the first run → repeated, the boot passes: `worst lateness 0 us (after a stalled run)`;*
  - the same stall with the repeat disabled → `worst lateness 8919 us: timers failed` (the stall really would have failed the proof); a stall in every run → `worst lateness 8900 us (after a stalled run): timers failed` after 64 runs (the budget is bounded);
  - ping-pong, a kernel that delays itself with no host load (the reviewing sessions' control and its neighbours): the pinger spinning 10 ms on every fourth round trip, interrupts on → `2541 us each, woken by IPI (boot flow away for 895 per mille of the run, run 8 of 8) (after a stalled run): wait queues failed`, the same on four processors (`2552 us each`, 903 per mille, run 8 of 8) and at 2× load (`4568 us each`, 852 per mille, run 8 of 8); the ponger doing the same → `2560 us each, woken by IPI (boot flow away for 15 per mille of the run, run 1 of 8): wait queues failed`, at once; a 25 ms hold with interrupts off on every tenth round trip, pinger `2552 us each` (979 per mille, run 8 of 8) and ponger `2554 us each` (5 per mille, run 1 of 8), both fail; both threads holding interrupts off for 25 ms on every twentieth round trip → `2552 us each` (489 per mille, run 8 of 8), fails: the hold that passed the second design. On one processor (`ORIGIN_QEMU_SMP=1`), every fourth round trip 10 ms slow → `2506 us each (one processor): wait queues failed`, at once;
  - ping-pong, the wake-up path: no reschedule IPI at all → `… did not finish within 5 s: wait queues failed` (quiet and at 2×: woken only by ticks, each round trip takes a tick period); every second wake's IPI lost → the same; every fourth wake's IPI lost → `3026 us each, woken by IPI (boot flow away for 0 per mille of the run, run 1 of 8): wait queues failed` (the undisturbed mean, at once), at 2× `4722 us each` (441 per mille, run 8 of 8), fails; a wake-up path 3 ms slow → `3066 us each, … run 1 of 8): wait queues failed` at once; 2.5 ms slow at 2× → `… did not finish within 5 s: wait queues failed`;
  - *a 2.5 s stall of the boot flow's processor in the first run → repeated, the boot passes: `49 us each, woken by IPI (boot flow away for 0 per mille of the run, run 2 of 8) (after a stalled run)`; both processors stalled 2.5 s with interrupts off in the first run (a descheduled vCPU, as the guest sees it) → the same, `51 us each, … run 2 of 8) (after a stalled run)`; the first run stalled 1 s and slow (a 3 ms slow wake path) → `46 us each, … run 2 of 8) (after a stalled run)`;*
  - the same 2.5 s stall with the repeat disabled → `2544 us each, woken by IPI (boot flow away for 982 per mille of the run, run 1 of 1): wait queues failed` (the stall really would have failed the proof);
  - a 2.5 s stall in every run → `2542 us each, woken by IPI (boot flow away for 983 per mille of the run, run 8 of 8) (after a stalled run): wait queues failed`; both processors stalled 1 s and a 3 ms slow wake path in every run → `4046 us each, … run 8 of 8) (after a stalled run): wait queues failed` (the budget is bounded).

In that matrix every ping-pong passed at its first run, with means of 41 to 55 µs on two or more processors (boot flow away for 0 per mille) and 4 and 5 µs on one, and every `prove_timers` line read `worst lateness 0 us`.

The other proofs this comparison shows failing under load were not touched: the timed wait (`prove_timed`, 81 ms against a bound of 80 in one boot of the old kernel at 2×, 69 ms at worst otherwise); the RTC proof (`too uncertain to confirm within 1 %`, one boot of the final kernel at 1×, and it stopped one control boot at 2×); the two-worker fairness check; and, at 4×, the APIC timer proof and the cross-CPU TSC check's 100 handoffs. At 4× in the last batch the ping-pong itself failed most boots that reached it, as described above. ### Serialized kernel console (2026-11-07)

- **What:**
  - `console` (binary): a `Console` collects one line (160 bytes) and sends it to COM1 under one spin lock, with interrupts disabled. Lines from different processors, or from an interrupt handler on the same one, never interleave; longer lines go out in whole 160-byte pieces.
  - Exception reports and the panic handler use `Console::urgent`. It tries the lock 2^22 times (on the order of 100 ms, longer than one line takes), then writes without it, so a processor that faulted inside the console, or waits on one that died holding the lock, still reports.
  - Every boot proof, the exception handler, the panic handler and the write system call now print through it. `origin-sync` gains `SpinLock::try_lock`.
- **A bug found on the way:** the first `try_lock` built its guard with `bool::then_some`, which evaluates its argument eagerly. A failed attempt therefore built a guard and dropped it, unlocking a lock that someone else held. The new host test (a held lock must refuse `try_lock` from another thread) caught it before the kernel used it; the guard is now built only on success.
- **Proof** (every boot): every online CPU prints 20 lines at once. Each line is `origin-kernel: console: CPU {id} line {k} of 20: ` followed by 60 copies of the letter `a + id`. xtask then checks the whole log:
  - every proof line arrived whole and in order, from every CPU;
  - no line of the log holds two `origin-kernel:` prefixes.

  Two new xtask unit tests cover mixed, lost, joined and over-long lines. In the boot log the two CPUs' lines alternate in runs (8, 1, 7, 1, 1, 1, 3, 6, …), so the printing really overlapped.
- **Control:** with the lock bypassed, two CPUs' bytes mix mid-line, and the boot test fails with "two kernel lines ran together".
- **Evidence:** `cargo xtask check` and `boot-matrix` (1, 2 and 4 CPUs) pass; boot to halt takes 4.8, 5.4 and 7.1 s.
- **Limitation:** interrupts stay off while one line is sent. In QEMU that is microseconds; at 115 200 baud on real hardware it is about 9 ms per 100 bytes. Production logging will go to a memory ring drained by a thread (CLAUDE.md §69).

### The early console: the firmware's framebuffer and a UART from the SPCR (ADR-0010, accepted by the owner; `boot/info`, `boot/uefi`, `paging::layout`, `fbconsole`, `font`, `spcr`, `serial`, `console`; xtask; CLAUDE.md §13, §19, §51, §58, §69; 2026-11-08)

ADR-0009 H6 required a console that does not depend on a 16550 at I/O port `0x3F8`, because neither first machine documents its COM port's address and a failed boot would have shown nothing.

- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, session `funny-benz-fa7d10`), 2026-11-08. Original code and font, no third-party crates (§3, §5).
- **Merged:** into `claude/interesting-carson-ae7c83` on 2026-11-09, on the owner's word (`8040882`; the merge changed no code from `a96bf7b`). On the merged tree `31c3d39`, `cargo xtask check` passes (827 tests, 0 failures, 6 ignored) and `cargo xtask boot-matrix` passes on a quiet host, the 8 `boot-console` scenarios included. Drawing a line took 226 to 245 µs on average and at most 808 µs (14 boots, QEMU TCG).
- **ABI:** boot info **0.4** appends `Framebuffer` (48 bytes at offset 128, `size_of::<BootInfo>() == 176`), with pixel format as channel masks. Written as Proposed under §84 and **accepted by the owner on 2026-11-08** (ADR-0010 E1, `docs/engineering/OWNER_DECISIONS.md` item 27), together with the mapping window and the UART policy (items 28 and 29).
- **What:**
  - `origin-boot-info`: `Framebuffer`, `FramebufferError`, `Framebuffer::check` (the contract: both the loader and the kernel run it), `overlaps_ram` (the "is it RAM" question for a device range).
  - `origin-boot-uefi`: `protocols` (GOP structures, `LocateHandle`), `framebuffer::describe` (GOP mode → boot-info framebuffer; RGB, BGR and bit-mask formats become masks), and `find_framebuffer`/`framebuffer_of` in `main.rs`: every Graphics Output handle is examined and the first usable one the firmware uses as a console wins (`EFI_CONSOLE_OUT_DEVICE`), else the first usable one. The mode is never changed. A framebuffer that overlaps RAM or cannot be mapped is dropped, not fatal.
  - `origin-paging::layout`: `framebuffer_mapping` (the first 2 GiB of the MMIO window, keeping the physical offset within 2 MiB so large leaves work), and `map_framebuffer` (run after everything else in both the loader's and the kernel's tables, so a failure costs only the framebuffer). Mapped uncached, kernel-only, writable, never executable. `MMIO_BASE` starts above the 2 GiB.
  - `framekernel::font`: an original 8 by 16 ASCII font, 96 cells (95 printable characters and a replacement glyph), written in the source as a "contact sheet" of `.`/`#` rows, compiled at build time, with tests that every printable glyph exists, is distinct and is the only ink in its cell. **Drawn by hand for this project** (glyph by glyph on the grid, as the source shows); no existing font's data, file, image or table was consulted or copied (§3, §51). `0` is slashed and `1`, `l`, `I` differ, for reading addresses and logs.
  - `framekernel::fbconsole`: `Screen` (geometry from a validated `Framebuffer`; scale 1 below 1440 rows, 2 below 2880, else 3), `Cursor` (one atomic, lock-free for urgent reports), drawing through `PixelSink`. The console never scrolls and never reads video memory: a newline paints a bar on the next row and the screen wraps, so a line costs one row's writes (ADR-0010 E3). Each UTF-8 lead byte draws the replacement glyph once, continuation bytes draw nothing, other non-printable bytes draw the replacement, `\r` does nothing.
  - `framekernel::spcr`: `parse` (revisions 1–4; interfaces 0/1 in revision 1 and DBG2 subtypes 0x0, 0x1, 0x12, 0x14 otherwise; the Generic Address Structure in I/O or memory space, stride and access width per the DBG2 notes; I/O ports below `0x1000` other than the four standard COM blocks refused; every other value refused by name), `UartAddress`, `Spcr::line_setup` (a stated rate and clock are programmed; otherwise a programmed latch is left alone, and a zero latch gets the table's rate on the PC clock for an I/O UART).
  - `framekernel::serial`: `configure(LineSetup)` (program a divisor or keep the firmware's settings), `write_bytes`, `line_settings`/`restore`, `divisor_for`, `EarlyLog`. `init` programs what it did before, after clearing a stray DLAB.
  - `console` (binary): `Sinks` under the console lock (UART, the early log, the firmware's own COM1 settings), `KernelUart` (port or MMIO registers), `ScreenCell` (the screen, set once), `CURSOR`, `UNOWNED` (the UART address for urgent reports with no lock), `attach_framebuffer`, `withdraw_framebuffer`, `adopt_firmware_uart`, `move_to`/`move_uart`. Every line: screen first, then the UART, then at most the log. A UART that stops taking bytes costs one bounded wait and is dropped (`uart_alive`), with a report on the screen; one that will not take the replayed log at the move leaves COM1 in charge; a screen that cannot be mapped is withdrawn before the kernel's tables load. The console measures its own drawing (`DRAWN_LINES`, `DRAW_CYCLES`, `DRAW_WORST`) and reports the average and worst per line in the console proof (rule 21).
  - `main.rs`: `uart.line_settings()` before the first programming, `attach_framebuffer` right after the boot info is validated, `adopt_firmware_uart` right after `init_paging`, the `Placement` for the kernel's own tables.
  - `xtask`: `screen` (`parse_ppm`; `model_rows`, which computes what the screen must show from the console's written rules (wrap, lazy wrap, the rule for every byte class) **independently of `fbconsole`'s code**; `decode`, which reads a dump back cell by cell against the font in the specification's literal colors; `check_frame`, `screen_text`), `dump_screen`, `Capture`, `Completed`, `boot-console` with six scenarios (below), and `boot-matrix` running them once. The main `kernel boot` scenario checks a screen dump in every cell of the matrix.
- **Specifications:** Microsoft "Serial Port Console Redirection Table" (spec revision 1.10, table revision 4, read in full 2026-11-08), Microsoft "Debug Port Table 2" (2023-04-10; subtypes, GAS notes for 16550), UEFI 2.11 §12.9 for GOP (the page refused the fetch; the ABI was confirmed against EDK II's `GraphicsOutput.h` and by the boot); ADR-0002 B4, ADR-0004 H2. Research: `docs/research/2026-11-08-early-console.md`.
- **Unsafe code:**
  - `console::KernelUart` (8 sites): port and MMIO register access; the invariant is `port`/`mmio`'s contract, established by `spcr::parse` (allowed ports, alignment) and `map_mmio` (uncached mapping), with `uart_for` checking RAM overlap.
  - `FramebufferMemory::write32`: a bounds- and alignment-checked volatile write; `attach_framebuffer` established the mapping.
  - `ScreenCell`: `Sync` over an `UnsafeCell` that is written once before readers exist (documented at the impl).
  - `boot/uefi/src/main.rs` (`find_framebuffer`, `console_device`, `framebuffer_of`): firmware calls and reads of firmware-owned protocol data, each checked for null and alignment; `describe` validates the values. `KernelUart`'s 8 register-access blocks in `console.rs`.
- **Tests:**
  - `framekernel` (host): `spcr` 8 tests including `hostile_tables_keep_every_promise` (200 000 mutated tables, sealed, on `crate::testing`, every accepted table keeps its invariants, and a divisor is only produced from a stated rate and a known clock); `fbconsole` 11 tests including `any_accepted_description_and_any_bytes_stay_inside_the_display` (15 000 hostile descriptions, arbitrary bytes, every pixel inside the visible rows and aligned); `font` 5 tests; `serial` six new tests.
  - `origin-boot-info` 2 new tests (`check` over 15 refusals and valid modes; `overlaps_ram`); `origin-paging` 3 new tests (mapping uncached with the physical offset kept, a mapping that does not fit is not a failed boot, largest framebuffer fits); `origin-boot-uefi` 4 new tests (`describe`); `xtask` 5 new tests (`parse_ppm`, the frame comparison and its negative cases, decoding oldest-first, noise cells).
- **Boot proofs (QEMU 11.1.3, OVMF edk2-stable202408):**
  - `cargo xtask boot-test`, every run: the kernel scenario adds the loader line and the kernel's `console: framebuffer ...` line, boots with COM1 and the monitor on stdio (`-serial mon:stdio`), and after `M1 entry complete` takes a screen dump (Ctrl-A C, `screendump`) and checks it **cell for cell, in the specification's literal colors**, against the rows the serial log implies, computed by `xtask` from the console's rules rather than with its code (`check_screen`, `screen::check_frame`). The console never moves what it has drawn, so a row only matches if every earlier line took the rows it should. The picture was also looked at by eye: legible text and the cursor bar right after the last line.
  - `cargo xtask boot-console` (each a whole signed boot): **the UART named by the SPCR** (a table added with `-acpitable`, a 16550 at port `0x2F8`, COM1's output in a file): all the kernel's output arrives on that UART, starting with the replay of the first lines, and COM1's log ends at the move line; **COM1 named by the SPCR itself** (the same-port path: left "as the firmware set it", nothing replayed); **a UART that answers but takes no bytes** (`isa-debugcon` on its status port, reading back 0): the replay fails, COM1 is given back, and the boot carries on; **an SPCR for an interface this kernel cannot drive**, **one naming a port with no UART** and **one naming registers in RAM**, each refused and named, leaving COM1 in use; **no display** (`-vga none`) and **no UART at all** (`-serial none`, the boot is judged only from screen dumps): both boot to the halt line.
  - **Cost** (rule 21): the console proof reports what drawing a line cost on that boot. At 1280x800 under QEMU's TCG on a quiet host, about 240 µs per line on average (233–243 µs over the first ten boots of a `boot-matrix` run) and under 1 ms at worst; a line drawn during a host stall takes as long as the stall (over 9 ms was seen under load). A line is drawn with interrupts off, like a serial line, and takes no longer on a big screen than one row's pixels; at real panels' widths the uncached writes are the bound, and write-combining (ADR-0010 trade-offs) would shrink them.
- **Negative controls** (each applied to the source or the table, run, shown to fail its proof, and restored from the git index): each applied, its proof run, the failure recorded, and the file restored from the git index.
  - *The framebuffer proof (`boot-test`'s screen check).* FB1, the kernel draws nothing: the bar is still on row 0, the log puts it on row 16. FB2, red and blue swapped: no row is the bar's color. FB3, the stride four bytes off: no bar. FB4, one line lost mid-boot: the bar is one row early. FB5, the kernel's own tables do not map the framebuffer: the bar stops where the framebuffer was withdrawn. FB6, glyphs drawn one pixel to the right: "the screen differs from the serial log at text row 0".
  - **FB2 and FB6 passed against the first version of the screen check**, which compared the dump with a frame rendered by the kernel's own drawing code, so a bug in that code could vouch for itself. That is why `screen::model_rows` and the literal colors exist; both controls were run against the new check and fail. The first version's other controls (FB1, FB3, FB4, FB5) had also failed.
  - *The SPCR proof (`boot-console`, a table naming a UART at `0x2F8`).* SP1, the kernel ignores the SPCR: nothing reaches the named UART. SP2, the parser reads the address one byte off: "nothing answers" there and the console stays on COM1, so the named UART receives nothing. SP3, the earlier output not replayed: the first lines are missing from the named UART. SP4, the console stays on COM1 after the move: the named UART receives nothing. SP5, the table says `0x3E8` while the UART is at `0x2F8`. SP6, a table for another interface accepted (the refusal the scenario expects never comes). SP7, COM1 not given back when the new UART takes no bytes. SP8, COM1 named by the SPCR treated as a new UART (its log replayed).
  - Host: `screen::every_wrong_picture_fails` (a lost line, a black frame, swapped channels, one row shifted a pixel, one wrong pixel, a second bar) and the SPCR tables each proof uses parse as the UART they name.
- **Gates:** `cargo xtask check` passes: 819 tests, 0 failed, 6 ignored. `cargo xtask boot-matrix` passes in full on a quiet host: Intel VT-d and AMD-Vi at 1, 2 and 4 processors, each `boot-test` with all 11 scenarios (the kernel scenario's screen check in each), `boot-x2apic` under leaves 1Fh and 0Bh, and `boot-console` (8 of 8 scenarios). Every kernel boot took 16–26 s. An earlier full run stopped in `boot-console`'s third scenario when another session's host-load test started during it (`an unsignalled 50 ms timed wait timed out after 82 ms`: a host-load failure of a proof this work does not touch, in a boot whose first lines were this work's own); the eight `boot-test` runs before it had passed. The rerun on a quiet host passed.
- **Security review:** by the author, and by one fresh reviewing agent (a read-only pass over the staged diff, given the ADR and the SPCR specifications, not my conclusions). It found no memory-safety bug. Its findings, all fixed: a UART that answers but takes no bytes silently lost the serial console (COM1 is now given back and a boot scenario proves it); a saved divisor of 0 could be restored onto COM1 (never restored now, and the format is compared as well as the divisor); the loader's entry stub could run out of table pages because the framebuffer's tables were allocated first (the framebuffer is mapped last on both sides); the reason a screen is withdrawn did not reach it (printed first now); a stray DLAB at the first programming (cleared first); a too-permissive I/O port list (now the four COM blocks and above `0xFFF`); and the rate logic, which replaced a working divisor from an assumed clock (a programmed latch is now left alone). Its observation that `wait_for_screen` sees failures only while they are on screen is documented at the function.  This is agent review, not an independent security review.
- **Limitations:** as ADR-0010, "What this does not prove": QEMU only. A wedged UART is shown with a debug-console port that answers the status register with 0, not a real device. **The firmware framebuffer may go dark on a real integrated GPU when `iommu::init` enables translation (scan-out by DMA through the unit; T14) or when the T4 work clears its bus mastering.** The MMIO UART path has no boot proof (QEMU has none on x86; tested with mocks). Output before `adopt_firmware_uart` reaches COM1 and the screen only; the UART named by the SPCR gets it replayed once the tables can be read, up to 8 KiB, with a count of what did not fit.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### The console: a line drawn a section at a time (`console`, `fbconsole`; `cpu`, `main`; xtask; CLAUDE.md §13, §53, §69, §72, §73, rule 21, P1, P2; ADR-0010 Amendment 1, accepted by the owner; 2026-11-09)

The kernel wrote every line's pixels with interrupts off, under the console lock. Under KVM on a real AMD EPYC 7763 (free GitHub runner, Actions run 42547942738; `docs/research/2026-11-09-testing-without-buying-hardware.md`, branch `claude/interesting-carson-ae7c83`, `61de1fa`) one line took 4.3 to 4.6 ms on average and up to 10 ms at worst, with interrupts off; the timer tick is 10 ms. TCG, QEMU's software CPU, showed 0.23 ms on the Mac and 0.57 ms on the runner, so the cost had been invisible. A line is about 40,960 pixels of uncached memory.

- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, session `epic-joliot-bff82c`), 2026-11-09. Original code, no third-party crates (§3, §5).
- **The bound:** a section writes at most `SECTION_PIXELS` = 256 pixels, 1 KiB of uncached memory, with interrupts off. The reasoning is in `console.rs`'s module documentation: at the cost measured on that runner (105 to 245 ns a pixel) that is 27 to 63 us, against a whole line's 4.3 ms. The bound is in memory written, because time on a real machine depends on the machine.
- **What:**
  - `framekernel::fbconsole` (library, pure and host-tested): drawing is now rectangles (`Stroke`, `Painting`) that can be left after any pixel and resumed; `Screen::write` is the same drawing with no budget, so the old tests check it. New: `Backlog<N>`, the bounded ring of text the screen has not shown yet and the character in progress, with `push` (a whole line or nothing, returning the position at which it is on the screen), `paint` (at most so many pixels, oldest first), `painted`, `clear`, and `note_lost` (a writer that cannot wait may lose a line on the screen, and the next line says so).
  - `framekernel/src/console.rs`: `Sinks::send` hands a line over in one critical section under the console lock: UART, early log, backlog, together, so both sinks get lines in one order. `Sinks::paint_section` draws one section. `send_and_draw` (ordinary writers), `send_urgent` (exception and panic reports). `Flow` says what a writer may do between sections: interrupts on (they are back on between sections), the boot flow (`Console::boot_flow`, a window once `allow_interrupt_windows` has run), or an interrupts-off context that cannot wait (`NoWaiting`: hands its line over and leaves). `with_sinks` takes the lock with interrupts off but waits for it with interrupts as the caller had them.
  - `framekernel/src/main.rs`: `Console::boot_flow` for `com1`, `allow_interrupt_windows` after the timer proof, `interrupt_self` for the proof, and `console::prove_sections` last before the halt.
  - `framekernel/src/cpu.rs`: `interrupts_enabled`; one call in the `IOAPIC_VECTOR` arm of `dispatch` (`console::on_proof_interrupt`).
  - `xtask`: the kernel scenario's markers; `settled_screen`, which waits for the screen to catch up with the log before the screen is checked (the UART now goes first); `check_screen` split so both can use the comparison.
- **The order of the sinks (ADR-0010 Amendment 1, accepted by the owner on 2026-11-09):** the UART goes first now; E3 said the screen. Under this design a line must be on the wire before its pixels: otherwise the UART would wait behind the pixels and everything between sections (interrupts, preemption, other writers' sections), against the requirement that the serial path must not get slower or less reliable. E3's reason (a UART must not hold up the screen) becomes: a UART delays the screen by one line's send at most, and a UART that stops is given up on after one bounded wait.
- **No new concurrency primitive:** everything shared is under the existing console lock, held for at most a section or one line's UART send, and nothing is held between sections, so no lock-free protocol was added and there is nothing for Loom to model. A writer preempted between sections holds nothing, so it cannot deadlock anyone; a line from any processor can be finished by any other.
- **Interrupt context and panics:** an interrupt handler (`Flow::NoWaiting`) takes the lock, hands its line over (UART at once, in order) and returns: it writes no pixels. The screen shows that line when the next writer that can wait paints that far. (Nothing prints from an interrupt handler outside the proof today; if something does in future and no later line follows, its line stays on the UART only until one does.) An exception or panic report (`Console::urgent`) waits a bounded time for the lock, puts its report on the UART, then draws the whole backlog, everything before the report and then the report, with interrupts off. If it cannot get the lock it sends without it, as before.
- **Unsafe code:** one new `unsafe` block pair: `main.rs::interrupt_self`, an x2APIC self IPI for the proof, on a vector whose handler only counts and acknowledges. `console.rs` and `fbconsole.rs` gain none.
- **Tests (host, `framekernel`):** in `fbconsole` (7 new tests, 18 in the module): painting in any steps, down to one pixel and steps of zero, draws exactly what writing draws, and a section writes no more than its budget (600 random cases); a section writes no more pixels than it is given, and a whole line takes 160 sections of 256; a line is fully drawn at the position its `push` returned and not before; text is taken whole or not at all; a lost line is owned up to before the next line that fits; any interleaving of pushes and painting steps keeps the order (400 random cases); clearing forgets the character in progress.
- **Boot proofs (QEMU, every `boot-test` kernel boot):** `console::prove` (mid-boot): a thread's line takes more than one section, and interrupts are on between its sections. `console::prove_sections` (last before the halt, so its lines are on the screen for the screen check): an interrupt made pending while the boot flow has interrupts off is taken after the line's first section, before the line is finished; its handler prints a line, which queues behind the interrupted line and is not drawn by the handler; a breakpoint in the middle of the next line prints its report through the urgent path; every section is at most 256 pixels, counted at the sink. The screen check compares the final screen with the serial log row by row, so the order of the handler's line, the broken-into line and the breakpoint report is checked.
- **Negative controls (each applied to a scratch edit of `console.rs`, booted, restored byte-identical):**
  - NC1, no window in the boot flow: "an interrupt waiting at its start was taken after section 0 ... console failed".
  - NC2, a section ignores its budget: one section of 81,920 pixels, "console failed".
  - NC3, interrupts off across a thread's whole line: "a thread's line took 159 sections with interrupts on between them: false ... console failed".
  - NC4, a handler draws its line itself: "its handler's line waited its turn: false ... console failed".
  - NC5, an urgent report drawn directly, bypassing the backlog: "the screen differs from the serial log at text row 37" (the report lands inside the line it interrupted).
  - NC6, the last line sent but never drawn: the screen is checked after `SCREEN_SETTLE` and fails: "the cursor bar is on row 45, and the serial log puts it on row 46".
- **Measurements (TCG on the Mac, M1 Max, QEMU 11.1.3; alternating runs, 5 of each; the console's own numbers in the kernel's boot log):** before: a line took one line's pixels took 231 us on average (228 to 234 across the boots) and 737 us at worst (696 to 787 across the boots), with interrupts off for all of them of pixel time with interrupts off for all of it. After: a line's pixels are written in about 160 sections: 368 us of drawing per line on average (349 to 430), which is the CPU-side cost of the drawing loop under TCG, about 1.6 times the old loop's, and the part an uncached write dwarfs on real hardware; and one section, which is all the pixels keep interrupts off for, took 2.3 us on average (2.2 to 2.7 across these 5 boots and the 16 boots of the matrix), against 231 us for a whole line before. The worst section per boot ranged from 43 us to 7.9 ms across the boots. A section cannot be longer than 256 pixels, counted at the sink, with interrupts off and nothing else running in it, so a stretch that long is the host descheduling the virtual processor (other sessions kept the host at a load of 4 to 10), not work the kernel chose to do. The whole boot did not get slower: the kernel boot took 26.2 s on average after and 28.4 s before. Under TCG a section's worst case is dominated by the host scheduling something else, and a line's pixel time is CPU-side loop cost rather than the uncached writes that matter on real hardware, so TCG cannot show the real improvement; the bound in pixels holds regardless.
- **Measurements under KVM (on the owner's word, 2026-11-09: `trial/real-x86` at `de9fbdf`, Actions run 42561010289, the console's own numbers; every figure names its processor):**
  - **AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core** (attempt 2; 8 of 8 boots passed: the TCG control and 7 KVM boots at 1 to 4 processors): a line's pixels took 3.73 to 3.93 ms of drawing on average per boot, about 91 ns a pixel, so the framebuffer costs there what it cost on the EPYC 7763, while one section, the most that ever holds interrupts off for pixels, took 23.4 to 24.6 us on average (256 pixels at 91 ns is 23.3 us). The worst section per boot was 189 to 226 us in the four boots with one to three processors and 2.9 to 3.05 ms in the three boots with four. At four the guest's processors compete with QEMU's own threads for the runner's four CPUs, so the likely cause is a virtual processor being descheduled in the middle of a section; that cannot be confirmed from inside the guest. The TCG control on the same runner: 420 us of drawing per line, 2.6 us per section.
  - **Before, for comparison, on a different model, AMD EPYC 7763** (Actions run 42547942738, before this change): 4.3 to 4.6 ms a line on average and up to 10 ms at worst, with interrupts off for all of it. Different processor models, so this is not a strict before and after; what changed is what interrupts are held off for, a whole line then and one section now.
  - **Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C** (attempt 1 of the same run): pixel writes cost about 2 ns (80 us for a whole line, 504 ns a section, in the one KVM boot that finished), so the guest's framebuffer is effectively cached on that machine and it cannot show this problem. Six of its seven KVM boots stopped earlier, at the SMEP proof in `prove_user_isolation` (#PF error 0x10), which this change does not touch: the known fault after `vm::map_user`, diagnosed and fixed by `b1fd62c` on `claude/interesting-carson-ae7c83` (PR #4), not yet on `main`.
- **Gates:** `cargo xtask check` passes on the final code: 975 tests passed, 0 failed, 6 ignored across the workspace, and Loom (26 models, all 35 negative controls caught). `cargo xtask boot-test`: 11 of 11 scenarios. `cargo xtask boot-matrix` passes in full: Intel VT-d and AMD-Vi at 1, 2 and 4 processors, `boot-x2apic` twice, `boot-bridge` on both IOMMUs, and `boot-console` 8 of 8 scenarios (12 min 49 s, host load 5 to 10 while it ran); the 16 kernel boots of the matrix all report sections of at most 256 pixels and the interrupt taken after section 1.
- **Limitations:** QEMU only. The real-hardware cost of a section is unknown until it is measured there (§74, rules 30, 40). The UART's time per line is still spent with interrupts off (9 ms for 100 bytes at 115 200 baud on real hardware; closed by the next entry, "The console: the UART a section at a time"); ADR-0010 E3's order is changed by an amendment the owner accepted on 2026-11-09. A line from an interrupt handler waits for a later line to be drawn.
- **Security review:** by the author only; no independent review yet. The attack surface is unchanged in kind: text from `debug_write` (developer builds only) passes through `Backlog` as bytes, and `begin` clamps the cursor, so a hostile line cannot put a pixel outside the screen; each pixel still goes through the sink's bounds check.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### The console: the UART a section at a time (`console`, `serial`, `linequeue`, `fbconsole`; xtask; CLAUDE.md §13, §53, §69, §72, rule 21, P0, P1, P2; ADR-0010 Amendment 2, accepted by the owner; 2026-11-09)

The console sent a line to the 16550 byte by byte, polling the transmit-holding register, with the console lock held and interrupts off. At 115 200 baud a byte takes 86.8 µs on the wire (10 bits), so 100 bytes take 8.7 ms, as long as the kernel's 10 ms timer tick. QEMU's UART takes a byte instantly, so no QEMU boot showed it.

- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, session `festive-chatelet-ac63d2`), 2026-11-09. Original code, no third-party crates (§3, §5).
- **Specifications:** PC16550D Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter with FIFOs (National Semiconductor, now Texas Instruments SNLS378): the line status register (bit 5, the transmit holding register or, in FIFO mode, the FIFO is empty), the FIFO control register, and the interrupt identification register's FIFO bits (7:6). No firmware or data dependency.
- **The bound:** one UART section, the longest the console's UART send keeps interrupts off, is **1 read of the line-status register and at most 16 writes to the data register: 17 register accesses, whatever the line's speed.** It never waits for the wire. The reasoning is in `serial.rs` (`TX_FIFO_BYTES`) and `console.rs`'s module documentation: in FIFO mode `LSR.THRE` means the transmit FIFO is empty (PC16550D, line status bit 5), so 16 bytes written one after another cannot overrun it; the first may move to the shift register at once and that only makes room. A UART that does not say its FIFOs work (the interrupt identification register's bits 7:6, read after the FIFO enable, not both set: a 16450, or the first 16550 whose FIFO does not work) gets 1 byte a section (`Uart16550::detect_fifo`). The bound is in register accesses, because what a register access costs depends on the machine. 16 is the FIFO, not a tuning choice: a smaller section would not shorten anything worth the lock and interrupt toggles it adds.
- **What:**
  - `framekernel::linequeue::LineQueue<N>` (new, host-tested): the bounded ring with positions, taken out of `fbconsole::Backlog`, which now uses it, so both sinks have one implementation of it.
  - `framekernel::serial`: `TxQueue<N>` and `Pumped`. `TxQueue::pump` is one section: it looks at the status once and, if the transmitter is empty, writes at most one load (`tx_load`), turning LF into CR LF across section boundaries; it never waits. `Uart16550::detect_fifo` and `tx_load`; `configure` reads the interrupt identification register after enabling the FIFOs, and `new` assumes no FIFO until it has.
  - `framekernel/src/console.rs`: `Sinks::send` now only queues (the UART's queue, 4 KiB, and the screen's backlog, in one critical section), and a line goes to both or, for a writer that can wait and finds no room, to neither. `Sinks::pump_uart` is one section under the lock. `send_and_draw` sends and then draws, a section at a time, each with the lock free in between. `send_urgent` keeps interrupts off from start to finish and takes the lock a section at a time. `Sinks::give_up_on_uart` is the one place a UART is dropped.
  - `xtask`: the kernel scenario's markers, `long_lines_whole` (each of the proofs' long lines appears once and whole) and `unwaited_lines_whole`; a new `boot-console` scenario, a UART that stops taking bytes.
- **On the framework crate (merged from `land/oidl`, ADR-0011 N14 step 1):** the console is safe code there (`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, `cargo xtask check` fails on `unsafe` outside `framekernel/frame/`). The screen is the framework's `SetOnce` and `SCREEN_WITHDRAWN` rather than this work's `ScreenCell`, the UART's ports a claimed `PortRange`, and the fallback to COM1 `FELL_BACK_TO_COM1`. The one thing this work needed that safe code cannot do, the self-interrupt the two proofs make pending, is `origin_frame::timer::interrupt_self`: a safe function with no arguments in the framework crate, whose vector is fixed (`IOAPIC_VECTOR`, which has a gate and a safe handler), so it can do no more than the device behind that vector can do at any moment. The framework dispatches device interrupts through registered handlers, so the proof's hook moved to `irq.rs`'s `on_interrupt`, registered for that vector by `irq::prove`, and the interrupt counts it reads are `irq.rs`'s. The two proofs therefore need `irq::prove` to have registered the vector, which every boot that reaches them has done.
- **What it had to keep, and how:**
  - *Lines never interleave on the UART and keep one order:* the only way to the UART is the queue, filled a whole line at a time under the lock. Any processor takes the next section from the front of the queue, so whoever holds it continues the line in front.
  - *Both sinks in the same order:* both queues are filled in one critical section.
  - *On the UART before `flush` returns for a writer that can wait:* it loops on sections until the position its line ends at has been written to the UART.
  - *An urgent report gets out with a bounded wait and does not depend on another processor:* it goes on until everything queued before it and the report itself are sent and drawn, with interrupts off throughout and the lock taken for one section at a time. Each take is bounded (`URGENT_ATTEMPTS`), and if it cannot be had the report goes out without it, as before.
  - *A UART that stops is given up on after one bounded wait, reported on the screen:* `TX_POLL_LIMIT` polls in a row across any number of sections, multiplied by the bytes of the last load (a full FIFO takes 16 times as long to get through as the one byte the polled driver allowed for; the first load has none before it and gets the wait for one byte). The writer that finds it out goes on only when the notice has been drawn.
  - *The early log and `adopt_firmware_uart`:* the log still records every line at hand-over, and the replay is still one unsectioned send (`emit`), under the lock with interrupts off. That is the one place the bound does not apply, and deliberately: it runs once, before the timer starts and before any other processor does, when no interrupt can be delayed and nobody can be waiting.
- **What changed for a writer that cannot wait** (an interrupt handler, the only one being the proof's): it hands its line over, sends one section and leaves. The rest of the line goes out with the next writer that can wait, or the next report. Before, its line was on the UART at once. The queue has room for 4 KiB; if it is full such a writer loses the line on the UART alone, and the next line that fits says so.
- **Tests (host, `framekernel`):** `linequeue` 4 tests; `serial` 15 new tests, among them: a section reads the status once and writes at most a load; a section that finds the transmitter busy writes nothing; an LF cut by the end of a section keeps its CR and its place; a line is on the UART at its position and not before; a line queued while another is on its way goes out behind it, whole; a wedged UART is given up on after exactly `TX_POLL_LIMIT` polls over many sections, and costs nothing after that; a UART that stops after a full load gets the wait that load needs; only a UART that says its FIFOs work gets more than a byte. A model of a 16550 (`Wire`: a 16-byte FIFO, a shift register that takes the next byte when it is free, an overrun counter, and time counted in register accesses) runs 300 random sets of lines at line speeds from the bus's own to 1042 accesses a byte: every section is at most 17 accesses, at most 16 bytes between status reads, no byte is lost and the wire carries the text exactly, CR LF included. `xtask`: `long_lines_pass_only_if_every_one_is_whole`, `unwaited_lines_pass_only_if_all_are_there_once_and_whole_in_order`.
- **Boot proofs (QEMU, every `boot-test` kernel boot):** `console::prove` (mid-boot): a thread's line takes more than one section on each sink with interrupts on between all of them; `prove_room`: lines from a writer that cannot wait fill the UART's queue, the next writer that can wait waits for room, and when it goes on the queue is empty and every line has reached the UART once and whole (`unwaited_lines_whole`). `console::prove_uart_sections` (near the end, so its lines are on the screen for the screen check): a line's bytes are on the UART when its writer goes on, counted at the data register; an interrupt made pending while the boot flow has interrupts off is taken after the first section of the UART's send, before the line is out; its handler's line comes after that line on the wire; a breakpoint in the middle of the next line prints its report through the urgent path, in order, and leaves nothing queued; the most bytes in one section, counted at the data register around each section, is the limit. `boot-console`, new: **a UART that stops taking bytes** (no UART on COM1 and a device at its status port reading back 0, for a boot judged only from the screen): given up on after exactly 100 000 polls, and on the screen at once.
- **Negative controls (each applied to a scratch edit, run, shown to fail, and restored from the git index):**
  - NU1, a section ignores the FIFO load (the whole line in one section): boot: "a thread's line took 0 sections on the UART ...: console failed"; host: `a_section_reads_the_status_once_and_writes_at_most_a_fifo_load` and five others fail.
  - NU1b, a section writes one byte too many: "a line took 7 sections on the UART, none over 17 bytes (the limit is 16) ...: console failed".
  - NU2, no window between the UART's sections: "an interrupt waiting at its start was taken after section 0 ...: console failed".
  - NU3, a handler's line sent past the queue, straight to the UART: "its handler's line waited its turn: false ...: console failed".
  - NU3b, a handler sends its whole line, waiting with interrupts off: "100 lines from a writer that cannot wait filled the UART's queue; the next writer waited for room: false ...: console failed".
  - NU4, a report sent past the queue: "a report left nothing queued behind it: false ...: console failed".
  - NU4b, a report queued and not sent: the same.
  - NU5, a writer goes on before its line is sent: "a thread's line took 0 sections on the UART ...: console failed".
  - NU5b, only the boot flow does: "40 lines from a writer that cannot wait filled the UART's queue; the next writer waited for room: true, and when it went on the queue was empty: false: console failed".
  - NU6, interrupts off across a thread's whole send: "a thread's line took 6 sections on the UART and 159 on the screen with interrupts on between them: console failed" (they were off).
  - NU7, a stopped UART is never given up on: host: two tests fail; boot: "the screen never showed the markers".
  - NU8, a stopped UART gets a wait on every line: "the screen shows \": console failed\"" (the console still thinks it has a UART and nothing is written to it).
  - NU8b, a stopped UART is given twice the wait: the screen shows "the UART was given up on after 200000 polls"; the scenario wants 100000.
  - NU9, 16 bytes given to any UART, FIFO or not: two host tests fail. NU10, no CR before an LF cut by the end of a section: five. NU11, the wait not scaled by the last load: one. NU13, bytes written while the transmitter is busy: six. (A boot cannot show NU9 or NU13: QEMU's UART has a FIFO and is never busy here.)
  - NU12, a writer that can wait does not wait for room in the UART's queue: the queue stays full, nothing drains it, every later line is lost on the UART, and the boot times out.
  - NU14, the writer that finds the UART stopped does not wait to show it: the screen shows "and the screen said so at once: false"; the scenario wants true.
  - NS1, no window between the screen's sections (the screen's proof was changed here, because the UART's windows would otherwise have let its interrupt in): "an interrupt made pending after its first section was taken after section 0 ...: console failed".
  - Host: `the_model_catches_a_load_larger_than_the_fifo` and `the_model_catches_a_fifo_load_written_to_a_uart_without_one` show the model sees an overrun, and `xtask`'s `long_lines_pass_only_if_every_one_is_whole` and `unwaited_lines_pass_only_if_all_are_there_once_and_whole_in_order` show its checks refuse lost, repeated, short and mixed lines.
- **How the bound was verified.** (1) The code: `pump` has one status read and one write loop, bounded by `tx_load`, which is only ever 1 or 16. (2) Host: the mock and the 16550 model above, with controls NU9 and NU1. (3) Every boot: the proof counts writes to the data register around each section, in the kernel, and fails over 16 bytes; control NU1b shows it failing at 17. (4) Every boot: the interrupt-window proof, with its control NU2.
- **What was not measured.** How long a section keeps interrupts off on a real machine: that is 17 register accesses, and what one costs on LPC, eSPI or a PCIe UART has not been measured here. How long a real UART's FIFO takes to drain, and that it behaves as the datasheet says when given 16 bytes at once (the model follows the datasheet; QEMU's UART has a FIFO but is instant, and in these boots it never reported busy). The whole of the UART's waiting behaviour on a real line: the busy path of `pump` has run in a boot only on the wedged device. KVM: not taken (it needs a push to `trial/real-x86`, which needs the owner's word). The kernel prints what a section cost and how many polls found the UART busy on every boot (`origin-kernel: console: UART:`), so the first boot on real hardware will report the real figures.
- **Measurements (TCG on the Mac, M1 Max, QEMU 11.1.3; the console's own numbers in the kernel's boot log):** 17 kernel boots of the `boot-matrix` run on the final code: 1922 to 2516 UART sections each, taking 12 to 27 µs on average with interrupts off and 70 µs to 2.8 ms at worst per boot, none over 16 bytes, and 0 polls that found the transmitter busy, because QEMU's UART is never busy here. These are QEMU's costs: 17 register accesses at about a microsecond of emulation each, the host's chardev write for each data byte included. The worst figures are the host descheduling the virtual processor (load 3 to 8 when sampled), not work the kernel chose to do. They say nothing about a real UART. The screen's sections in the same boots took 2.2 to 2.4 µs on average.
- **Independent review:** one fresh reviewing agent read the staged diff with the requirements and not my conclusions. It found no defect in the order, the bound or the locking. Its findings, all fixed: the notice that the UART stopped could stay off the screen until something else was printed (now the writer that finds out draws through it, and the boot proof shows it, NU14); a report held the lock for its whole send, up to 355 ms, long enough for a second report on a healthy processor to give up on the lock and write over it (now a report takes the lock a section at a time); a refused move to another UART re-enabled COM1 even if COM1 had already been given up on, and a replay failing on COM1 itself was not reported on the screen; two comments that had become false. This is agent review, not an independent security review.
- **Concurrency:** no new primitive. Everything shared is under the existing console lock, held for one section at a time, and no lock is held between sections, so there is nothing new for Loom to model. The counters added are statistics, read only by the proofs.
- **Unsafe code:** none added. The one new thing touching hardware is `Uart16550::detect_fifo`, a read of the UART's interrupt identification register through `UartRegisters`.
- **Security review:** by the author and the agent review above; no independent security review yet. Text from `debug_write` (developer builds only) reaches the UART through the queue as bytes and is not interpreted. A user program cannot fill the queue with more than the lines it writes: `debug_write` runs with interrupts on and waits like any other writer.
- **Gates:** `cargo xtask check` on the final code: 996 tests passed, 0 failed, 6 ignored across the workspace, and Loom (26 models, all 35 negative controls caught). `cargo xtask boot-test`: 11 of 11 scenarios. `cargo xtask boot-matrix` passes in full: Intel VT-d and AMD-Vi at 1, 2 and 4 processors, `boot-x2apic` twice, `boot-bridge` on both IOMMUs and `boot-console` 9 of 9 (17 min 49 s). On the tree merged with the framework crate (`land/oidl`): `cargo xtask check`: 1088 tests passed, 0 failed, 6 ignored, the gate on `unsafe` clean and Loom as above; `cargo xtask boot-test` 11 of 11 under Intel VT-d and under AMD-Vi; `cargo xtask boot-console` 9 of 9; and controls NU1b, NU2, NU3 and NS1 rerun there, with two for the ported pieces, each failing as it should (NP1, the proof's hook gone from `irq.rs`'s handler: "its handler's line waited its turn: false ...: console failed"; NP2, the framework's self-interrupt doing nothing: "an interrupt waiting at its start was taken after section 0 ...: console failed"). `boot-matrix` was not run again on the merged tree.
- **Limitations:** QEMU only (§74, rules 30, 40). A line from a writer that cannot wait reaches the UART only when another writer sends it, or a report does; if neither comes, it stays queued, as it already could on the screen. If such a writer finds the queue full, its line is lost on the UART (it is still on the screen), and the next line that fits says so; a boot cannot show that path, because the screen check needs the two sinks to agree: the queue's part of it is tested on the host, and the few lines of `Sinks::send` around it are not exercised.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### TLB shootdown and global kernel pages (ADR-0004 H5; CLAUDE.md §28, 2026-11-07)

- **The gap closed:** before this, a guard page made while application processors ran (every `spawn` makes one) was invalidated only on the processor that made it. Another processor could keep the old translation, a 2 MiB one included, and run through the guard without a fault. The negative control below shows QEMU really keeps such stale entries.
- **What:**
  - `origin-paging`: `Attributes::kernel_global`, `Translation::global`, and `AddressSpace::leaf_census` (present leaves by half and by global bit). The layout builder marks the whole kernel half (direct map and image) global.
  - `cpu`: `enable_global_pages` (CR4.PGE, cleared then set, which also drops every translation cached under the loader's tables), `flush_tlb_all` (toggles CR4.PGE when it is set, since a CR3 load keeps global entries; else reloads CR3), `invlpg`, and the gate for vector 0xF0.
  - `tlb` (binary), the shootdown:
    - one request at a time, under an initiator lock; a processor waiting for the lock serves the request in progress, so two initiators never deadlock;
    - each request has a generation; every processor records the last one it served, and the initiator waits for every target's record (panicking after about a second, because carrying on would not be memory-safe);
    - targets are the processors whose schedulers run, each sent a fixed IPI by its x2APIC ID. A processor marks itself online and then flushes everything, so no request falls between the two.
  - `vm`: `unmap` and `make_guard` shoot down once the address-space lock is released; `make_guards` unmaps several pages with one full flush. `map_firmware` and `unguard` map global pages.
- **Specifications:** Intel SDM Vol. 3A §4.10.2.4 (global pages), §4.10.4 (invalidation: INVLPG, CR3 and CR4.PGE writes), §4.10.5 (propagation to multiple processors), the x2APIC ICR; Vol. 2A, INVLPG.
- **Proof** (every boot):
  - Every processor turned on global pages, and the kernel's tables hold 4269 to 4296 kernel-half leaves, all global, and none in the lower half.
  - Every application processor reads three heap pages, then stops touching them. The boot processor unmaps one with a single-page shootdown and two with one full flush. Every processor's next read of each page must fault: 3 of 3 at 2 CPUs, 9 of 9 at 4.
  - Measured in QEMU TCG (comparisons only): a single-page shootdown took 11 000 to 48 000 TSC cycles at 2 to 4 CPUs, a full flush 92 000 to 113 000.
- **Negative controls**, each restored and each failing the boot test:
  - No IPIs sent: "0 of their 3 reads faulted and 3 saw a stale translation".
  - The direct map left non-global: "upper_local: 4199 … TLB failed".
  - An earlier attempt at that control changed `map_firmware`. It passed, because this boot maps no new firmware page, and so proved nothing; it was redone on the layout builder.
- **Test evidence:** 16 `origin-paging` tests (the census, and global bits surviving a large-page split); `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** PCIDs for user address spaces (every CR3 switch still drops all non-global entries); shootdowns for user mappings of a process running on several processors (processes are single-threaded so far); INVPCID.

### Kernel wait queues and cross-CPU wake-ups (CLAUDE.md §25, §26, §30; 2026-11-07)

- **What:**
  - `runqueue` (library): a `Blocked` state; a per-slot generation, bumped by every `push`, so a wake-up names its thread exactly and a stale one never wakes the slot's next thread; and a pending-wake flag, so a wake-up that arrives before its thread has blocked makes the next `block` return at once.
  - `sched`: `block` (software interrupt 0x84), `current_thread`, `ThreadRef`, and `wake`. Waking a thread blocked on another processor sends that processor a reschedule IPI (vector 0xF1), whose handler acknowledges and switches.
  - `wait` (binary): `WaitQueue::wait_until(condition)` checks the condition under the queue's lock and registers the thread there before blocking; `wake_one` takes a waiter under the lock, releases it, then wakes it. Lock order: a wait queue's lock, then what its condition reads. These queues are kernel-internal. (The protocol moved unchanged to `origin_sync::wait` on 2026-11-08, where Loom can run it: see "Loom models" under `origin-sync`.)
- **Proof** (every boot):
  - A producer on CPU 1 sends 10 000 numbers through an 8-slot ring to a consumer on CPU 0, each blocking when the ring is full or empty. All arrive in order, in 19–32 ms.
  - Two threads on CPUs 0 and 1 pass a turn back and forth 1000 times: 44–73 µs per round trip, woken by IPI, against a bound of 2 ms.
  - On one CPU the producer and consumer alternate exactly (1250 blocks each), and a round trip takes 4 µs.
- **Negative controls**, each failing the boot test:
  - No reschedule IPI: the transfer slows from 19 to 180 ms, and the ping-pong does not finish within 5 s (a woken thread waits for its processor's next 10 ms tick).
  - No pending wake-ups: a wake-up is lost and the transfer stalls at 6202 of 10 000 items. So the race between registering and blocking really happens even in QEMU, and the pending-wake rule is what closes it.
- **Test evidence:** 2 new run-queue tests (blocking and waking; a stale generation and the boot context refused); `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Timed waits (added later the same day):**
  - A blocked slot may carry a deadline tick, and the tick that reaches it makes the thread ready. `sched::block_until` converts a monotonic-clock deadline into ticks (RDI of the block request), and `WaitQueue::wait_until_deadline` returns `TimedOut` once the deadline passes with the condition still false.
  - Proof: an unsignalled 50 ms wait timed out after 57–58 ms, and a 2 s wait signalled after about 20 ms returned in 8–19 ms, not timed out (1, 2 and 4 CPUs).
  - Control: deadlines ignored by the run queue → the 50 ms wait never returns → "wait queues failed".
  - One new run-queue test covers a deadline, a wake-up before it, a late wake-up kept, and the one-tick minimum.
- **Not done:** sub-tick deadlines (TSC-deadline one-shot timers), priority inheritance, the user-visible waiting of ADR-0005 P9, and Loom models of the protocol.

### PCI Express enumeration (M5 groundwork; CLAUDE.md §32; 2026-11-07)

- **What:**
  - `origin-paging`: a `Cache` memory type (write-back at PAT entry 0, or uncached at entry 3 through PCD and PWT); `Attributes::mmio`; `Translation::uncached`. `split_large` now keeps PCD, PWT and the PAT bit, which moves from bit 12 to bit 7. Before, it dropped PCD and PWT, which would silently have made split device mappings write-back.
  - `cpu::check_pat`: every processor's IA32_PAT must hold write-back at entry 0 and uncached at entry 3 (the reset values). The kernel then refuses to map device registers rather than reprogramming caches behind the firmware.
  - `vm::map_mmio`: a bump allocator in the MMIO window (ADR-0004 H2), with 2 MiB pages where the physical alignment allows.
  - `pci` (library), over an abstract `ConfigSpace`: MCFG allocations, checked (1 MiB-aligned base, no wrap, end bus not below start); ECAM offsets, refused outside the window or misaligned; header decoding; enumeration (functions 1–7 only on multi-function devices, nothing when function 0 is absent); BAR sizing for 32- and 64-bit memory and I/O BARs, including 16-bit I/O decoders. Sizing turns decoding off meanwhile, then restores every BAR and the command register, writing zeros to the status register's write-one-to-clear bits.
  - `pcie` (binary): MCFG, then segment 0's window (refused if it overlaps RAM in the boot map), mapped uncached; every function listed with its sized BARs; afterwards each BAR and the command register is read back and compared.
- **Bugs found by the new tests before they reached the kernel:**
  - An unimplemented BAR (mask 0) was reported as 4 GiB, because the mask was widened to 64 bits before the zero check. The same flaw was in the I/O path.
  - The PAT bit and PCD/PWT were lost on a split (above).
- **Specifications:** PCI Firmware Specification 3.3 §4.1.2 (MCFG); PCI Express Base 6.x §7.2.2 (ECAM) and §7.5.1 (configuration headers, BAR sizing); Intel SDM Vol. 3A §11.12 (PAT) and §4.9 (paging memory types).
- **Proof** (every boot, QEMU q35 under OVMF):
  - The ECAM is at 0xe0000000 (256 MiB, buses 0–255), mapped at 0xffffe00000000000 with 2 MiB uncached pages; IA32_PAT is 0x0007040600070406 on every processor.
  - The 5 functions found: host bridge 8086:29c0; VGA 1234:1111 (BAR0 prefetchable 16 MiB, BAR2 4 KiB); ISA bridge 8086:2918; AHCI 8086:2922 (BAR4 I/O 32 B, BAR5 4 KiB); SMBus 8086:2930 (BAR4 I/O 64 B).
  - Every BAR and command register read back unchanged.
- **Negative controls**, each failing the boot test:
  - BARs not restored after sizing → "restored: false".
  - Uncached mappings encoded without PCD and PWT → "uncached false".

  Whether sizing turns decoding off is invisible in QEMU; a host test checks it on a device model that records any probe made while decoding is on.
- **A mistake in the boot test, caught by the matrix:** the PCIe markers were first listed before the scheduler's last line, which the boot prints earlier, so every boot would have failed. The controls had failed on their own failure strings, so they did not show it. The markers now follow the boot order. Lesson: run the good path after adding markers, before running controls.
- **Test evidence:** 4 `pci` tests and 1 more `origin-paging` test; 83 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** bridges' bus numbers and hot-plug, MSI/MSI-X, PCIe capabilities, AER, an IOMMU (no DMA confinement yet; done 2026-11-08, see "Intel VT-d DMA and interrupt remapping"), and segments other than 0.

### NVMe driver (M5; CLAUDE.md §33; 2026-11-07)

- **What:**
  - `nvme` (library): CAP decoding, the version register, doorbell offsets, CC and AQA encodings, submission entries (Identify, Create I/O Completion and Submission Queue, Read, Write, Flush), PRP entries for transfers of up to two pages, completion decoding with the status field, the queue indexes (one slot always empty, the phase flipping at each wrap), and Identify Controller and Namespace parsing (bounds-checked; an inactive namespace, an out-of-range format index or a block size outside 512 B–64 KiB is refused).
  - `storage` (binary), a first-party polled driver (ADR-0001 D2):
    - binds to the first NVMe controller PCIe listed; turns on memory decoding and bus mastering; maps BAR 0 uncached;
    - resets the controller and awaits CSTS.RDY within CAP.TO (failing on the fatal-status bit); creates 32-entry admin queues and one 64-entry I/O queue pair;
    - masks the pin interrupt and polls each completion: the phase dword first, a deadline of 2 s, and a check that the command ID is its own;
    - DMA pages are zeroed heap pages that are never freed; a fence orders writes before every doorbell; no reference is ever made into memory the device may write.
  - xtask `disk`: a 16 MiB GPT test disk built independently of the kernel (protective MBR, primary and backup headers and entry arrays with bitwise CRC-32, two partitions, and a per-LBA pattern), attached as `-device nvme,serial=ORIGIN0001`. The image is fresh for every boot. The two Origin partition-type GUIDs are provisional, for this disk only (the M9 partition-layout decision fixes the real ones).
- **Specifications:** NVM Express Base 2.x (§3.1.4 registers, §4.2 and §4.6 queue entries and the phase tag, §5.2 admin commands); NVM Command Set 1.x (Read, Write, Flush, Identify Namespace); NVMe over PCIe Transport 1.x (doorbells, PRPs); UEFI 2.11 §5.3 (GPT, for the test disk).
- **Proof** (every boot):
