  - Controller: 00:02.0 1b36:0010, NVMe 1.4.0, with a 64-bit BAR 0 that OVMF placed at 0xc000000000 (above 4 GiB); model "QEMU NVMe Ctrl", serial "ORIGIN0001".
  - Namespace 1: 32 768 blocks of 512 B.
  - Through I/O queue 1: LBA 0 holds the MBR signature, LBA 1 "EFI PART", and 8 of 8 blocks at LBA 2048 match the pattern xtask wrote.
  - LBA 32704 was written, flushed and read back unchanged; a read at LBA 32768 (past the end) completed with status type 0, code 80h (LBA out of range).
- **Negative controls**, each failing the boot test:
  - Reading from LBA 2049 instead of 2048 → "0 of 8 blocks … match".
  - Bus mastering really off → "a command timed out". The driver reports the timeout; it does not hang.
  - A first version of that control only left out the bus-mastering bit. OVMF had already set it, so the control passed and proved nothing; it was redone so that it clears the bit.
- **Test evidence:** 7 `nvme` tests (91 library tests in all) and 3 xtask `disk` tests (CRC-32 check value, GUID byte order, a self-consistent GPT); `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** MSI-X interrupts, several I/O queues (one per CPU), PRP lists for transfers over 8 KiB, controller-reset recovery, power states, health logs (SMART), an IOMMU (done 2026-11-08, see "Intel VT-d DMA and interrupt remapping"), and a block layer above the driver.

### GUID Partition Tables (CLAUDE.md §39; UEFI 2.11 §5.3; 2026-11-07)

- **What:**
  - `gpt` (library): a table-driven CRC-32, independent of xtask's bitwise one, with incremental updates; GUIDs in their mixed-endian form, shown in canonical text.
  - `parse_header` follows UEFI 2.11 §5.3.2: signature, revision 1.0, header size 92 bytes to one block, the header CRC (the CRC field zeroed), and MyLBA. Also a layout check: the usable range lies inside the disk, after the primary structures and before the backup header; the entry array lies inside the disk, outside the usable range, and over neither header; entries are at least 128 bytes and a power of two; the array is at most 64 KiB.
  - `parse_entries`: the array CRC; every used entry inside the usable range and not ending before it starts; no two entries overlapping; names read as UTF-16LE.
  - `Header::agrees_with`: the two copies must describe the same disk, entries and CRC, and point at each other.
  - `storage`: reads both copies over NVMe and checks each and their agreement, then lists the partitions. With only one valid copy, the disk is reported from it and the proof fails.
- **Proof** (every boot):
  - Both copies are valid (the backup at LBA 32767) and agree.
  - The disk is 28a71590-fa80-422c-a428-8dff96984d99, usable blocks 34–32734.
  - Partition 1 is "Origin system A", type ab846206-03ad-4cf6-b80b-5da764646190, blocks 2048–10239. Partition 2 is "Origin data", type 1a0f3667-a459-431f-b1fb-c1d11e0d699a, blocks 10240–32734.
  - All of this is exactly what xtask wrote, so two independent GUID and CRC implementations agree.
- **Firmware finding:** the first control flipped one bit in the primary entry array. It passed, because OVMF had restored the primary copy from the backup before the kernel ran, as UEFI 2.11 §5.3.2 allows. The test image is fresh for every boot, so the repair does not persist. Keep this in mind for the installer and recovery (M9, M12): firmware may rewrite GPT structures on its own.
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): both entry arrays corrupted, which the firmware cannot repair → "primary copy invalid (ArrayCrc), backup copy … invalid (ArrayCrc) … GPT failed".
- **Test evidence:** 5 `gpt` tests: the CRC check value and incremental updates; GUID text; a valid disk with agreeing copies; header checks (signature, revision, size, the CRC and the bytes it does not cover, MyLBA, entry size and count, layout); entry checks (ranges, overlap, capacity, a flipped array bit, a short array). Also `cargo xtask check` and `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** restoring a corrupt copy (the kernel only reports it), MBR-only disks, a block layer and volumes above partitions, and a filesystem.

### Seeded mutation tests for the firmware and device parsers (CLAUDE.md §72; 2026-11-07)

- **What:** `testing` (test-only) holds xorshift64\* and a mutator: bit flips, random and boundary bytes, truncation, extension and chunk copies, one to four per case. Each parser gets a test that it never panics on mutated valid input and that anything it accepts keeps its invariants:
  - **GPT:** the header CRC really matches; the usable range lies inside the disk; partitions lie inside it and never overlap. Half the cases re-seal both CRCs after mutating, so the semantic checks behind them are reached: over 500 headers and 300 tables were accepted per default run.
  - **ACPI:** an accepted RSDP sums to zero over both checksum ranges; MADT processors are each listed once (half the cases re-sealed); an accepted FADT's century register is in the standard bank.
  - **PCI:** accepted MCFG windows are 1 MiB-aligned and do not wrap; random sizing masks give only powers of two.
  - **NVMe:** accepted Identify Namespace data has 512 B–64 KiB blocks and at least one block; Identify text fields are printable; any completion decodes.
  - **RTC:** every date from 1970 to 2099 round-trips through each register encoding (BCD or binary, 12- or 24-hour, with or without a century register). A single corrupted register decodes only to a real date, and both outcomes are reached over 10 000 times.
- **Scale:** the default run is about 20 000 parser cases plus 100 000 RTC cases, in 0.8 s with all 101 library tests. `ORIGIN_MUTATION_SCALE=n` multiplies the counts. A 50× release run (about a million parser cases and 5 million RTC cases) passed in 9 s.
- **Result:** no parser bug was found. The two first-run failures were in the tests themselves (shared Identify data, and random registers that are almost never a date) and were redesigned.
- **Not done:** coverage-guided fuzzing (cargo-fuzz needs nightly, against CLAUDE.md §12), and Kani proofs of the same properties (§73).

### MSI-X and interrupt-driven NVMe completions (CLAUDE.md §31 interrupt management, §33; 2026-11-07)

- **What:**
  - `pci` (library): the capability-list walk. It needs the status bit, starts from the pointer at 34h, stops at a loop, a pointer into the header or 48 entries, and reads bytes through dword accesses. Also the MSI-X capability (entries, table and PBA BARs and offsets, with BIRs above 5 refused) and the x86 MSI message: address `FEEh` with the destination APIC ID (IDs above 255 refused until interrupt remapping exists), and fixed edge-triggered data for vectors 16–254.
  - `nvme`: Create I/O CQ with interrupts (PC, IEN and the vector in CDW11).
  - `pcie::enable_msix`: sets the enable bit and clears the function mask; `pcie::msix`.
  - `cpu`: `DEVICE_VECTOR` 0x40. Its handler acknowledges, calls `storage::on_interrupt` (count, record the CPU, wake the wait queue), then reschedules.
  - `storage`:
    - `run` split into `submit` and `poll`, so a thread can block between them;
    - the controller kept in a lock once bound;
    - `setup_interrupts`: every MSI-X entry masked, then entry 1 routed to the target CPU and unmasked; MSI-X on; I/O queue pair 2 created with interrupts on vector 1;
    - the I/O thread submits under the driver lock and blocks with `wait_until_deadline`. Its condition is the completion queue itself, so a completion that lands before the thread blocks is never missed.
  - `sched::stop_boot_processor`: the boot processor's scheduler now stays active through the storage proofs.
- **Specifications:** PCI Express Base 6.x §7.5.1.1 (capability pointer), §7.7.2 (MSI-X); Intel SDM Vol. 3A §11.11 (message address and data); NVM Express Base 2.x §5.2.1 (Create I/O CQ: PC, IEN, IV).
- **Proof** (every boot): q35's NVMe has 65 MSI-X vectors, with the table in BAR 0 at offset 2000h. A thread on CPU 1 (CPU 0 with one processor) made 64 reads of 8 blocks through queue 2, each blocking until its interrupt: exactly 64 interrupts, all on the target CPU, and 512 of 512 blocks matched the pattern.
- **Measured in QEMU:** 89 µs per read on one CPU, about 375 µs when the thread waits on an idle AP. The difference is probably QEMU waking a halted vCPU, not the driver.
- **Negative control:** vector 1 left masked → no interrupt arrives, and the first wait times out → "0 reads … none arrived … NVMe failed".
- **Process note:** the MSI-X markers were first placed before the GPT markers, which the boot prints earlier. This time the good-path run made before the controls caught it, as the lesson from the PCIe step requires.
- **Test evidence:** 1 more `pci` test (capability walk, loops, header pointers, bad BIRs, messages) and 1 more `nvme` assertion; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** per-CPU queues with a vector each, interrupt remapping (x2APIC IDs above 255; done 2026-11-08, see "Intel VT-d DMA and interrupt remapping"), MSI (non-X) devices, and moving the admin queue to interrupts.

### Per-CPU NVMe queues and concurrent I/O (CLAUDE.md §33 multiqueue, §66 per-CPU queues; 2026-11-07)

- **What:**
  - `nvme`: Set Features, Number of Queues (feature 07h), and decoding of the allocation in its completion.
  - `storage`:
    - before any I/O queue exists, the driver asks for queue pairs 1 (polled), 2 (the MSI-X proof) and one per processor, and fails if the controller allocates fewer;
    - `submit_on` and `poll_on` work on one queue pair, so a processor's own queue needs no global lock;
    - per processor `k`, MSI-X entry `2 + k` is sent to that processor and I/O queue pair `3 + k` completes to it;
    - the completion interrupt wakes the wait queue of the processor it arrived on, and counts per processor.
  - Each processor's thread submits under its own queue's lock and blocks until its interrupt; the wait's condition is its completion queue.
- **Proof** (every boot):
  - Asked for 4 queue pairs (6 at 4 CPUs); QEMU allocated 64.
  - Every online CPU at once: 32 reads of 8 pattern blocks through its own queue pair, all matching, and one block of its own written, flushed, cleared and read back. Its 35 interrupts (32 reads, write, flush, read-back) all arrived on that CPU.
  - Totals: 1 CPU 32 reads in 4 ms; 2 CPUs 64 in 52 ms; 4 CPUs 128 in 54 ms. Twice the work in the same time at 4 CPUs, so the queues run concurrently (QEMU throughput figures are only comparisons).
- **Negative control:** every per-CPU vector sent to CPU 0 → CPU 1's thread is never woken: "0 reads … 0 interrupts on CPU 1 … NVMe failed".
- **Test evidence:** 1 more `nvme` assertion group (Set Features encoding and allocation decoding); `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** a block layer that routes requests to the submitting CPU's queue, PRP lists and larger transfers, command timeouts with abort and controller reset, and NUMA placement of queue memory.

### Weighted fair scheduling: stride scheduling and an idle context (CLAUDE.md §26; 2026-11-07)

- **What:** `runqueue` (library) picks the next context by stride scheduling, a deterministic proportional-share policy (Waldspurger and Weihl, MIT LCS/TM-528, 1995; the published algorithm, not anyone's code):
  - every context has a weight (1–1024, default 8) and a pass value; each quantum it uses (a tick or a yield) advances the pass by 2^20 / weight;
  - the ready context with the lowest pass runs next, ties going round-robin from the current one, so equal weights are exactly round-robin;
  - a context that becomes ready (new, woken, or due after a sleep) starts at no less than the lowest pass among the ready ones: sleeping earns no credit;
  - slot 0 can be the processor's idle context, which runs only when nothing else is ready; each AP's idle loop now is one. Leaving idle mode admits slot 0 at the floor.
  - `sched::spawn_weighted` sets a thread's weight.
- **Bugs found by the new host tests:**
  - A new thread's starting pass was computed with the new slot already counted as ready. The floor then included that slot's stale pass of 0, so the newcomer started 70 quanta behind and took 180 of 300 quanta.
  - The idle context, which is charged only for quanta nobody else wanted, monopolized the processor when it stopped being idle (20 of 20 ticks).

  Both are fixed. Three test expectations were wrong instead and were corrected: an off-by-one tick, the share arithmetic, and an old test that encoded pure round-robin order.
- **Proof** (every boot): three never-yielding workers with weights 1, 4 and 16 share one CPU for 2 s. Their shares are 45–50, 185–191 and 758–763 per mille, against ideal 47, 190 and 761 (1, 2 and 4 CPUs). Every earlier scheduler proof still passes.
- **Measured:** with an idle context on each AP, two workers there now get about 1.6 M iterations each in the 500 ms window, against 1.0 M before. The idle loop no longer takes a third of the processor.
- **Negative control:** weights ignored (one stride for all) → shares 341, 327 and 331 → "scheduler failed".
- **Test evidence:** 3 new run-queue tests (exact shares 100 : 400 : 1600 over 2100 quanta, and after a weight change; the idle context; no credit for sleeping and new threads starting level); 106 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** interactive and background classes on top of the weights, load balancing between processors, priority inheritance, and an EEVDF evaluation (§26).

### Block layer: a page cache over NVMe (CLAUDE.md §39, §40; 2026-11-08)

- **What:**
  - `blockcache` (library): the cache's index — a fixed-capacity map from a page number to a slot, with LRU order and write-back bookkeeping. `access` returns Hit, Fill (an empty slot), Replace (evict a clean slot) or Evict (write back a dirty slot first); `mark_dirty`, `mark_clean`, `dirty_slots` (oldest first) and hit/miss counts. No data, no `unsafe`.
  - `block` (binary): each cache slot is a 4 KiB DMA page (8 × 512 B device blocks). A read returns the cached page, fetching it on a miss after writing back the page it evicts; a write does a read-modify-write and dirties the page; a flush writes every dirty page back and flushes the controller. `storage` gained the polled device access it needs (`geometry`, `dma_page`, `transfer`, `flush_device`, `dma_read`/`dma_write`).
- **Bugs found by the library's model test before the kernel ran:** none in the cache. Three first-run failures were all in the test model (a second stray `access` per write inflated the counts, the mirror was sized to the unclamped capacity, and one stats expectation was miscounted) and were fixed.
- **Proof** (every boot): a 4-slot cache over the NVMe disk. Reading all 32 pattern blocks of 4 pages does 4 device reads (one per page) and every block matches; re-reading the 4 resident pages does no device I/O (32 hits). A 5th page evicts the LRU clean page with one read and no write-back. A block written through the cache, then flushed (one device write), is read back changed after its page is evicted.
- **Negative controls**, each failing the boot test:
  - cache hits still fetch from the device → cold reads jump from 4 to 32 and re-reads do 4 more;
  - written pages never marked dirty → "flushed (0 device writes) ... read back changed: false".
- **Test evidence:** 6 `blockcache` tests, including a 20 000-operation model check over a 20-block working set in 8 slots (every slot and dirty bit mirrored, no block cached twice, the hit rate sane); 112 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Limitation and not done:** the block layer holds its lock across polled I/O and is driven from the boot flow; a production one routes each request to the submitting processor's queue and blocks instead of polling. Also not done: readahead, a writeback thread on a timer, per-file or per-inode caching, and a filesystem above it.

### CPU feature discovery and FPU/SIMD state across context switches (CLAUDE.md §14, §24; 2026-11-08)

- **The correctness gap closed:** the scheduler saved only general-purpose registers in the interrupt frame, never the FPU/SSE/AVX state. Two threads both using SIMD would corrupt each other's registers across a preemption. The negative control shows this happens on almost two thirds of checks when the state is not restored.
- **What:**
  - `features` (library): decodes CPUID leaves 1, 7, 0Dh and 8000_0001h into a `Features` set, grades the x86-64 microarchitecture level (v1–v3, from the psABI supplement), gives the XCR0 to set and the XSAVE area size. Host-tested against a synthetic v3 CPU and degraded ones.
  - `cpu`: `gather_cpuid`; `enable_simd` (CR0.EM clear, MP set; CR4.OSFXSR, OSXMMEXCPT and, where XSAVE exists, OSXSAVE; XCR0 ← x87|SSE|AVX via XSETBV); `fpu_save`/`fpu_restore` (XSAVE/XRSTOR with the full mask, else FXSAVE/FXRSTOR) and `fpu_init_area` (a clean FCW and MXCSR). The kernel stays soft-float; this only adds a capability.
  - `sched`: each slot has a 64-byte-aligned FPU area, allocated at spawn and initialized clean; a switch saves the outgoing context's state and restores the incoming one's; the area is freed with the stack when the thread is reaped. Each processor's boot/idle context gets an area before the heap baseline is measured, so the leak check stays fair.
- **Proof** (every boot): the feature report with the x86-64 level, then three SIMD threads on one processor, each holding four values in spread-out XMM registers (0, 3, 7, 15), spin checking them for 300 ms across 100–307 context switches: 1.3–1.6 M checks, 0 corruptions.
- **Correction and enforcement (2026-11-08, ~09:45 IST):** the note that stood here — that QEMU's TCG `-cpu max` "presents x86-64 level 2" — was wrong. QEMU's own feature expansion (`query-cpu-model-expansion`) shows that `max` has every v3 feature. The kernel misread it: the level required **OSXSAVE**, which mirrors CR4.OSXSAVE — how *user space* sees that the OS enabled XSAVE — and the kernel decodes CPUID before it sets that bit, so it read 0 on every CPU and every v3 CPU was graded v2. The check now requires the capability, **XSAVE** (the bit the kernel uses to decide to enable OSXSAVE); `Features::requirements` lists each level's requirements once, and `arch_level` and the new `missing_baseline` both derive from it. The baseline is now **enforced**: below v3, or if XCR0 does not hold x87, SSE and AVX state after enabling, the boot refuses to continue and names what is missing (`: CPU baseline failed`, a failure marker). Boot proof: `CPU: x86-64 level 3 (baseline v3 true)`, which the boot test now requires. Negative control: `ORIGIN_QEMU_CPU=max,-avx2` (a new `xtask` override) boots a CPU without AVX2 — `x86-64 level 2 (baseline v3 false)` and `this CPU is below the x86-64-v3 baseline Origin OS requires (CLAUDE.md §14); missing: AVX2: CPU baseline failed` — and the boot stops there; the boot test fails in 3 s. Host tests: a kernel-entry CPUID (OSXSAVE clear) is v3; without XSAVE it is not and `XSAVE` is named; several gaps are named in order; and over 20 000 random CPUID words the level and the named gaps always agree. XCR0 is 0x7 (x87, SSE, AVX) and the XSAVE area 2696 bytes.
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): the incoming context's FPU state not restored on a switch → 812 443 of 1 318 469 checks saw another thread's XMM values → "scheduler failed".
- **Test evidence:** 4 `features` tests (a v3 CPU decoded and graded, levels 1 and 2, absent leaves, the XSAVE-size sanity check); 116 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** lazy FPU (deliberately — eager save/restore is used), the AVX upper halves tested separately from the full XSAVE image, AVX-512 (XCR0 leaves it off), and a per-CPU "FPU used" optimization to skip saving an untouched state.

### Panic diagnostics: a frame-pointer backtrace (CLAUDE.md §69; 2026-11-08)

- **What:**
  - `unwind` (library): `walk` follows the frame-pointer chain (each frame is `[RBP]` = the caller's RBP, `[RBP + 8]` = the return address), through a caller-supplied word accessor that returns `None` to stop, and halts at a null, unaligned or non-increasing RBP or one more than a bound above the last. Pure, host-tested.
  - `cpu::capture_backtrace`: reads the current RBP and walks it with an accessor bounded to a 256 KiB window above the starting frame, so a corrupt chain cannot fault.
  - `_start` is now a tiny naked shim that zeroes RBP, aligns the stack and calls `kernel_main`. So every backtrace (a panic's included) terminates cleanly at `kernel_main` instead of reading the loader's leftover frame.
  - The panic handler prints the kernel base and the backtrace addresses, which the KASLR base turns into image offsets offline.
- **Proof** (every boot): a three-deep `#[inline(never)]` call chain whose innermost frame captures a backtrace yields at least four return addresses, every one at or above the kernel image's virtual base.
- **A bug found and fixed on the way:** the first proof required every captured address to be in a `base .. base + 2 GiB` window, but that upper bound wrapped past the top of the address space for a KASLR base near `0xFFFFFFFF80000000`, making the window empty; and the walk stepped into `_start`'s frame and recorded the loader's leftover word (`0x1e093037`) as a return address. The naked `_start` fixed the second (the chain now ends at `kernel_main`), and the check became "at or above the kernel base".
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): the walk's frame-step bound set to 0 so it cannot move between frames → only 1 frame → "backtrace failed".
- **Test evidence:** 5 `unwind` tests (a clean chain, the chain end, the capacity bound, a wild frame pointer, an unreadable word); 121 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** symbol names (addresses are printed for offline symbolization), DWARF `.eh_frame` unwinding for frame-pointer-less code, and a full crash dump (registers plus stack) to storage.

### In-memory virtual filesystem (CLAUDE.md §39; M8/M9 groundwork; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `vfs` (library): a tree of directories and files in RAM, with the path handling and node operations the runtime and services will build on. Pure, no `unsafe`.
  - `components` parses an absolute, `/`-separated, UTF-8 path, skipping empty parts, with `.`/`..` and a per-component length limit.
  - `create`, `mkdir`, `mkdir_all`, `write` (grow and zero-fill a gap), `read` (offset and partial), `truncate`, `stat`, `list` (sorted), `remove` (a file or an empty directory; never the root). `resolve` follows `.` and `..` (the root's parent is itself). Distinct `FsError`s; a node and file-size limit; freed slots are reused and a failed create leaks nothing.
  - No on-disk format is decided here: an on-disk filesystem (its own format ADR) will implement the same operations later.
- **Proof** (every boot, on the heap): builds `/etc/origin/hostname`, writes and reads it back through a `..` path, lists the directory, stats it, removes everything, and checks the node count returns to the root alone (no leak).
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): a stray node left after the removals → "removed all back to 2 node: vfs failed".
- **Test evidence:** 6 `vfs` tests, including path parsing at the length limit, offset/gap read-write, the error taxonomy, the node limit with slot reuse, and a 4000-operation deterministic workload kept consistent; 127 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** an on-disk filesystem and its format ADR, open-file handles and a current-directory, permissions and ownership, symbolic links, mmap, and wiring the VFS to system calls (ADR-0005) and the block cache.

### Software rasterizer (CLAUDE.md §50 Origin UI, §52 the compositor's software fallback; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `raster` (library): a 2D rasterizer over a borrowed 32-bit `0xAARRGGBB` surface with a stride (a view into a larger framebuffer works). `clear`, `fill_rect`, `blend_rect` (straight-alpha "over"), `stroke_rect`, `blit`, with every operation clipped to the surface, so out-of-bounds coordinates are safe. `blend` rounds `(a·s + (255−a)·d + 127)/255` per channel. Pure, no `unsafe`.
- **Cross-check:** `demo_scene` draws a fixed scene (clear, three fills that run off the edges, a frame, a translucent band, a blitted checker sprite). The host test renders it to a 160×48 surface, checks it is deterministic, and proves its CRC-32 (`0x912df877`); the kernel renders the same scene on the heap and checks its CRC equals that constant, so the two renderers agree bit for bit.
- **Proof** (every boot): "raster: 160x48 scene rendered, CRC 0x912df877 (expected 0x912df877)". The value is identical on every machine (pure computation, no timing or KASLR), so the boot test matches it exactly.
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): one fill's blue channel changed by 1 → CRC `0x53d95223` → "raster failed".
- **Test evidence:** 5 `raster` tests (fills and clipping at every edge, the blend arithmetic, a clipped blit, surface-construction validation, the deterministic demo and its CRC); 132 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** a text/font engine (CLAUDE.md §51), drawing to a real framebuffer (no GOP framebuffer in boot info yet), damage tracking and the compositor (§52), and hardware-accelerated rendering.

### PS/2 keyboard: scancode decoding and i8042 bring-up (CLAUDE.md §56; 2026-11-08)

- **What:**
  - `ps2` (library): scan-code set 1 decoding. A `Decoder` turns bytes into key events (make/break, the `0xE0` extended prefix handled across calls, the `0xE1` pause sequence ignored), a US QWERTY `to_char` with a `Modifiers` state machine (Shift, Ctrl, Alt, Caps Lock, with Caps Lock affecting only letters and Shift the symbols). The tables are authored from the published set-1 assignments, not copied.
  - `i8042` (binary): controller bring-up after `ExitBootServices` — disable both ports, flush, read and rewrite the config byte (clearing the IRQ and translation bits for now), the controller self-test (0xAA → 0x55), the keyboard-port test (0xAB → 0x00), then enable the keyboard port. Every status-register wait is bounded (a million polls), so a missing controller cannot hang the kernel.
- **Proof** (every boot): "i8042: config 0x77; self-test 0x55 (want 0x55), keyboard port test 0x00 (want 0x00)". QEMU's emulated controller answers deterministically.
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): the self-test command byte changed from 0xAA to 0xAB, so the controller returns the port-test result 0x00 instead of 0x55 → "i8042 failed".
- **Test evidence:** 7 `ps2` tests (lower case with releases, Shift capitals and symbols, Caps Lock on letters only, Ctrl typing nothing, the extended keys, make/break and function keys, and typing the whole string "Origin OS!"); 139 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** live keystrokes need the keyboard IRQ (vector routing through the I/O APIC, not wired yet), the keyboard device reset and LED/typematic control, scancode set 2 without translation, USB HID keyboards, and other layouts.

### The HPET: discovery and a rate cross-check (CLAUDE.md §68; 2026-11-08)

- **What:**
  - `hpet` (library): parses the ACPI HPET table (the MMIO base from the GAS at offset 44, with the address-space and alignment checked) and the main-counter arithmetic (the period in femtoseconds from the capabilities register, period → frequency, a counter delta → nanoseconds, rate agreement). Pure, host-tested.
  - `time::prove_hpet`: finds the HPET through ACPI, maps its registers uncached, enables the main counter, and measures a counter delta against a TSC-timed ~20 ms window, requiring the HPET-measured and TSC-measured elapsed times to agree within 2 %.
- **Proof** (every boot): "HPET: at 0xfed00000, 100 MHz counter (period 10000000 fs); 20 ms elapsed by the HPET, 20 ms by the TSC". QEMU's HPET is a 100 MHz counter; the two clocks agree.
- **A boot-test lesson:** mapping the HPET first took the MMIO window's first slot (0xffffe00000000000), so the PCIe ECAM then mapped one slot higher and a marker that had hard-coded the ECAM's virtual address stopped matching. The virtual address is an allocation detail, so that marker now matches "uncached true, 2 MiB pages" without it. (The debug that found this — printing the first unmatched marker on a timeout — was removed.)
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): the second counter read forced equal to the first (a frozen counter) → "0 ms elapsed by the HPET, 20 ms by the TSC: HPET failed".
- **Test evidence:** 4 `hpet` tests (a valid table, bad addresses and short tables, the counter arithmetic at 100 MHz and 14.318 MHz, rate agreement); 143 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** HPET comparators as timer interrupt sources (one-shot and periodic), using the HPET as the wall-clock reference, and the ACPI PM timer as a further fallback.

### Network packet layer (CLAUDE.md §54; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `net` (library): header parsing and building for Ethernet II, IPv4 (no options), ICMP echo and ARP (IPv4 over Ethernet), and the Internet checksum (RFC 1071), including a streaming `checksum_parts` for a header plus payload without copying. Every parser is bounds-checked, requires a correct checksum where one applies, and never panics on a short or malformed buffer. Pure, no `unsafe`.
- **Self-validating proofs:** the checksum is anchored by its defining property — a block carrying its own checksum sums to zero — and by small hand-verifiable cases (one word 0x0001 → 0xFFFE, odd-byte padding), with the streaming form matching the contiguous one across an odd split. IPv4, ICMP and ARP round-trip (build → parse) with their checksums, and corrupting any checksummed byte makes parsing reject. No external vectors are needed.
- **Kernel proof** (every boot, on the heap): a 65-byte Ethernet/IPv4/ICMP echo request is built from host A to host B, B parses it and builds a reply, and A matches the reply to its request with the 23-byte payload intact and every checksum valid.
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): the ICMP checksum left unwritten → the echo request fails its checksum on parse → "payload and checksums intact false: net failed".
- **Test evidence:** 5 `net` tests (the checksum and its streaming form, an IPv4 round trip with a corrupted-byte rejection and an options rejection, an ICMP echo build/parse/reply, ARP request/reply, and a full Ethernet/IPv4/ICMP loopback echo); 148 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** a NIC driver (so nothing is on a wire yet), TCP and UDP, IP fragmentation and options, routing, DHCP and DNS, and IPv6 (CLAUDE.md §54).

### TCP: segments and a minimal connection state machine (CLAUDE.md §54; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `tcp` (library): TCP header parse/build with the IPv4 pseudo-header checksum, and a `Tcb` connection state machine (RFC 793 states). It drives the three-way handshake, one in-order data exchange and the FIN teardown, returning explicit outgoing segments (owning the send-sequence advance) and what to deliver. Pure, no `unsafe`.
- **Scope, stated honestly:** the connection core only — no retransmission, congestion control, out-of-order reassembly, window scaling or options beyond ignoring them on receive. It establishes, carries ordered data and closes.
- **Self-validating proofs:** a segment round-trips through build/parse with the pseudo-header checksum (which binds the IP addresses — parsing with the wrong addresses is rejected, as is a corrupted byte); `seq_len` counts SYN and FIN. `loopback_demo` connects two TCBs through an in-memory pipe: handshake to ESTABLISHED, A sends a payload B receives in full, A closes and B follows, ending with B CLOSED and A in teardown. No external vectors needed.
- **Kernel proof** (every boot, on the heap): "tcp: loopback connection established, 30-byte payload delivered, and closed: true".
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): `connect` sends no SYN flag → the handshake never completes → "closed: false: tcp failed".
- **Test evidence:** 4 `tcp` tests (segment round trip with checksum and address binding, `seq_len`, `loopback_demo` over several payload sizes, and the full establish/data/close loopback); 152 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** retransmission and timers, flow and congestion control, reassembly, the socket API and port demultiplexing, and moving segments over a real NIC.

### UDP, and a monotonic timer queue (CLAUDE.md §54, §68; 2026-11-08)

- **UDP** (`net`): datagram parse/build with the IPv4 pseudo-header checksum and the length field, a zero stored checksum accepted (RFC 768), a computed zero sent as all ones. Self-validating: round-trip with address binding and corrupted-byte and bad-length rejections. The kernel's net proof now also round-trips a UDP datagram.
- **Timer queue** (`timers`): a deadline-ordered set of `(id, deadline)` timers — `arm` (re-arming moves a timer), `cancel`, `next_deadline`, and `expire(now)` which removes and returns the due ids in deadline order. Kept sorted (O(1) peek, O(n) arm/cancel; a heap is a later optimization). Pure, no `unsafe`.
  - Host tests include a 5 000-operation workload checked against a `BTreeMap` model after every step (length, next deadline and the exact fired set).
  - Kernel proof (every boot): three timers armed at 5/10/15 ms on the monotonic clock, plus one cancelled, fire in order [10, 20, 30] with the cancelled one never firing; worst lateness 0 µs (the poll loop reads the clock tightly).
- **Negative controls**, each failing the boot test: a UDP checksum left unwritten is rejected on parse (the net control already covers the ICMP path; UDP's is covered by host tests); `cancel` made a no-op so the cancelled timer fires → order [10, 20, 99, 30] → "timers failed".
- **Test evidence:** 6 `net` tests (UDP among them) and 4 `timers` tests; 157 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** wiring the timer queue under the scheduler's sleeps and socket timeouts (it stands alone so far), a binary-heap implementation, and UDP/TCP port demultiplexing to sockets.

### Integration: a `/sys` info tree in the VFS, and a verification pass (2026-11-08)

- **What:** a boot step builds a read-only `/sys`-style tree in the in-memory VFS from facts several subsystems discovered — `/sys/mem/free_mib` (the frame allocator), `/sys/cpu/tsc_mhz` (the clock), `/sys/bus/pci/count` (`pcie::device_count`) and `/sys/block/nvme0/size_mib` (`storage::geometry`) — then reads a value back and checks it parses to the discovered number. It shows the VFS carrying a live system namespace built from real hardware state, tying the memory, clock, PCIe, NVMe and VFS subsystems together.
- **Proof** (every boot): "sysfs: built /sys with 4 facts (4 subtrees): mem/free_mib=503, cpu/tsc_mhz=999, bus/pci/count=6, block/nvme0/size_mib=16; read back pci count Some(6)". The PCIe count (6) and disk size (16 MiB) are deterministic in QEMU; free MiB and the TSC MHz vary and are reported, not asserted.
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): a wrong value stored for the PCIe count → the read-back (7) no longer matches the discovered count (6) → "sysfs failed".
- **Verification pass (2026-11-08):**
  - The whole workspace: 27 test suites, 396 tests, 0 failures (1 ignored).
  - An 8-processor boot (`ORIGIN_QEMU_SMP=8`): all 8 online, the scheduler on every one, the clock consistent across 8 (0 backwards), and 8 per-CPU NVMe queues doing I/O at once.
  - A 40x parser-mutation soak (`ORIGIN_MUTATION_SCALE=40`, release): ~800,000 parser cases and ~4,000,000 RTC cases over the firmware/device parsers, 0 failures, in about 7 s.

### I/O APIC interrupt routing (CLAUDE.md §24, §31; 2026-11-08)

- **What:**
  - `acpi`: MADT parsing extended to I/O APIC structures (type 1: id, MMIO base, GSI base) and interrupt source overrides (type 2), with `gsi_for_irq` resolving a legacy ISA IRQ to its global system interrupt and flags (an override, else identity).
  - `ioapic` (library): the redirection-table register indexes, the version register's max-entry field, MPS INTI flag decoding (polarity and trigger), and the redirection-entry bit layout (vector, fixed delivery, physical destination APIC id, polarity, trigger, mask). Host-tested.
  - `irq` (binary): finds the I/O APIC via the MADT, maps its registers uncached, programs a redirection entry through IOREGSEL/IOWIN (high dword first), and the 8254 PIT channel 0 as a 100 Hz rate generator.
- **Proof** (every boot): the I/O APIC is id 0 with 24 entries at 0xfec00000; the PIT's IRQ0, remapped to GSI 2 by a MADT override, is routed to vector 0x41 on the boot processor, and 20 periodic interrupts arrive in ~204 ms (polling with interrupt windows, never halting). The entry is then masked and the PIT stopped; nothing schedules on it yet.
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): the redirection entry left masked → 0 interrupts in 2 s → "I/O APIC failed".
- **Test evidence:** 7 `acpi` tests (I/O APIC and overrides among them) and 3 `ioapic` tests; 163 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** routing the keyboard IRQ1 to a handler for live keystrokes (the i8042 bring-up is done; this is the remaining link), level-triggered PCI INTx routing, per-CPU interrupt affinity and balancing, and an EOI path for the I/O APIC's own remote-IRR on level interrupts.
- **Under interrupt remapping (2026-11-08):** this proof still runs before the IOMMU, in compatibility format. Once the IOMMU is up, the same pin is routed again in remappable format through an IRTE; see "I/O APIC interrupts through VT-d interrupt remapping".

### The ACPI PM timer: a second time-source cross-check (CLAUDE.md §68; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `acpi::parse_fadt` extended to read `PM_TMR_BLK` (the PM timer's I/O port, accepted when `PM_TMR_LEN` is 4) and the `TMR_VAL_EXT` flag (24- vs 32-bit counter); `acpi::PM_TIMER_HZ` (3.579545 MHz). `time::prove_pm_timer` reads the counter across a TSC-timed window and requires the PM-timer-measured and TSC-measured elapsed times to agree within 2 %. A new `ind` (32-bit `in`) port helper.
- **Proof** (every boot): "PM timer: 24-bit at port 0x608, 3.579545 MHz; 20 ms elapsed by the PM timer, 20 ms by the TSC". QEMU's PM timer is a 24-bit counter at 0x608; the kernel masks the single wrap and the two clocks agree. This is now the third independent clock the kernel validates against the TSC (the RTC second, the HPET, the PM timer).
- **Negative control** (failing the boot test): the second counter read forced equal to the first → "0 ms elapsed by the PM timer, 20 ms by the TSC: PM timer failed".
- **Test evidence:** the `acpi` FADT test checks the new fields; 163 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs.
- **Not done:** using the PM timer as the wall-clock reference when the TSC is not invariant, and handling the PM timer's overflow interrupt.

### CPU topology from CPUID (CLAUDE.md §24, §27; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `topology` (library) decodes CPUID leaf 0Bh sub-leaves into the bit widths that split an x2APIC ID into SMT thread, core and package, with `split`, `are_siblings`, and `analyze` (group a set of processors into package/core/thread counts and check every triple is unique). A flat fallback when the leaf is absent. Pure, no `unsafe`. `cpu::cpuid_subleaf` reads a leaf with a sub-leaf in ECX.
- **Proof** (every boot): the online processors' x2APIC IDs decompose consistently. QEMU `-smp N` presents N single-thread cores in one package: "topology: 2 logical, 2 cores, 1 packages (1 threads/core, 2 logical/package); consistent true" (and 4 cores at `-smp 4`).
- **Why no boot-level negative control:** distinct x2APIC IDs always decompose to distinct `(package, core, thread)` triples under any `smt_width ≤ core_width` (the split is injective, and `decode` enforces the bound), so the `consistent` check can only fail on duplicate IDs — a firmware fault, not something a code change toggles. The failure path is covered by the host test, where `analyze` with duplicate IDs returns `unique = false`.
- **Test evidence:** 3 `topology` tests (width decode and ID splitting, the flat fallback, and `analyze`'s package/core/thread counts with a duplicate-ID rejection); 166 library tests; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-matrix` at 1, 2 and 4 CPUs (and an earlier 8-CPU boot).
- **Not done:** using the topology for scheduler placement (SMT-aware and cache-aware, §27), the cache hierarchy from leaf 04h, and hybrid-core capacity (§27).

### CPU topology from CPUID leaves 1Fh, 0Bh and 80000026h (`topology`; `cpu`, `smp`, `main`; xtask; library + kernel; CLAUDE.md §24, §27, §72, §74; ADR-0008 C2; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** an extension of the entry above (which read leaf 0Bh only) in `framekernel::topology` (library, `forbid(unsafe_code)`):
  - `CpuTopology::detect(cpuid)`, driven by a CPUID reader: the kernel passes `cpu::cpuid_subleaf`, host tests a modelled processor;
  - `Layout`: from thread to package, the bits below each domain's ID field, one type for three encodings. Leaves 1Fh and 0Bh give upper bounds (the shift to the next wider domain); AMD's 80000026h gives lower bounds (the shift to each level's own ID), so the two are decoded apart. AMD's complex is the module domain. Leaf 0Bh shows the core field reaching to the package;
  - the choice of leaf: 80000026h, then 1Fh, then 0Bh, then none, each checked against its maximum and its own validity rule, never by vendor. A malformed leaf is skipped and recorded in `problem`;
  - unknown domain types absorbed into the known domain directly below (Intel's paper §1.3.2);
  - `CoreIdentity`: leaf 1Ah's or leaf 80000026h's core type as a raw code, native model, and AMD's efficiency ranking. No names (§24); Intel's text says the code implies nothing;
  - `Placement` (package, die group, die, tile, module, core, thread), `Census`, and `agree` (each processor against its MADT APIC ID and against the first processor).
- **Kernel:** `cpu::record_topology` runs on every processor on itself (the boot processor in `prove_topology`, each AP in `smp::ap_entry` before its handshake answer) and stores the decoded record under its `CpuIndex` (`cpu::topology_of`, a spin lock per slot; no new `unsafe`). `smp::listed_apic_ids` gives the MADT's whole list. `prove_topology` reports the layout, each online processor's placement, the MADT census, the core types, and the checks.
- **Research ledger:** `docs/research/2026-11-08-cpu-topology-leaf-1fh.md`.
- **Specifications:** Intel SDM Vol. 1 Chapter 21 (253665-093US, September 2026; CPUID.0BH, 1AH, 1FH), Intel *Processor Topology Enumeration* (337015-002), AMD APM Vol. 3 (24594 Rev 3.39, October 2026, read from a mirror and since confirmed byte-identical to AMD's own copy; SHA-256 in the ledger).
- **Host tests:** 19 `topology` tests: QEMU's exact leaves and census; a leaf above the maximum not believed (the XSAVE reply, and 80000026h reading 1Fh's list); every domain; unknown domains (Intel's Examples B, C, D); every malformed list skipped and reported; 80000026h's convention, hybrid flag, core type and ranking; the leaf 1Ah rules; each way `agree` can fail; mixed thread widths on a hybrid only; and a randomized test over 3000 layouts through all three encodings. xtask: `the_topology_markers_follow_the_machine`. `cargo xtask check`: 596 tests, 0 failures, 6 ignored (579 before).
- **Boot proof, `cargo xtask boot-x2apic`** (two boots, one machine: `-smp 1,maxcpus=150,sockets=2,dies=3,modules=5,cores=5,threads=1` with processors at APIC IDs 256 and 412, cold-plugged). With `-cpu max,vendor=GenuineIntel`, which raises QEMU's CPUID maximum to 1Fh:
  - `topology: layout from leaf 1Fh: thread bits 0, core bits 3, module bits 3, die bits 2, package from bit 8`
  - `topology: CPU 2 (APIC ID 412): package 1, die 2, module 3, core 4, thread 0`
  - `topology: the MADT lists 150 processors: 2 packages, 6 dies, 30 modules, 150 cores, 150 threads`
  - `topology: core types: reported by 0 of 3 processors; hybrid false`
  - `topology: against the MADT: 3 processors checked, 0 recorded nothing, 0 have another APIC ID, 0 another layout, 0 an undecodable leaf, 0 no core type although hybrid, 0 a duplicate placement; consistent true`
  - `topology: 3 logical, 3 cores, 2 packages (1 threads/core, 256 logical/package); consistent true`

  With the default `-cpu max` (AMD vendor, maximum leaf 0Dh) the same machine reads through leaf 0Bh alone: `layout from leaf 0Bh: thread bits 0, core bits 8, module bits 0, die bits 0, package from bit 8`, `CPU 2 (APIC ID 412): package 1, die 0, module 0, core 156, thread 0`, and `2 packages, 2 dies, 2 modules, 150 cores, 150 threads`. xtask derives every expected value from the `-smp` fields alone. A third processor exists so that a die, module and core mix-up shows: at APIC ID 256 they are all 0.
- **`cargo xtask boot-matrix`** (Intel and AMD IOMMUs, 1, 2 and 4 CPUs): each CPU's placement through leaf 0Bh, e.g. `CPU 3 (APIC ID 3): package 0, die 0, module 0, core 3, thread 0` at `-smp 4`.
- **Negative controls.** Each is a temporary change. With it applied, `cargo xtask boot-test` (`ORIGIN_BOOT_TEST_TIMEOUT=45`) exited 1 on the sparse machine with `-cpu max,vendor=GenuineIntel`, and C9 and C10 on the default machine; it was then restored and `git diff` was empty:
  - **C1, an AP that never records itself** (no `cpu::record_topology()` in `ap_entry`): `CPU 1 (APIC ID 256): it recorded nothing about itself`, `2 recorded nothing`, `consistent false: topology failed`.
  - **C2, leaf 1Fh ignored** (1Fh removed from the leaves tried): `layout from leaf 0Bh`, so the `leaf 1Fh` markers never appear and the boot times out at its deadline.
  - **C3, the module and die codes swapped**: the list is then out of order (die before module): `3 an undecodable leaf`, the fallback to 0Bh, `consistent false: topology failed`.
  - **C4, an APIC ID that is not the MADT's** (the recorded MADT value off by one on each AP): `2 have another APIC ID`, `consistent false: topology failed`.
  - **C5, an AP that draws another layout** (EAX of leaf 1Fh sub-leaf 1 raised by one on the APs): `CPU 2 (APIC ID 412): package 1, die 2, module 1, core 12, thread 0`, `2 another layout`, `consistent false: topology failed`.
  - **C6, the census counts modules as dies**: `2 packages, 30 dies, 30 modules`, so the `6 dies` marker never appears and the boot times out.
  - **C7, a hybrid claim with no core type** (CPUID.07H:EDX\[15\] forced set for every processor): `core types: reported by 0 of 3 processors; hybrid true`, `3 no core type although hybrid`, `consistent false: topology failed`.
  - **C8, an AP that reports the boot processor's ID** (EDX forced to 0 on the APs): `CPU 2 (APIC ID 412): package 0, die 0, module 0, core 0, thread 0`, `2 have another APIC ID, ... 2 a duplicate placement`, `consistent false: topology failed`.
  - **C9, leaf 0Bh ignored** (default `-smp 2` machine): `layout from no topology leaf`, `2 packages`, so the `core bits 1` markers never appear and the boot times out.
  - **C10, no maximum-leaf check** (default machine, so leaf 1Fh is read beyond level 0Dh and returns leaf 0Dh's XSAVE data): `2 an undecodable leaf`, `consistent false: topology failed`.
- **QEMU facts worth keeping** (ledger §3): `-cpu max` under TCG is AuthenticAMD with maximum basic leaf 0Dh, so leaf 1Fh is out of its range even with dies and modules; an Intel-vendor model (or `min-level=0x1f`) reaches it; a read above a maximum returns the highest basic leaf's data, never zeros; leaf 80000026h does not exist in QEMU 11.1.3 (`xlevel=0x80000026` gives zeros); leaf 1Ah reads zero and the hybrid bit has no name; `max` and `EPYC-Genoa` leave TopologyExtensions clear under TCG.
- **Unsafe inventory:** nothing new. `framekernel::topology` is `forbid(unsafe_code)`; the per-CPU table is a spin lock per slot; CPUID goes through the existing `cpu::cpuid_subleaf`.
- **Not done:** topology-aware placement (§27); hybrid-core capacity, which needs the CPUID.06H feedback interface or ACPI CPPC; leaf 8000001Eh, deliberately (AMD processors without 80000026h or 0Bh are below the 2026+ target, and they fall back to a flat layout); the ACPI PPTT; the MADT's "online capable" processors; **QEMU-only (§74): leaf 80000026h, leaf 1Ah, mixed SMT widths, tiles, die groups and any hybrid processor are host-tested from the specifications and were not run on hardware.** `hybrid false` under QEMU says nothing about hybrid processors.
- **Review:** not yet independently reviewed.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code, written from the Intel SDM, Intel's topology paper and AMD's APM (T1, T2, A1 in the ledger); no operating-system code was read or copied (CLAUDE.md §3).
- **Commit:** `d1984cd` (code and ledger), and the records commit after it.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### CPU cache hierarchy from CPUID leaf 04h (CLAUDE.md §24, §27; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `cache` (library) decodes leaf-04h deterministic-cache sub-leaves into each cache's level, type (data/instruction/unified), size, line size, ways and how many logical processors share it. The size is the product of ways, partitions, line size and sets. Pure, no `unsafe`. The kernel reports the hierarchy in its topology step.
- **Honest QEMU note:** QEMU's TCG `-cpu max` reports no leaf-04h caches (it is an Intel-specific deterministic-cache leaf the emulator leaves empty), so the kernel line reads "cache: 0 caches; consistent true" under emulation. The decoder is therefore validated by host tests, not a boot proof; on real 2026 hardware (CLAUDE.md §74) leaf 04h is populated and the same code reports the real caches. It is an informational line, not a gated boot marker, for that reason.
- **Test evidence:** 2 `cache` tests (a typical L1/L2/L3 hierarchy decoded to exact sizes and sharing, and `decode_all` stopping at the terminator with the size-equals-geometry invariant); 168 library tests; `cargo xtask check`.
- **Not done:** cache-aware scheduler placement (§27), AMD's leaf 8000001Dh, and TLB/prefetch descriptors (leaf 02h).

### OriginFS v0: a read-only on-disk filesystem parser (ADR-0006, **Proposed**; CLAUDE.md §39, §40, §41, §84; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `originfs` (library) is a read-only parser for the OriginFS v0 on-disk format and an image builder for its tests. A `BlockDevice` trait yields 4 KiB blocks; `Fs::open` validates the superblock (magic, version, block size, CRC-32 over the first 60 bytes, and that the inode table lies before the data region inside the volume); `inode`, `read_file`/`read_whole` (direct and single-indirect blocks, with a zero-filled hole for a 0 pointer), `entries` (linked `rec_len` directory records) and `resolve` (path walk reusing `vfs::components`, `.`/`..`). Pure, no `unsafe`; every field is range-checked through `.get(..)`/`u{32,64}_at`, so no parse panics on a malformed image. Inode field offsets follow ADR-0006 F3 exactly (direct pointers at byte 24, after kind/_reserved/links/size/blocks; single-indirect at 120). The superblock/inode **encoders** are `#[cfg(test)]` — the shipped read path never encodes; only the test `Builder` does.
- **Status / §84:** ADR-0006 is **Proposed**; this is a format decision, so the owner must accept it before anything is Accepted. The parser and builder are **host-only and not registered in the kernel binary** (`main.rs` does not reference `originfs`), so OriginFS is not mounted and the no-panic kernel object is unaffected. It will plug in beneath `framekernel::vfs` once the ADR is accepted. No negative boot control, for the same reason — there is no boot path to break.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code, written from the classic Unix inode-filesystem design (a superblock, a fixed inode table, direct and single-indirect block pointers, linked directory entries with `rec_len`) described conceptually in the BSD FFS / ext2 lineage; no source is used (CLAUDE.md §3). Reuses the first-party `gpt::crc32` and `vfs::components`.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 4 `originfs` tests — build→parse→list→read a directory tree (a small file, a nested file, and a 15-block+123-byte file that exercises the single-indirect block, read whole byte-exact and with a block-straddling partial read); `.`/`..` resolution; distinct `NotFound`/`BadPath`/`IsDirectory`/`NotDirectory`/`BadInode`/`Io` errors; a corrupt-superblock rejection (flipped magic byte, and a flipped CRC-covered field with a stale CRC) and a too-small device as `Io`; and a punched direct pointer reading back as a zero-filled hole. 172 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`.
- **Not done (ADR-0006 F6):** the write path, allocation bitmap, journalling and crash consistency (§41), double-indirect (so files are capped at ~2 MiB in v0), snapshots, permissions beyond the kind, and mounting beneath the VFS (pending owner acceptance). The CRC is the first-party IEEE CRC-32 used for internal consistency; it is not a cryptographic integrity check.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### NUMA from the ACPI SRAT (CLAUDE.md §24 NUMA topology, §28 NUMA policies; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `acpi::srat_cpu_affinities` and `acpi::srat_memory_affinities` (library) parse the System Resource Affinity Table: Processor Local APIC Affinity (type 0, with the split 8-bit/24-bit proximity domain), Processor Local x2APIC Affinity (type 2), and Memory Affinity (type 1, 64-bit base and length, enabled/hot-pluggable/non-volatile flags). Each walks the structures from offset 48 (36-byte header + 12 reserved) with the same bounds discipline as the MADT walker — every structure's length is checked against the remaining table and against its type's minimum, so no parse panics on a malformed table. New typed errors `SratEntry(offset)` and `TooManyEntries`. Pure, no `unsafe`.
- **Integration:** `prove_numa` (kernel) finds the SRAT through `firmware::acpi_table(rsdp, b"SRAT")` (RSDP → XSDT → table, all checksum-checked), lists the CPU and memory affinities, and reports the distinct proximity domains, the placed CPUs, the memory ranges and the total memory, with a consistency check: every online processor must appear as an enabled CPU affinity and some memory must be present. A machine with no SRAT (uniform memory, or QEMU without `-numa`) is reported as one implicit node.
- **Proof** (every boot): QEMU is now booted with two `-numa` nodes (two 256 MiB `memory-backend-ram` objects summing to `-m 512M`; the vCPUs auto-distribute, valid for any `-smp`, verified at 1/2/4/8). The kernel reads QEMU's real firmware SRAT: `origin-kernel: numa: 2 nodes, N cpus, 3 memory ranges, 511 MiB; consistent true` at `-smp` N = 1, 2, 4 and 8 (every online CPU placed across the two nodes). The line is a gated boot marker; `: numa failed` is a failure marker.
- **Negative control:** starting the SRAT walk 4 bytes early (`SRAT_ENTRIES` 48 → 44) makes the first "structure" a zero-length run in the reserved area, so the parser returns `SratEntry(44)`; the kernel then prints `numa: invalid SRAT; consistent false: numa failed` and `cargo xtask boot-test` fails (exit 1 on the failure marker). Restored to 48, the boot passes. This confirms the marker checks the real parse, not a constant.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code, written from ACPI 6.6 §5.2.16 (SRAT and its three x86-relevant affinity structures); no source is used (CLAUDE.md §3). Reuses the first-party `acpi` table-checking (`check_table`, `xsdt_entries`) and `firmware::acpi_table`.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 2 new `acpi` tests — a two-node SRAT with type-0, type-2 and type-1 structures (the 32-bit type-0 domain split, a present-but-disabled CPU, an x2APIC affinity, 64-bit memory base/length, hot-plug/NV flags, and an unknown type skipped), and malformed/overflow rejection (a short type-0, a length running past the table, a full buffer → `TooManyEntries`, and a short type-1). 9 `acpi` tests and 174 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-test`; `boot-matrix` (1, 2, 4) and an 8-CPU boot; the negative control above.
- **Not done:** using the affinities for memory-allocator placement and scheduler locality (§27, §28, §66) — this is the discovery half; a NUMA-aware frame allocator and placement policy come next. The SLIT inter-node distance matrix is parsed (below); the HMAT memory-latency table is not.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### NUMA distances from the ACPI SLIT (CLAUDE.md §27 migration cost, §28 NUMA policies; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `acpi::parse_slit` (library) parses the System Locality Information Table into a borrowed `Slit { localities, matrix }` with `distance(i, j)`: the u64 locality count at offset 36 and the row-major N×N byte matrix, both bounds- and overflow-checked (a locality count whose N×N would overrun the table, or overflow `usize`, is refused, not panicked). The diagonal is the normalized local distance 10; 255 means unreachable. Pure, no `unsafe`.
- **Integration:** `prove_slit` (kernel) finds the SLIT through `firmware::acpi_table(rsdp, b"SLIT")` and checks the diagonal is 10 and every off-diagonal ≥ 10. No SLIT (uniform distance) is reported as such.
- **Proof** (every boot): QEMU is booted with `-numa dist,src=0,dst=1,val=21` (it mirrors 1→0), so it emits a real SLIT: `origin-kernel: slit: 2 localities, local 10 (true), 0->last 21; consistent true` at `-smp` 1/2/4/8. Gated boot marker; `: slit failed` is a failure marker.
- **Negative control:** shifting the matrix read one byte (`table.get(44..end)` → `45..end`) misaligns the diagonal, so `local 10` reads `false`; the kernel prints `slit: ... consistent false: slit failed` and `cargo xtask boot-test` fails (exit 1). Restored, it passes.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code from ACPI 6.6 §5.2.17; no source used (CLAUDE.md §3). Reuses the `acpi` table-checking and `firmware::acpi_table`.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 2 `acpi` tests — a 2-locality `[10,21,21,10]` matrix and a 3-locality asymmetric matrix round-tripped cell for cell with out-of-range `distance` returning `None`; a truncated matrix and a `u64::MAX` locality count both refused as `Length`. 11 `acpi` tests and 176 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-test`; `boot-matrix` (1, 2, 4) and an 8-CPU boot; the negative control above.
- **Not done:** using the distances to order NUMA-aware placement and migration decisions (§27, §66); the HMAT table (bandwidth/latency) is not parsed.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### NUMA locality map (CLAUDE.md §27, §28, §66; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `numa` (library) turns the parsed SRAT affinities and the SLIT into the placement questions an allocator or scheduler asks: `node_of_cpu` (APIC ID → enabled affinity's node), `node_of_address` (physical address → the enabled memory range that contains it), `nearest_nodes` (fill a buffer with the SLIT locality indices in ascending distance from a given node, a stable insertion sort so equal distances keep ascending order), and `self_is_nearest` (every node's nearest node is itself — the invariant an allocator relies on, that local memory is never further than remote). Pure, no `unsafe`, no allocation; it decides nothing about the hardware, only about placement over already-parsed ACPI data.
- **Integration:** `prove_slit` (kernel) now also derives the map from the real SLIT and reports node 0's nodes in ascending distance and the self-nearest invariant, folding `self_is_nearest` into the gated consistency check: `slit: 2 localities, local 10 (true), 0->last 21, self-nearest true, from 0 [0, 1]; consistent true`.
- **Negative control:** inverting the sort comparator in `nearest_nodes` (`<` → `>`) makes node 0's order `[1, 0]` and `self-nearest false`, so the kernel prints `consistent false: slit failed` and `cargo xtask boot-test` fails (exit 1). Restored, it passes. This proves the reported order reflects the real distances, not a constant.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code (CLAUDE.md §3), building only on the first-party `acpi` types.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 4 `numa` tests — CPU and address lookup (a disabled affinity and an unlisted/unmapped address return `None`, a range is half-open), distance ordering from two different origin nodes with a capped output buffer, stable ordering of equal distances, and a broken SLIT (a remote node closer than self) failing `self_is_nearest`. 180 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-test`; `boot-matrix` (1, 2, 4); the negative control above.
- **Not done:** wiring the map into the frame allocator (local-node-first allocation) and the scheduler (locality-aware placement/migration, §66) — the map is the decision layer; the allocator and scheduler changes that consume it come next.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### Streaming UTF-8 decoder for the text engine (CLAUDE.md §51; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `text` (library) is a streaming, error-locating UTF-8 decoder. `decode_first` reads one Unicode scalar from a byte slice and returns either `(char, len)`, `Incomplete(present)` (a valid but truncated prefix), or `Invalid(skip)` (ill-formed, with the maximal-subpart length to skip). `validate` walks the slice and returns a std-shaped `Utf8Error { valid_up_to, error_len }`; `is_valid` is the boolean form; `chars_lossy` iterates scalars, substituting one U+FFFD per maximal ill-formed subpart without allocating. Well-formedness (Unicode 18.0 §3.9): overlong encodings, surrogates (U+D800..U+DFFF) and scalars above U+10FFFF are rejected by constraining the second byte per lead byte (0xE0/0xED/0xF0/0xF4). Pure, no `unsafe`, no allocation.
- **Why not `core::str`:** the text engine must decode a file, a paste or terminal bytes that may be partial or corrupt, keep going past the first bad byte, and report *where* the error is — none of which `core::str::from_utf8` (all-or-nothing) offers. This is the decoding primitive the editor, terminal and font shaper build on; it is **not yet wired into a kernel text/UI path** (the UI itself is later milestone work), and the kernel's own console output continues to use `core::str`.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code from the Unicode 18.0 well-formed byte-sequence table (§3.9, Table 3-7) and the recommended U+FFFD substitution (TR#36 / the WHATWG Encoding rule); no implementation source is used (CLAUDE.md §3), and no Unicode data tables are needed (the rules are expressed as byte-range constraints).
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 5 `text` tests. Besides the hand-written cases (every sequence length and the U+0080/07FF/0800/FFFF/10000/10FFFF boundaries; overlong, surrogate, over-max, stray-continuation, truncated and bad-continuation rejection with the exact `Incomplete`/`Invalid` lengths; lossy substitution), an oracle test runs 20 000 biased-random byte strings through both `validate` and `core::str::from_utf8` and asserts they agree on validity, `valid_up_to` and `error_len`, and that `chars_lossy` equals `String::from_utf8_lossy` and, for valid input, `str::chars` — a byte-exact equivalence to the standard library's decoder, used only as a test oracle (CLAUDE.md §4/§5). 185 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`. Host-only, so no boot proof or negative control (there is no boot path to break; the std oracle is the control).
- **Not done:** grapheme-cluster and word segmentation (UAX #29), line breaking (UAX #14), normalization, bidi and shaping (§51) — this is the byte→scalar layer those build on; UTF-16/UTF-32 transcoding; and East Asian width. These need Unicode property data (permitted infrastructure, §4) with provenance, added when the segmentation work lands.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### Gap buffer for editable text (CLAUDE.md §51 text editing, caret movement; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `editbuffer` (library) is a gap buffer: the text lives in one `Vec<char>` with a movable gap at the caret, so insert and delete at the caret are amortised O(1) and only caret movement shuffles scalars across the gap. `EditBuffer` offers `insert`/`insert_str`, `delete_back` (backspace) and `delete_forward`, `move_left`/`move_right`/`move_to` (clamped), `get`, `len`/`caret`, and `Display` (so `to_string` is free). It stores Unicode scalars, so a caret position is a scalar index — the internal model of a text field or line editor; grapheme-aware movement is a later display layer over `text`. Pure, no `unsafe`.
- **Why:** the terminal, text fields and the eventual editor need an editable text model with a caret; a gap buffer is the standard structure, and keeping it scalar-indexed (not byte-indexed) means a caret never lands inside a multi-byte scalar. Host-tested groundwork; **not yet wired into a kernel input/UI path** (the UI is later-milestone work).
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code (CLAUDE.md §3); the gap-buffer technique is textbook, no source used.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 4 `editbuffer` tests. Besides the hand-written cases (ASCII editing with backspace/forward-delete at both ends; a non-ASCII string — `café ∀😀` — edited mid-string with scalar-correct lengths and `get`; caret clamping and mid-gap insertion), a model-based test runs 50 000 random operations (insert, both deletes, both moves, jump-to) against a `Vec<char>` + cursor oracle and asserts the text length and caret match after **every** operation, then the whole text and every position at the end. 189 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`. Host-only, so no boot proof (the oracle is the control).
- **Not done:** selection ranges, undo/redo, line-aware operations, and grapheme-granular movement (needs UAX #29). Wiring it into a terminal line editor or a text-field control comes with the UI milestone (§50).
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### Hardware entropy source: RDSEED/RDRAND with bounded retries (CLAUDE.md §59; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `entropy` (library) holds the retry/fill logic as pure functions over an abstract `Source` (`try_next() -> Option<u64>`): `draw` retries a transiently-failing source up to a budget (Intel's `RDRAND_RETRIES` = 10, so 11 attempts) and returns `None` only if every attempt fails (never the value 0); `fill` fills a byte buffer word by word, taking the low bytes of the last word for a partial chunk, and reports whether the whole buffer was filled. No `unsafe` (the instructions live in the binary). The kernel binary's `cpu::rdrand`/`cpu::rdseed` are the real one-shot attempts (RDRAND/RDSEED + SETC, register/flag-only, CPUID-gated), and `prove_entropy`'s source prefers RDSEED and falls back to RDRAND.
- **Why:** the kernel had no entropy source of its own — only the loader draws KASLR bits. §59 wants secure randomness; this is the true-random primitive that a future DRBG, ASLR offsets, stack canaries, TCP initial sequence numbers and nonces draw from. It is a **true-random source, not a DRBG**: it returns hardware bits or fails, and never substitutes a constant. A reseedable stream (SP 800-90A Hash_DRBG over `origin-crypto`'s SHA-256, with KATs and review, §59) is deliberately left as a separate, reviewed change, not invented here.
- **Proof** (every boot): the kernel draws 16 values through `draw` over RDSEED/RDRAND and checks they all arrived, are non-zero and are distinct — the smoke that separates a live source from a dead one: `entropy: RDSEED true, RDRAND true; 16 draws (16 RDSEED, 0 RDRAND), all true, distinct true, nonzero true; consistent true` at `-smp` 1/2/4. (QEMU TCG `-cpu max` supplies RDSEED, which satisfied every draw on the first attempt.) A processor with neither instruction is reported honestly as "no source claimed", not failed. Gated boot marker; `: entropy failed` is a failure marker.
- **Negative control:** replacing the drawn value with a constant (0) at the consumer makes the batch non-distinct and zero, so the kernel prints `distinct false, nonzero false; consistent false: entropy failed` and `cargo xtask boot-test` fails (exit 1). Restored, it passes. This proves the dead-source smoke actually rejects a constant stream.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code (CLAUDE.md §3); the bounded-retry loop follows Intel's RDRAND/RDSEED guidance (Intel SDM / the DRNG software implementation guide). The binary's asm mirrors the loader's existing RDSEED/RDRAND use.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 5 `entropy` tests over a scripted mock source — `draw` stops at the first success, counts exactly `retries + 1` attempts, and gives up with `None`; `fill` writes a partial final chunk from a word's low bytes (one draw per 8-byte chunk), fails cleanly when the source dies mid-buffer, and an empty fill makes no attempt. 194 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`; `boot-test`; `boot-matrix` (1, 2, 4); the negative control above.
- **Unsafe:** two inline-asm blocks (`cpu::rdrand`, `cpu::rdseed`), each a single instruction + SETC writing only a register and the carry flag, CPUID-gated, with SAFETY notes; neither is `pure`.
- **Not done:** a DRBG for a reseedable stream (§59), wiring entropy into user-process ASLR, stack canaries and TCP ISN (§54, §58), and a health/continuous test (SP 800-90B). The loader's KASLR entropy stays separate for now.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### Glob pattern matching (CLAUDE.md §39; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `glob` (library) matches names and paths against a glob pattern: `*` (any run except `/`), `?` (one char except `/`), `[...]` classes with ranges and `!`/`^` negation (a leading `]` is literal, a trailing `-` is literal), and `\` escapes. A literal `/` is the only thing that matches `/`, so one pattern stays within a path segment unless it spells the separators out (`src/*.rs`); no `**` yet. `matches(pattern, text)` and a `filter` helper. The matcher compiles the pattern to tokens, then runs the single-star-pointer backtracking algorithm with the `/` guard on star extension, so it is linear in practice and terminates on adversarial patterns. Pure, no `unsafe`.
- **Why:** a shell, the package manager's file lists, and VFS/search filtering all need name and path matching; keeping the wildcards from crossing `/` is the POSIX pathname behaviour callers expect. Host-tested utility; a caller (shell/package tooling) wires it in later.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code (CLAUDE.md §3); POSIX `fnmatch`-style semantics, standard algorithm, no source used.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 6 `glob` tests — literals and `?` (exactly one, never `/`); stars (empty, extensions, no crossing `/`, collapsed runs, `src/*/*.rs`); classes (sets, ranges, double ranges, `!`/`^` negation, literal leading `]` and trailing `-`, never `/`, unterminated `[` as a literal); escaping of `*`/`?`/`[]` and inside a class; Unicode (`café`, a Greek range) and the `filter` helper; and a pathological-backtracking case (`*a*a*…*b` on 64 `a`s) that must terminate with the right answer. 200 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`. Host-only, so no boot proof (the cases are the control).
- **Not done:** `**` (crossing `/`), brace expansion `{a,b}`, case-insensitive matching, and a directory-walk that applies a multi-segment pattern against the VFS. These are callers of `matches`, added with the shell/package work.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### IPv4 longest-prefix-match routing table (CLAUDE.md §54 routing; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `route` (library) is an LPM routing table: a binary (bit) trie over the 32-bit IPv4 address. `Table<V: Copy>` with `insert(prefix, prefix_len, value)` (host bits beyond the length ignored; re-inserting a prefix replaces it; `/0` is the default route) and `lookup(addr)` returning the value of the most specific matching route. A lookup walks at most 32 nodes, remembering the deepest marked node it passes. The value is generic, so a caller stores whatever a route needs (a gateway and an interface). Pure, no `unsafe`; `alloc` for the node pool. Reuses `net::Ipv4`.
- **Why:** the network stack needs a forwarding decision — given a destination address, which route (gateway/interface) applies — and routing is by longest prefix. §54 lists routing; this is the table a future IP output path and a `route`-like tool consult.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code (CLAUDE.md §3); the LPM bit-trie is textbook, no source used.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 4 `route` tests — most-specific wins (default < /8 < /16 < /24), no default means no match, host bits ignored and re-insert replaces plus a /32 host route; and an **oracle test** building 2 000 random tables (up to 24 routes, lengths 0–32, a crowded prefix space so nesting and collisions are common) and checking `lookup` against a brute-force longest-match scan over 30 random addresses each — the trie must agree with the reference on every (table, address). 204 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`. Host-only, so no boot proof (the brute-force scan is the control).
- **Not done:** route deletion and prefix aggregation, path-compressed (Patricia) nodes for memory, ECMP, metrics/administrative distance, IPv6 (a 128-bit trie), and wiring it into an IP forwarding/output path with ARP/NDP next-hop resolution (§54).
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### DNS message parsing with bounded name decompression (CLAUDE.md §54 DNS; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `dns` (library) parses a wire-format DNS message into owned values: the header (with `is_response`/`recursion_desired`/`rcode` helpers), the questions, and the resource records (A → `Ipv4`, AAAA → 16 bytes, CNAME/NS/PTR → a decompressed name, anything else → its length). `read_name` resolves RFC 1035 §4.1.4 label compression. Every length is `.get`-checked, so no parse panics. `parse` reads `qdcount` questions then `ancount + nscount + arcount` records. Pure, no `unsafe`; `alloc` for owned names/lists. Reuses `net::Ipv4`.
- **Safety (untrusted input, §34/§54):** name decompression is bounded — a compression pointer must point **strictly backwards** (target < the pointer's own offset) and a jump counter is capped, so a self-referential, forward or cyclic pointer is rejected (`None`) rather than looped on; a decoded name is capped at 255 bytes; reserved pointer-type bits (0x40/0x80) are rejected. This is the property that turns a classic DoS (a DNS decompression bomb) into a clean parse failure.
- **Why:** a resolver client needs to read responses; this is the read path it builds on (it does not send queries or cache yet). A natural companion to `net`/`udp` and the `route` table.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code from RFC 1035 §4; no source used (CLAUDE.md §3).
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 4 `dns` tests — a round-trip (a no-compression builder writes a response with a question, an A record and a CNAME; parse recovers the header flags/rcode, the names, the A address and the CNAME target) which **caught a real rdlength offset bug** (read at `pos+8`, not `pos+6`); a backward compression pointer (an answer whose name points to the question) resolved correctly; hostile/truncated names refused (a self-pointer, a forward pointer, a label past the end, a short header — all `None`); and a 50-deep chain of strictly-backward pointers that must terminate at the root. 208 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`. Host-only, so no boot proof (the round-trip and the malformed cases are the control).
- **Not done:** a message builder/encoder for sending queries (the test builder is minimal and test-only), EDNS(0), DNSSEC, the full record-type set, and wiring into a resolver with UDP/TCP transport and a cache (§54).
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### Mutation soaks for the new parsers, and a `read_whole` allocation cap (CLAUDE.md §72; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** seeded "never panics on mutated input" soaks (the existing `crate::testing` `Rng`/`mutate`/`cases` harness, scaled by `ORIGIN_MUTATION_SCALE`) for the untrusted-input parsers added this run: `acpi::srat_and_slit_mutations_never_panic` (SRAT and SLIT, 10 000 cases × 2 bases), `dns::mutations_never_panic` (`parse` and `read_name` over 20 000 mutated messages), and `originfs::mutations_never_panic` (4 000 mutated images through `Fs::open`, `entries`, `read_whole`, `read_file` and `resolve`). All parse paths use `.get`/checked arithmetic, so arbitrary bytes yield `Ok`/`Err`, never a panic.
- **Hardening found by the soak:** `originfs::Fs::read_whole` allocated `inode.size` bytes from the on-disk inode; a mutated (or malicious) inode with a huge `size` would drive an unbounded allocation (an abort). It now refuses a size beyond what v0 can address (12 direct + 512 single-indirect blocks, ~2 MiB) with `OutOfRange` before allocating. `read_file` was already bounded by the caller's buffer, and `entries` by the 524-block addressing limit.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** the three soaks pass at scale 1 and at `ORIGIN_MUTATION_SCALE=10` (≈340 000 parser cases); 211 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### Fixed-size bit allocator (CLAUDE.md §40 allocation bitmap, §29 resource allocation; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `bitmap` (library) is a dense bit allocator: `Bitmap::new(len)` holds `len` bits; `alloc` returns the lowest free bit (scanning 64-bit words, `(!word).trailing_zeros()` for the lowest clear bit of the first non-full word); `set`/`clear` return whether the bit changed (so a double-set or double-free is reported, not silently miscounted); `get` and `free` report state; an exact free counter is kept. Padding bits past `len` in the final word are permanently set, so they are never handed out. Pure, no `unsafe`; `alloc` for the word vector.
- **Why:** the OriginFS write path needs a free-space map (§40), and process-id / handle pools need an id allocator (§29); this is the shared primitive. Lowest-free allocation keeps ids and blocks dense and reproducible.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-08. Original code (CLAUDE.md §3); standard bitmap technique, no source used.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-08):** 4 `bitmap` tests — lowest-free allocation with reuse after a free; filling exactly `len` bits across a partial final word (every index once, no padding bit, then full); `set`/`get` tracking the free count and out-of-range no-ops; and a model-based test running 60 000 random `alloc`/`set`/`clear`/`get` operations against a `[bool; 200]` oracle (spanning three words with a partial last), asserting `alloc` returns the lowest free index and the free count matches after every op. 215 library tests in all; `cargo xtask check`. Host-only, so no boot proof (the oracle is the control).
- **Not done:** multi-bit (contiguous run) allocation for extents, a hint/cursor to avoid rescanning from 0, and a two-level summary for very large maps. Wiring into OriginFS's (future) write path and a pid/handle allocator.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

### ustar (tar) archive reader (CLAUDE.md §21 initial deployment, §46 package parsing; 2026-11-08)

- **What:** `ustar` (library) is a read-only POSIX tar reader. `Reader::next_entry` / `parse` walk the 512-byte header+data records, verifying the `ustar` magic and the header checksum, parsing the octal size, joining the `prefix`/`name` fields, and yielding each `Entry { name, size, typeflag, data }` with a borrowed data slice; the archive ends at a zero block.
