Each detail now reads only the reports it is about, the summary comes after them, and all seven were run again on that code with the results above.

A forced schedule: the client waits for `peer_closed` on the refused connection's own end straight after the connect, so the directory has always run first. With the order the proof had, the write that followed is `peer_closed` and the boot fails with that same line. The client now writes on that end before it passes the other one; with the wait still in place the boot passes, 56 of 56. The wait is not in the committed script. The script was wrong, not the kernel: the directory closes a refused end without waiting, and a write to a channel whose other end is closed is `peer_closed`.
- **Cost:** the exchange as QEMU figures with no budget (rule 21): from the first launch until all three processes had ended, the kernel's waits for their ends included, so an upper bound on thirteen messages between three processes, with three launches. The eight logs that survive the merge commit's boot-matrix (QEMU's software CPU on an M1 Max) show 5,329 to 5,848 µs in seven and 12,259 µs in one, a console machine whose SPCR names registers in RAM; single boots during development took 4,693 to 12,364 µs. How much of it is the messages and how much the launches and the waits was not measured. ADR-0011 N8's round-trip figure belongs to the first service domain (step 4), on the declared hardware.
- **Known limits:** how a launcher fills a directory and how a provider receives connections are not decided (D11): the proof's arrangement is used by nothing else. The ring-3 directory and service are scripts until step 4 brings Rust to ring 3, so the lookup is proven on the host. Fairness between a directory's clients and what a client checks a service's identity against (S9) are open. `launch::place` leaves the pages it mapped before a failing `map_page` in the child until the child is dropped: harmless while only kernel code launches, to be documented or cleaned up when the Loader Service, which may retry, calls it. Nothing ran on physical hardware.

## Memory objects (ADR-0011 N14 step 3, task S3-5b; 2026-11-10)

- **What:** the owner's decisions C6–C8 (ADR-0005 Amendment 4, accepted 2026-11-09, decision sheet items 61–63) and the five shapes they left open, D1–D5 (Amendment 5, accepted 2026-11-10, items 101–105), on S3-5a's address spaces. **ABI change:** `user-abi` goes from 0.4 to 0.5; `origin.kernel`'s lock records 0.5, and 0.0 to 0.4 are unchanged.
  - **Research and threats first:** `docs/research/2026-11-10-memory-objects.md` (§16: Fuchsia's `zx_vmo_create`, `zx_vmar_map` and `zx_vmar_protect`, Linux's `mmap(2)` page and its `max_map_count` entry, and Amit, Tai and Wei on shootdowns; documentation and abstracts only), then the threat rows M1–M15 in `docs/engineering/THREAT_MODEL_SYSCALLS.md`, written before the code and given their status once the proof, its controls and the host tests ran. The shapes C6–C8 left open went to the owner as one list, and no system-call code or lock change was committed before the answer.
  - **Interface** (`sdk/interfaces/origin.kernel.oidl`, 0.5): `memory_object_create = 11 (request: object_request) -> object`, `memory_map = 12 (process, object, request: map_request) -> address`, `memory_unmap = 13 (process, address, length)` and `memory_protect = 14 (process, address, length, access)`; the `map_access` and `map_flags` bits, the sized `object_request` and `map_request`, and the constants `memory_object_rights` and `page_size`. `origin-abi` mirrors them; `framekernel/syscalls`' cross-check pairs them with the generated crate, and OIDL's differential test models the new calls' register checks.
  - **Rules** (`framekernel/src/mapping.rs`, host-tested): decoding a `map_request` in D5's order, whole pages, the user half with every sum checked, random placement in `[0x1000_0000_0000, 0x7000_0000_0000)`, a process's records of its whole mappings (`room` says why one more is refused: an ended process, then the limit), and the change budget, a generic cell rate priced at one unit per shootdown and per processor it may interrupt.
  - **Kernel** (`framekernel/src/memory_object.rs`): an object's frames are allocated and zeroed when it is made and charged to its creator's committed bytes (`process::Account`), refunded with the object's last reference; a mapping holds its object; every call needs `write` on the process handle it names; a fixed address never replaces a mapping (the records and the page tables both checked), and a random one is drawn from RDSEED or RDRAND, after the limit; unmap and protect are priced against the caller's budget before anything changes and refused with `should_wait` if it cannot pay, and what each change cost is charged afterwards; a stalled shootdown is `timed_out`, and only unmap can then be `no_memory` (D5). `process::MemoryLimits` gives nothing unless the creator says so; a process's mappings close before it counts as ended.
  - **The proof** (`framekernel/src/ipc_proof/memory_objects.rs`): ring-3 programs scripted through the system calls, and the kernel's own calls for the costs; see the boot lines below. Each detail reads only the reports it is about, and one line checks every other call and how each program ended. The memory calls' hostile corpus (`ipc_proof.rs`, `hostile_memory`) runs in a process of its own: the first corpus already fills a process's report log of 128 values.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code agent (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-10, in worktree `sad-lalande-b83a31`, branch `claude/s3-5b-memory-objects`, from the step-3 batch at 490c4d0 with `land/s3-part2` (02d9ba8, Amendment 5) merged in. Original code, from ADR-0004, ADR-0005, `docs/spec/OIDL.md` and the ledger.

- **Test evidence:** `cargo xtask check` and `cargo xtask boot-matrix` pass on the code tip (1fd5d6a), each on the first attempt, every step taking its turn on the machine: 1,210 host tests; Loom's 39 models with all 60 controls caught; the no-panic, dependency, interface and unsafe gates; 18 kernel boots in the matrix (Intel VT-d and AMD-Vi with 1, 2 and 4 processors, the x2APIC, bridge, legacy-free and console machines), each with 57 of 57 proofs and the 49 hostile memory calls returning their statuses. Each code commit passed on its own tree, first time: rustfmt; clippy (`-D warnings`, kernel target and host); the host tests of the kernel library, `origin-abi` and `origin-syscalls`; the interface and unsafe gates and xtask's tests; OIDL's clippy and tests and the directory crate where the definition changed; and a QEMU boot where the kernel changed (56 of 56 at the interface commit, 57 of 57 from the proof on).
  - Boot lines: two processes share an object by passing its handle, and each reads what the other wrote; a protect to read-only refuses an increase, and the next write faults at the mapping; after an unmap, the next read faults there; a fixed address over a mapping is refused, and the mapping keeps what was written to it; execute is refused; two random placements are apart, page-aligned and in their region; closing the handle leaves the mapping working; the quota refuses an object past its bound and takes one again once an object is closed, a closed object still mapped keeps its charge, and a third mapping past the limit of two is refused; once the process has ended its account owes nothing; mapping into another process needs `write` on its handle, and with it the two share the frame; unmapping there needs it too, and the other's next read faults; a hostile unmap loop is refused with `should_wait` once its budget (8 units, 2 a second) is spent, with its mapping still there, and served again once the budget has refilled; every other call returned what its script says, and each program ended as it should; a thread reading a shared object on another processor faults at the page once it is unmapped from its space, and the object stays mapped in its creator's; the leak check holds.

  - Host: `mapping`'s tests (each malformed request refused for its own reason; the rights a mapping needs; the last user page and nothing past it; a random place fits its region; prices per round and per processor; the budget's burst, rate and charges, saturating; whole, bounded, never overlapping records; `room`'s order).
- **Negative controls** (each on a scratch copy of the code tip, in a turn of its own on the machine, with the copy's xtask printing every line; every one fails the boot, and the baseline passes 57 of 57):
  1. A mapping gets fresh frames, not the object's: `each reads what the other wrote: false`, and the three other details that read a word written through another mapping (the mapping a refused fixed address leaves, the mapping left after the close, the frame shared with another process). Every call still returns what its script says.
  2. Protect changes the record but not the page tables: `protect to read-only ... makes a write fault at the mapping: false`, and the summary line (A exits instead of faulting).
  3. Unmap removes the record but leaves the pages mapped, read-only: `unmap makes a read fault there: false`, `the other's next read faults: false`, the shared object's reader `faulted at the page: false`, the hostile loop's lines (its next map finds the page still there) and the summary line.
  4. A fixed address replaces what is there: `a fixed address over a mapping is refused ...: false`, the summary line, and the corpus's `over it`.
  5. Execute, and write with execute, are taken as read and read-write: `execute is refused: false`, the summary line, and the corpus's `write and execute -> OK` and `execute -> OK`.
  6. No entropy, so every placement draws the same place: `two random placements are apart ...: false`; Q's second random mapping collides too (`a third mapping ... refused: false`), and the summary line.
  7. Closing a memory object's handle releases its memory under the live mappings (its frames scrubbed): `closing the handle leaves the mapping working: false`, and nothing else.
  8. No quota on committed memory: `... a third mapping past the limit of two is refused: false` (Q's quota line), the summary line, and the corpus's `past the quota`.
  9. A process's mappings are not released when it ends: `once the process has ended its account owes nothing: false`, and nothing else.
  10. Map into a process without `write` on its handle: `with it the two share the frame: false`, the summary line, and the corpus's `a process handle without WRITE -> OK`.
  11. Unmap in a process without `write` on its handle: `unmapping there needs it too ...: false`, the summary line, and the corpus's `unmap without WRITE -> OK`.
  12. The budget is never enforced: `refused with should_wait ...: false` and `served again ...: false` (the unmap the loop should have been refused succeeds), and the summary line.
  13. A refused unmap has already removed the pages: `refused ..., changing nothing: false` (H faults reading its page), `served again: false`, and the summary line.
  14. The budget never refills (its clock stands still): `it is served again once the budget refills: false`, and the summary line.
  15. Each mapped page leaks a reference to its frame: the leak line (heap and frames not back); the scheduler's own heap check then fails too, and the boot stops there.
  16. Protect may add access: `protect to read-only refuses an increase ...: false`, the summary line, and the corpus's `protect back to writable -> OK`.
  17. Map ignores the read and write rights of the object's handle: the corpus's `write without WRITE -> OK`; the proof's own programs held every right, so no proof line turned. The review's fixes, below, gave the proof a line for it.

  A first run of controls 1–15 on the first version of the proof failed the boot each time, but its details were partly computed from whole scripts: control 11 failed the line through "with it the two share the frame" and left "unmapping there needs it too" printing true. Each detail now reads only its own reports, the summary line checks the rest, and all eighteen were run on the final code with the results above.
- **Cost:** QEMU figures with no budget (rule 21), from the 18 boots of the tip's boot matrix (QEMU's software CPU on an M1 Max). The kernel's own map, protect and unmap of 16 pages, in a space no processor holds: map 72–112 µs (median 84), protect 64–100 µs (median 77), unmap 45–69 µs (median 57). The unmap of a shared object's page from a space a thread is reading it in: 39 and 42 µs on the one-processor machines, where no other processor holds the space; 37–128 µs with 2 to 4 processors in 15 boots; and 1,266 µs once, on the console machine whose SPCR names COM1 itself (2 processors). That one figure was looked into on 2026-11-11 and did not come back. On the review branch's code (`4062c6b`; `cded704` after it changes documents only): 20 rounds, each one turn on the machine that boots that console machine, a plain machine with 2 processors and a plain one with 4, once each. All 60 boots passed. The same unmap took 26–65 µs on the console machine (median 35), 23–106 µs on the plain machine with 2 processors (median 30) and 24–95 µs on the one with 4 (median 45.5); over the 60, the median is 36.5 µs, nine in ten are under 85 µs and the longest is 106 µs. The host's one-minute load average, read as each boot ended, was 2.0–11.8 (median 4.1). Two rounds on the branch's earlier tip (`efae0ee`, six boots) read 26–78 µs and are not among the 60. A round before those is not counted at all: the scratch copy the rounds boot still ran a negative control's kernel, because its restore had copied the files' times with them and cargo saw nothing to build. The restore no longer copies times, and a round now stops unless the copy's code is the worktree's. So the 1,266 µs is one boot in 82 with 2 to 4 processors, and no cause was found. Under QEMU's software CPU each processor is a thread of the host, and this unmap waits for the other processor to acknowledge it, so a host that held that thread back for a millisecond would read like this; that is a guess, and no boot here shows it. The kernel's own three calls on this code, over the same 60 boots: map 28–56 µs (median 33.5), protect 45–105 µs (median 52), unmap 24–58 µs (median 28). The code is not the code measured above (for one, a mapping's pages are now entered by one call, where each page was looked up in the page tables and then entered by a call of its own) and the host's load was not the same either, so the two sets are not a comparison. Physical-hardware figures are step 4's, on the declared hardware.
- **Known limits:** demand commit, sealed objects and executable mappings (the Code Integrity Table) come later (C7); unmap and protect act only on whole mappings; `MAX_TABLES` (32 table frames a space) is not raised, so a process maps about seven objects at random; the budget's defaults for programs are the Loader Service's (step 4); per-initiator shootdowns, which would remove T16's shared turn, are open. QEMU cannot reach the map without hardware entropy (`not_supported`), a stalled shootdown (`timed_out`) or the `no_memory` that can follow it. The framework returns the same error for a space whose 32 table frames are used up and for no free frame, so both are `limit` where D4 would have the second `no_memory`; telling them apart is a framework change. Nothing ran on physical hardware.
- **Review:** by the coordinating AI session, by reading, 2026-11-10 (`docs/engineering/REVIEW_S3-5B_2026-11-10.md`). It had the author's report in hand, so it is not an independent review. No human has reviewed this code.
- **The review's finding D and its low observations**, on `claude/s3-5b-review-low` from `2248729`, one commit per change. Findings A, B and C are the framework's; the kernel's side of them is the entry after this one.
  - *Finding D, a mapping could outlive the call that could not report it* (`93c6b2a`): `memory_object::map` takes its caller and a `report`, and calls the report with the address while the mapping's record is still reserved, so no other call can change the mapping first. If the report fails, `withdraw` unmaps the pages without asking the budget, removes the record and drops the object, and the call returns the report's error. `memory_map`'s `address` has no `@also_on` (`docs/spec/OIDL.md` §4.4), so nothing is written on that path. What the take-back cost is charged to the caller afterwards (`settle`, with nothing paid beforehand). Threat row M16. Not chosen: asking the budget first, as before, which is the finding; and writing the address before the pages are entered, which would write a result on a map that then fails.
  - *One copy of the map path* (`0a347de`): `93c6b2a` took the report as a generic parameter, which gave the kernel three copies of `map`, two of them the proof's. The proof's cost line then timed a copy nothing had run before, and its map figure rose from 70–120 µs (the boots above, and some 40 control boots) to 234–252 µs in four boots; protect and unmap did not move. With the report a `dyn` there is one copy, the one the ring-3 programs have already run, and the figure is 48 µs in the tip's one boot so far (protect 62 µs, unmap 32 µs). That is read as QEMU's software CPU translating code on its first run; no boot timed a warmed copy of the generic version, so the reading rests on the figure's return alone.
  - *A busy mapping, and eight colliding draws* (no change in these commits): a change to a mapping another thread is changing returned `invalid_args`, and eight random places that all collide returned `limit`. D5 named neither case. Both went to the coordinator for the owner (CLAUDE.md §84), each with a recommendation. The owner answered on 2026-11-10 (items 155 and 156, a note on D5 in ADR-0005 Amendment 5): the first is `should_wait`, and the second stays `limit`. Both are in the entry after this one.
  - *A map racing another into the same space* (`2ac4d6a`): recorded as intended, in two comments. Nothing can be mapped between `reserve`'s look at the page tables and `map_pages`: a process's own pages are all mapped before it has a thread (`Process::map_page` needs the only reference to the space), and every later page is mapped under its mapping's reserved record, which `reserve` does not overlap. `map_pages`' catch-all `invalid_args` is not reached in this version. The framework call that maps a run wholly or not at all (finding B) has since removed the separate look and `map_pages` (`ed45075`, the entry after this one).
  - *Control 17 was caught by the corpus only* (`53fac8d`): B duplicates its handle twice, once without `write` and once without `read`, and asks for a writable mapping through the first and for a mapping through the second; both must be `access_denied`. The proof's second line gained "a handle without write maps nothing writable, and one without read maps nothing".
  - *A rate above 10⁹ units a second made every unit free* (`0875705`): `Budget::new` takes such a rate as 10⁹, so a unit costs at least a nanosecond and the burst always bounds what is spent at once. Bounded where the budget is made, not recorded as a step-4 requirement only: the bound then holds whatever the call that sets a rate does. That call may still prefer to refuse such a rate (threat row M8). Host test `no_rate_makes_a_unit_free`, for 10⁹, 10⁹ + 1 and `u32::MAX`.
  - *Evidence:* 2026-11-10, under QEMU's software CPU on an M1 Max; nothing ran on physical hardware. The tree of each of the five commits passes `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, clippy for the host, the kernel's target and xtask with warnings denied, and the kernel's 412 host tests. `53fac8d`'s tree and the tip's were each booted once (`kernel boot`, 2 processors): 57 of 57 proofs both times, in 65.8 s and 57.6 s, every line of the memory proof true and its leak line level (heap 197,168 bytes before and after). The first three commits were not booted one by one. `cargo xtask check` on the tip (`0a347de`) passed: 1,211 host tests in 43 suites, none failed, 8 ignored (one more than S3-5b's 1,210, the rate's test); all 39 Loom models passed and all 60 of their controls were caught; the unsafe gate found no `unsafe` outside the framework and 321 sites in it, and no commit here touches the framework; both interface gates found the generated files byte for byte.
  - *Negative controls,* each a change to a scratch copy of the tip's code, never committed; one `kernel boot` each, with xtask made to print every line of the proof. Each was run twice, on `53fac8d`'s code and on the tip's, with the same result:
    - 19. A map that cannot be reported is taken back through the priced unmap, as before the fix: `a map whose address cannot be written to its caller leaves no page and no record, though the caller's budget pays for nothing: false`, the charge beside it still true, and no other line; the boot is refused.
    - 20. The take-back is not charged: `what taking it back cost is charged, and the caller's next unmap must wait: false`, the detail before it still true, and no other line; the boot is refused.
    - 21 (host). `Budget::new` without the bound: `no_rate_makes_a_unit_free` fails with `1000000001: above the burst`; with the bound it passes.
    - 17 again. Map ignores the read and write rights of the object's handle: the corpus's `write without WRITE -> OK` as before, and now the proof's `a handle without write maps nothing writable, and one without read maps nothing: false`. `two random placements are apart, page-aligned and in their region: false` and the summary line turn with it: the two mappings that should have been refused use up B's limit of four, so B's later random map is refused.
  - *What no boot shows:* the system call's own write of the address failing. Ring 3 cannot make it fail at will: the pointer is checked against the caller's page tables first, and the page must go or become read-only between that check and the write. The proof drives `memory_object::map`, the call `memory_map` makes, with a report that fails.
  - *`unsafe`:* none added. Both modules still forbid it, and the gate's count is unchanged.
- **The kernel's side of the review's findings A, B and C, and the owner's items 155 and 156**, on `claude/s3-5b-review-low` after two merges of `land/s3-part2`: `da404f3` (of `cdf4ed9`: the framework's fixes, merge `759d319`) and `d585c9a` (of `010cf91`: the owner's answers, a note on D5 in ADR-0005 Amendment 5). One commit per change. The coordinating session set the five items and passed on the owner's two answers; the owner's item 142 is the statuses.
  - *A mapping's pages are entered by one call* (`1e9fd61`): `put` hands `UserSpace::map_shared_run` the object's frames for the request (`MemoryObject::run`, their places from `mapping::frames`) in place of a loop over its pages. A refused run was never entered, so the unmap that cleaned up after a page failed part-way is gone, and with it a shootdown no budget had agreed to (finding B). Host test `a_request_maps_its_own_pages_of_the_object`.
  - *Statuses* (`b956c83`): what the space refused a run for is read once (`refused`, into `mapping::Refused`), and each cause has its status (`Refused::status`). The space's bound on page tables is `limit`; no free frame, or no room in the kernel's heap, is `no_memory` (D4, the owner's item 142); a run over a mapped page is `invalid_args` at a fixed address and another draw at a random one. `origin.kernel` already declares `limit` and `no_memory` for `memory_map`, so the interface is unchanged. Host test `a_refused_run_has_the_status_of_what_refused_it`.
  - *No look at the page tables before a map* (`ed45075`): by reading, every user page of a space enters it through `UserSpace::map_page` (the program's code, data and stack by `Process::map_page`; the start record in `launch.rs`) or through `UserSpace::map_shared_run`, and both write the space's own records. The one other `map_user` (`frame/src/vm.rs`) writes the kernel's own space. So the space's refusal covers what `reserve`'s look at the page tables covered, with no time between a look and the map, and the look is removed. A random place over a page of the program's own is still drawn again; the bound and a want of memory end the call at once.
  - *Finding A needed no kernel change:* the arms of `unmap`, `protect` and `withdraw` for `ChangeError::Stalled` already removed the record, or gave it its new permissions, and returned `timed_out`. With the framework's fix every page then has its final entry, so `timed_out` means what D5 says (threat row M14). The two arms no call reaches were given the framework's own words: it refuses only before anything changes (comments only, in `ed45075`).
  - *The order this gives:* D5 puts the quotas before the placement, and the bound on page tables is not one of D4's quotas, which a process's creator sets; D5 does not name its place. As built, a fixed run over a mapped page, in a space that is also at its bound of page tables, is `invalid_args`: the space looks at its records before it makes tables, so a run refused for a mapped page makes none. Told to the coordinating session.
  - *The proof's line for runs* (`da78c26`): "a fixed run over a page of the program's own is refused whole, and the page stays; a mapping of an object's later pages maps those pages' frames; a run past the space's page tables is refused with limit and leaves no page and no record". It is made through `memory_object::map`, the call `memory_map` makes, in processes the proof builds and never runs: no ring-3 program of the proof has a page of its own where a run could go, and the bound is reached by mappings 2 MiB apart, a page table each, of which the proof tries up to 64. The frames are read from the space's own records (`Process::frame_of`); the later pages' frames are compared with a mapping of the whole object, so the object needs no accessor for the proof. ADR-0013's row and xtask's marker name the line.
  - *A mapping in another call's hands waits* (`2b41e3c`; the owner's item 155): `Mappings::begin` now finds a mapping whether or not it is busy, and for a busy one returns `should_wait` and takes nothing. Before, a busy mapping was not found, and the call said `invalid_args`: no such mapping. Busy is a mapping whose map has not written its address yet, or one an unmap or a protect holds. `memory_unmap` and `memory_protect` ask for the mapping before they price the change, so the refusal spends nothing; `memory_protect` asks before it compares the access with what the mapping allows, which is not settled while another call changes it. A range that is not exactly one mapping is still `invalid_args`. Host test `a_mapping_another_call_is_changing_says_wait`; two older assertions that expected `invalid_args` for a busy mapping now expect `should_wait`.
  - *Its line in the proof* (`a160f41`): "an unmap and a protect of a mapping whose map has not returned yet are told to wait (should_wait); so are those of a mapping another change holds; the refusals changed nothing and spent nothing". It needs no second thread: a map's report runs while the mapping's record is still reserved, and the proof takes the record with `begin`, as a change takes it. The process's budget holds one unit and gains one a second. One unit is what unmapping its one page costs in a space no processor holds, so had a refusal spent anything, the unmap that ends the part would be told to wait. ADR-0013's row and xtask's marker name the line.

## The Framekernel framework crate and its gate (ADR-0011 N6, N13, N14 step 1; 2026-11-09)

- **What:** the privileged framework the kernel is built on, and the gate that keeps it the only place with `unsafe`:
  - `framekernel/frame/` (package `origin-frame`, plus its lock package `origin-sync`, kept separate only because Loom builds it alone) holds every `unsafe` operation that has moved so far. Everything under `framekernel/` that is not on the allowlist is `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, and nothing the framework depends on is above it.
  - The gate (`developer-tools/xtask/src/unsafety.rs`, part of `cargo xtask check`, or `cargo xtask unsafe-gate` alone): `unsafe` tokens or `global_asm!` outside `framekernel/frame/` fail, except in the files on `developer-tools/xtask/unsafe-allowlist.txt` at exactly their count; the list can only shrink, which is checked against its own git history; a module off the list must carry `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; `cargo tree` proves the kernel's dependency layers (`LAYERS` in the gate). Seven negative controls fail it (an unsafe in an unlisted file; a file added to the list; a raised count; a count that fell without the list being lowered; `forbid` removed; a framework dependency outside its layer; a kernel crate naming the lock package directly).
  - **Moved into the framework:** the CPU core (`cpu.rs`: GDT/TSS/IDT, exception and trap entry, MSRs, FPU, probes, user copy; `timer.rs`; `vm.rs`; `tlb.rs`'s mechanism; `memory.rs`; `phys.rs`), with the pure code they depend on (`apic`, `descriptors`, `features`, `clock`, `frames`, `heap`, `unwind`, `usercopy`), moved down rather than left above it. New: `addr` (`PhysAddr`, `Iova`), `mmio::MmioRegion`, `dma::{DmaFrame, DmaPage}`, `port` (claimed `PortRange`, `Cmos`), `stack` (`GuardedStack`, `FpuArea`, `GuardablePage`, first frames), `userspace::UserSpace`, `objref::ObjectRef`, `irq` (per-vector device interrupt registration), `trap` (the scheduler, system-call and report upcalls), `once::SetOnce`, `monotonic`.
  - **Interrupt registration:** `cpu::dispatch` names no layer above it: device interrupts go through `irq::register`/`irq::run`, the scheduler, the system-call layer and the exception report through `trap::Hooks`, installed once at boot. The trap entry resumes a frame only if it saved that frame itself or the scheduler's thread creation built it (`stack::GuardedStack::publish_first_frame`): a wrong answer from the scheduler above is refused with a panic instead of being loaded. A stack is freed only when no processor is on it and no saved frame lies on it (`cpu::stack_in_use`), and a user address space only when no processor has it loaded: a safe caller that drops one too early leaks memory rather than leaving a processor on freed memory.
  - **The eight memory-unsafe safe functions of the review:** `vm::map_mmio` returns a typed region (refusing RAM from the first call, and any range overlapping one already handed out); `vm::unmap` is an `unsafe fn` (the AP trampoline's mappings are returned through `IdentityMapping::unmap`); `make_guard`/`make_guards`/`unguard` are framework-internal (`GuardedStack`, `GuardablePage`, `cpu::protect_interrupt_stacks`); `Process::map` and the rest of a process's memory are `UserSpace` (typed `UserFrame`, `&mut self` to change it, copies checked against its own tables with faults recovered, refused unless it is the space loaded on this processor); `iommu::map` accepts only a `DmaFrame`; `storage::dma_read`/`dma_write` are gone (`DmaPage::copy_out`/`copy_in`); `memory::free_frame` takes an `OwnedFrame` (`allocate_frame` returns one, not `Copy`, so no double free); `cpu::set_kernel_stack` takes a `&GuardedStack`. Also: `vm::install` and `memory::reclaim_loader_memory` are `unsafe fn`, `phys::init` and `memory::init` are first-call-wins, and `vm::firmware_bytes` refuses anything but firmware memory.
  - **Migrated:** `storage`, `virtionet`, `block`, `dma`, `pcie`, `firmware`, `i8042`, `irq`, `time`, `console`, `sched`, `tlb`, `process`, `ipc`, `syscall`, `user`, `wait` are `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

- **Not yet migrated (the allowlist):** `smp.rs` (22: the AP trampoline's `global_asm!`, its data-page writes, INIT and start-up IPIs, the AP entry), `main.rs` (31: `_start`, `kernel_main`, `read_boot_info`, the frame-allocator and page-table bring-up and their proofs), `iommu.rs` (8) and `iommu/amd.rs` (3) (remapping structures and their cache flushes; N12 keeps IOMMU programming privileged, so these two and their pure dependencies, `vtd`, `amdvi`, `dmar`, `ivrs`, `pci`, are the next move into the framework) and `ipc_proof.rs` (3: the ring-3 test programs' `global_asm!`). `unsafe` remaining outside the framework: 67 sites in 5 files; `cargo xtask unsafe-gate` prints it.
- **How the safe APIs were checked for soundness:** by reading each against the rule "no safe caller can break memory safety through it, whatever it passes, in whatever order, from whichever processor", with these results, and by the tests named below; this is the author's reasoning, not an independent review. Every type's module documentation states its argument.
  - *Device memory* (`MmioRegion`, `framebuffer_region`): constructed only over mapped uncached device ranges refused if RAM; accessors bounds-checked and aligned (host-tested over a buffer); a device writing them concurrently is not a data race because they are volatile accesses to non-Rust memory. Registers have one owner per physical range (`Claims`), so a device's lying BAR cannot reach the IOMMU or ECAM once those are claimed at boot.
  - *DMA pages* (`DmaFrame`): zeroed kernel pages kept for ever; only volatile accessors, no reference ever covers one; `iommu::map` accepts only these. Their `Copy` handle cannot be freed.
  - *Frames, stacks, user spaces, FPU areas, objects*: linear or owned types with no way to fabricate one; the dangling-resource cases (`GuardedStack`, `UserSpace`) are resolved by `Drop` checking the framework's own records and leaking on doubt (a safe failure).
  - *Interrupt and scheduler boundary*: the only frames the trap entry can resume are the ones it recorded (`SAVED_FRAMES`), per processor, consumed on resume; a thread exiting is never recorded; `cpu::record_saved_frame` is crate-private. The hooks are safe functions: the framework assumes nothing about their logic except that they return some frame, which it checks.
  - *Ports*: claims are exclusive and exclude the system's ports (legacy DMA, PIC, PIT, CMOS, PCI configuration); the reserved list is enforced by `claim` (host-tested). `Cmos` is one handle.
  - *User copies*: `UserSpace::copy_in`/`copy_out` check the range against this space's own tables and refuse unless the space is loaded here; a racing unmap by another thread is recovered as a fault at the copy instruction.
  - Known limits of this reasoning, stated: `probe_read` (one fault-tolerant byte read of non-device memory) is a racy read in the abstract machine if a writer races it, accepted as a volatile-style hardware read used only by proofs; a device that misbehaves within its own IOMMU domain remains the IOMMU's concern, not the framework's; on a platform with no IOMMU, a device can DMA anywhere, as owner decision 9 records. The saved-frame table is per processor and sized from the run queue (at most 16 contexts on a processor, sleeping and blocked ones included, against 32 slots), which holds today because threads do not migrate and nothing removes a thread that is not running: load balancing (§26) and killing a blocked thread will each need a framework call to move or forget a frame, and until then a frame from another processor is refused with a panic, a safe failure. Each switch makes two scans of that table with locked compare-exchanges, at most one per thread on the processor; no benchmark was run on it (§53, §66).

Deviation, recorded: the locks are a separate package inside the framework's directory, because the Loom scratch workspace builds that package alone; the framework re-exports them and the gate lets no other kernel crate name them directly. N12's closed list is kept: the AP trampoline, IOMMU programming and early boot are privileged, and still partly outside the framework at this commit (the allowlist).
- **Dependencies:** none new. Host tools `std` only. The framework's dependency layers are `origin-abi`, `origin-boot-info`, `origin-paging`, `origin-sync` and `origin-version`.
- **Toolchain:** Rust 1.99.1 (stable, edition 2024), `cargo xtask check`, QEMU 11.1.3 (TCG) + OVMF.
- **Test evidence:** on the final tree (8552796 and the records on it), with Rust 1.99.1 and QEMU 11.1.3 (TCG) + OVMF, host load average about 4: `cargo xtask check` passes (989 passed, 0 failed, 6 ignored; Loom: 26 models, 35 negative controls caught; the gate's seven negative controls above); `cargo xtask boot-matrix` passed in full on its first attempt: both IOMMUs at 1, 2 and 4 processors, `boot-x2apic` under both CPU models, `boot-bridge` with both IOMMUs, and the 8 `boot-console` scenarios. Those boots exercise the migrated code: NVMe and virtio-net over typed registers and DMA pages, the IOMMU proofs, the I/O APIC routing proofs, AP start-up, preemption, FPU state, the TLB proof, ring-3 processes and IPC, and the leak checks at the end of each proof. No test or boot-proof bound changed; the TLB proof's touching loop now reads through `cpu::probe_read` (the same byte load, fault-tolerant) instead of a raw volatile read. **Not proven:** nothing here ran on physical hardware (rule 30). The soundness arguments are the author's, not independently reviewed. ADR-0011's S8 asks for Loom and Kani where they apply to the framework's safe APIs: not done yet for the new types (`SetOnce`, the saved-frame table); `SetOnce` has a threaded host test, `MmioRegion` and the port claims host tests. The framework crate is outside the no-panic check, like the kernel library before it: `cpu::resume` panics on a frame the kernel never saved, a kernel bug it must not continue past.

## The rest of the `unsafe` migration: no `unsafe` left outside the framework (ADR-0011 N6, N12, N13, N14 step 1 finished; 2026-11-09)

- **What:** the five files the entry above left on the allowlist are gone from it, and the allowlist with them. No file under `framekernel/` (or the leaf crates the kernel links) outside `framekernel/frame/` holds an `unsafe` token or a `global_asm!`, and `framekernel`'s crate root is `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, which the compiler enforces for every module above the framework. `cargo xtask check` fails on any `unsafe` outside `framekernel/frame/`; `developer-tools/xtask/unsafe-allowlist.txt`, its ratchet and `xtask unsafe-list` are removed, since nothing is left for them to count.

  | File | Before this entry | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | `framekernel/src/main.rs` (now `kernel.rs`) | 31 | 0 |
  | `framekernel/src/smp.rs` | 22 | 0 (moved) |
  | `framekernel/src/iommu.rs` | 8 | 0 (moved) |
  | `framekernel/src/iommu/amd.rs` | 3 | 0 (moved) |
  | `framekernel/src/ipc_proof.rs` | 3 | 0 |
  | **Total outside the framework** | **67** | **0** |

  Across both entries: 351 sites in 23 files to 0. `framekernel/frame/` holds 300 (237 before this entry).
- **How each file went:**
  - `ipc_proof.rs`: the ring-3 programs' assembly is `origin_frame::proof_programs`; safe code can only read their bytes.
  - `iommu.rs`, `iommu/amd.rs`: the VT-d and AMD-Vi drivers are `origin_frame::iommu` (N12: IOMMU programming is privileged), taking their pure table and encoding modules (`acpi`, `amdvi`, `bitmap`, `dmar`, `ivrs`, `pci`, `vtd`) and `firmware` down with them as `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` modules, re-exported from `framekernel` under their old names. Configuration space stays with the PCIe layer above; `iommu::init` takes a function that reads it.
  - `smp.rs`: the AP trampoline, its data page, INIT and start-up IPIs and the AP entry are `origin_frame::smp` (N12), with `apstart`, `cpumap` and `topology` moved down the same way. Each AP goes on to a function the layers above name, so the framework never names the scheduler.
  - `main.rs`: the boot flow is `framekernel/src/kernel.rs`, ordinary safe code in the library, and the library now holds the whole kernel above the framework (its kernel-only modules are `cfg(target_os = "none")`). `_start` is the kernel image's link root, `framekernel/frame/entry/main.rs`, a target of the `framekernel` package whose source sits in the framework's directory: it holds three `unsafe` sites, and has to be a binary that links the kernel above the framework, so it cannot be part of `origin-frame` itself. Early boot's privileged steps (the boot info, the CPU's tables, SIMD, the frame allocator, the kernel's page tables, the heap, SMEP/SMAP and their proofs, reclaiming the loader's memory) are `origin_frame::early` (N12), with `boot` moved down.
- **Soundness of the new safe interfaces:** by reading each against the rule "no safe caller can break memory safety through it, whatever it passes, in whatever order, from whichever processor". This is the author's reasoning, not an independent review.
  - *Early boot (`early::Early`):* one exists per boot. `Entry` has a private field and no constructor: it is only ever the loader's RDI, which `_start` passes straight through (`repr(transparent)`, `sysv64`); neither type is `Send`. Each step runs once and does nothing before the steps it needs have run, and nothing the caller passes is trusted: boot data is read and validated once inside the framework, `enable_simd` gathers CPUID itself (a forged `Cpuid` could undersize the FPU area), and the allocator and page tables never leave framework hands. So `phys::init` and `memory::init` are now framework-internal, and `KernelTables` is opaque. `reclaim_loader_memory` needs an `smp::Online`, which only `smp::start` makes.
  - *Interrupts and the IDT:* `cpu::enable_interrupts`, `idle`, `idle_disabling`, `interrupt_window` and `breakpoint` do nothing until `cpu::init` has loaded the kernel's IDT, and `timer::init` refuses before then, so no interrupt can reach the firmware's handlers. Without that, a safe caller could have made one arrive before the kernel owned the vectors.
  - *AP start-up (`smp::start`):* runs once, only on the boot processor, and takes the processors from the firmware's MADT, the memory map from the validated boot data and the delays from a TSC rate the framework measured itself (`timer::calibrated_tsc_hz`, first measurement stands): no argument can aim INIT at a running processor or shorten the wait before the trampoline's data page is rewritten. A second call starts nothing. `cpu::assign`, the interrupt-stack guards and the identity mappings are now framework-internal.
  - *IOMMU (`iommu`):* every remapping structure is private, a domain's tables map only `DmaFrame`s (kept for ever, and never a Rust object), and `init` runs once. What the PCIe layer's configuration reader answers decides only which unit and requester an attachment names, never what memory a domain can reach. A wrong interrupt route is a logic error of its caller: it can only deliver a vector that has a gate.
  - *Proof programs:* their bytes are in the read-only image, so a `&'static [u8]` of them is sound.
- **Behaviour added:** the boot prints and the boot test requires `origin-kernel: boot steps: out of turn refused true; a second run refused true`, a proof run on the machine: before any boot step has run, `start_heap`, `prove_user_isolation`, `build_kernel_tables` and `timer::init` refuse; after the boot, `smp::start`, `iommu::init`, `init_memory`, `build_kernel_tables`, `start_heap`, `prove_user_isolation`, `reclaim_loader_memory` and `enable_simd` change nothing on a second call. `: boot steps failed` is a failure marker.

- **Architecture decisions:** ADR-0011 N6, N12, N13, N14 step 1. Deviation, recorded: the image's link root is a second crate holding `unsafe` (three sites, `_start`), because N6's framework crate cannot name the kernel above it; it sits under the same gate directory.
- **Dependencies:** none new; the framework's layers are unchanged.
- **Toolchain:** Rust 1.99.1 (stable, edition 2024), QEMU 11.1.3 (TCG) + OVMF.
- **Test evidence:** on the tree at 25afabe (the records are committed on it and touch only `docs/`), with Rust 1.99.1 and QEMU 11.1.3 (TCG) + OVMF, host load average 5 to 7: `cargo xtask check` passes (985 passed, 0 failed, 6 ignored; 5 tests of the removed allowlist mechanism went and 1 test of the simplified gate came; Loom: 26 models, 35 negative controls caught); `cargo xtask boot-matrix` passed in full: both IOMMUs at 1, 2 and 4 processors, `boot-x2apic` under both CPU models, `boot-bridge` with both IOMMUs, and the 8 `boot-console` scenarios. No test or boot-proof bound changed: the backtrace marker's exact 4 frames still hold because `_start` calls `kernel_main` directly, and the new boot-steps line is a required marker that 17 boots of the matrix printed. Negative controls, each applied to a clean tree and undone: an `unsafe` block and a `global_asm!` in kernel modules, and `forbid(unsafe_code)` removed from the crate root, each fail the gate; an `unsafe impl` in a pure module and an `unsafe fn` in `origin-abi` and in `origin-paging` stop the build before the gate runs (those crates forbid `unsafe_code`, and xtask links them); a kernel crate naming the lock package and a framework dependency outside its layer fail the dependency check; the compiler alone refuses an `unsafe` block in a kernel module. **Not proven:** nothing here ran on physical hardware (rule 30). ## AMD-Vi checked against AMD 48882 Rev 3.11, and DMA made coherent under both IOMMUs (2026-11-09)

- **What:** every AMD-Vi encoding, the IVRS parser and the AMD IOMMU bring-up and runtime sequence compared with the specification, and the findings fixed, in `framekernel/frame/src/amdvi.rs`, `ivrs.rs`, `iommu/amd.rs` and `iommu.rs` (in the framework crate since ADR-0011 N14 step 1); the VT-d counterpart of one finding fixed in `vtd.rs` and `iommu.rs` there. The full list, with what was found and not changed, is the AMD-Vi research ledger's §7; the VT-d row is in its ledger's check table.
  - DMA is coherent: AMD-Vi leaves set FC (bit 60); VT-d leaves set SNP (bit 11) where `ECAP.SC` is reported.
  - Enabling the AMD IOMMU keeps the Control bits the firmware owns (the SMI filter, BlkStopMrkEn), and turning it off leaves them too.
  - Every AMD IOMMU is probed before any is enabled, and all use one IRTE size; an IOMMU is refused for HATDis, a capability revision above 1 (QEMU 11.1 reports 0), or a capability block holding another register base.
  - The register range kept free of BARs is 512 KiB where the IOMMU has performance counters.
  - With NpCache, a map that makes table pages invalidates the whole domain with PDE set.
  - The command ring checks the head before each batch and refuses all commands after a halt.
  - Events are decoded by each code's own layout; interrupt faults are recognised in every address form; a blocked device's interrupt (an invalid device request, Type 101b) is recorded as a blocked interrupt.
  - The walker refuses special addresses, and its model refuses reserved bits.
- **Specifications:** AMD I/O Virtualization Technology (IOMMU) Specification, 48882 Rev 3.11 (April 2026), §2.1.3, §2.1.4.2, §2.1.5, §2.2.2–§2.2.5, §2.2.9, §2.3, §2.4, §2.5, §3.2, §3.4, chapter 5 (Tables 3, 10, 17, 18, 19, 21, 44, 56–68, 94, 98, 102, 103). Intel VT-d Architecture Specification Rev 5.20 (D51397-019), §3.7, §3.10, §9.8. Both read from the owner's copies in `specifications/` (outside version control), whose SHA-256s match the copies the code was first written from.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-09. Three review agents compared the code with the text; every finding was checked against the text again before a change. Original code from the specifications; no operating system's IOMMU code was read or copied (CLAUDE.md §3).
- **Test evidence:** host tests in `amdvi.rs` and `vtd.rs`, new or extended: the leaf's FC and the directory entries without it; the VT-d leaf's SNP with and without SC; reserved bits refused by the model; special addresses refused; every event code's fields. Eight negative controls, each a fix reverted in turn, each failing a test: FC dropped, FC in directory entries, reserved bits ignored, PR, I or the DomainID read for every code, SNP dropped, SNP whatever SC says. `cargo xtask check` passes (969 tests, 0 failures, 6 ignored), as do `boot-test` under Intel VT-d and under AMD-Vi (11 of 11 scenarios each) and `boot-matrix` (both IOMMUs at 1, 2 and 4 processors, then the sparse, bridge and console machines). Kernel-level changes QEMU cannot exercise have no boot-level negative control (below).
- **Not shown under QEMU:** QEMU 11.1's `amd-iommu` has no SMI filter, no performance counters, no HATDis, one IOMMU, and records address 0 for every event, so the SMI-filter, register-range, multi-IOMMU and interrupt-address changes are host-tested or reasoned from the text only, and need a hardware run (§74).
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

## Boot info 0.5: memory the firmware sets apart (UEFI 2.8 `EFI_MEMORY_SP`, 2.11 `EFI_MEMORY_HOT_PLUGGABLE`; 2026-11-09)

- **What:** the loader reads each memory descriptor's attribute as well as its type (`boot/uefi/src/memmap.rs`, `kind_for`). Conventional memory marked specific-purpose becomes the new region kind `SpecificPurpose` (14); conventional memory marked hot-pluggable becomes `HotPluggable` (15). Specific-purpose wins when both are set (`boot/info/src/lib.rs`). The kernel already allocated only from `Usable` and direct-mapped a fixed list of kinds, so it neither allocates from nor maps the new kinds. Boot info goes from 0.4 to 0.5 (`origin-version.toml`).
- **Specifications:** UEFI 2.11 §7.2, the memory attribute definitions. The two attribute values were checked against EDK II's `UefiSpec.h`, because uefi.org refuses automated reading of the 2.11 text: `docs/research/2026-11-09-uefi-2.8-to-2.11.md`.
- **Decision:** ADR-0002 B4, boot info 0.5, accepted by the owner on 2026-11-09 (decision sheet item 69, CLAUDE.md §84).
- **Author / date:** Claude Code (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-09. Original code; no firmware code was copied (CLAUDE.md §3).
- **Test evidence:** host tests cover `kind_for` on plain, specific-purpose, hot-pluggable and doubly marked conventional memory, and on other types; a whole translation in which marked ranges stay apart from the RAM around them and like ranges merge; the region kinds' round trip; and the kernel's usable-page count, which leaves out both new kinds. Negative control: translating by type only, as before, fails the new test. QEMU's firmware marks no memory either way, so no boot shows these kinds; the boot tests show the change leaves an ordinary boot unchanged.
- **Licensing:** MIT OR Apache-2.0.

## Address spaces that change while they run (ADR-0011 N14 step 3, task S3-5a; ADR-0004 H2; 2026-11-10)

- **What:** the framework part of N14 step 3's memory work, on `claude/s3-5a-address-spaces`, in `framekernel/frame/{src,sync/src}`, `framekernel/paging` and the kernel's address-space callers. No system call uses it yet: S3-5b adds them.
  - **The kernel half is fixed at boot (H2).** Every PML4 entry 256–511 gets a table before the kernel's tables go live (`AddressSpace::reserve_upper_half`, 256 more frames in the table pool); `vm::install` records the entries once; every space copies them. A kernel mapping made later, in a slot of its own, is found through tables every space already points at.
  - **Spaces that change under their own threads.** `UserSpace` holds `state` (tables and records, short, with interrupts off, never across a shootdown) and `editor` (one change at a time; whoever waits for it serves shootdown requests in its loop). `map_page`, `map_shared`, `unmap` and `protect` take `&self`.
  - **The shootdown protocol is `origin_sync::shootdown`**, generic over what it asks of a processor (`TlbHardware`), so the Loom models run the real code; `origin_frame::tlb` instantiates it. `Scope::Space(root)` asks only the processors with that root loaded or in the middle of leaving it (`switch_space`, with a `SeqCst` fence paired with the one in `shoot`).
  - **Deferred free.** `Shootdown::retire` runs the release only after every target has answered; on a timeout it leaks the value for good and reports `Stalled`. The reference count behind `ObjectRef` is `origin_sync::refcount::RefCount`, and a shared frame goes with its last reference, each mapping's being given up after its own shootdown (`SharedFrame`).
  - **Charging a hostile loop (for S3-5b).** Every change returns `Change { pages, shootdowns, interrupts }`, and `processors_loaded` says what the next change would interrupt.
- **Soundness of the new safe interfaces:** by reading each against the rule "no safe caller can break memory safety through it, whatever it passes, in whatever order, from whichever processor". The author's reasoning, not an independent review; the review of these APIs that the ledger advises is still to come.
  - *`UserSpace::map_page`, `map_shared`:* only pages of the user half. The frame is fresh and zeroed (or a referenced `SharedFrame`). A leaf that was not present is in no TLB.
  - *`UserSpace::unmap`:* the range is checked to be whole pages of the user half and is walked by what is mapped. A leaf is cleared under `state`, and its frame is released only by `retire`, after the shootdown. `state` is not held across it. On `Stalled` nothing is released.
  - *`UserSpace::protect`:* only the writable and no-execute bits of a 4 KiB user leaf change, from `Access`, which has no writable and executable value; a shootdown follows every change.
  - *`UserSpace::{read_u64, write_frame, translate, frame_of, copy_in, copy_out, check_user}`:* `state` is held around every direct-map access, and a frame cannot be freed while `state` leads to it. The user copies stay as they were: they run through this space's own page tables and recover from a fault, and a frame is not reused before this processor has answered.
  - *`UserSpace::{activate, without_probe_slot, shares_kernel_half, processors_loaded}`:* `activate` needs a live reference; `without_probe_slot` clears only slot 480, where nothing else is ever mapped, so loading it leaves the kernel mapped.
  - *`SharedFrame`:* `new` gives a zeroed frame; `claim` only a frame the allocator says is free, then zeroed; `Clone` and `Drop` are the count; the contents are reached only by volatile copies.
  - *`vm::KernelProbe`:* one at a time, a fresh frame, read-only, at one fixed page in a slot nothing else uses; `Drop` unmaps with a shootdown of every processor, then frees.
  - *`vm::{kernel_half, kernel_half_unchanged}`:* the entries are set once, then only read.
  - *`memory::{claim_frame, is_frame_free}`:* a frame is handed out only if the bitmap says it is free, so it still has one owner.
  - *`tlb::interrupts_taken`, `cpu::flush_tlb_non_global`:* a counter; a CR3 reload with its own value.
  - *`origin_sync::shootdown::Shootdown`, `refcount::RefCount`, `origin_paging`'s `reserve_upper_half`, `protect`, `same_kernel_half`:* safe code; the `Shootdown` instance is private to `origin_frame::tlb`.
- **The rule on locks during a shootdown:** `state` is never held across one. `editor` is, by design, because that keeps a later change from overtaking the TLBs: its waiters serve shootdown requests while they wait, so an interrupts-off waiter still answers. Whoever calls `unmap` or `protect` must hold no other lock that a processor may spin on with interrupts off; the compiler cannot check that, and breaking it times out as `Stalled` and leaks, which cannot corrupt memory.
- **`unsafe`:** the framework holds 318 sites by the gate's count, 312 at the branch point. The six new: `SharedFrame::write_u64` and `read_u64` (a volatile access to a frame a live reference keeps allocated, at an offset checked to be inside it), `KernelProbe`'s drop (`vm::unmap` of its own page, which nothing relies on: only `probe_read`, which recovers from a fault, was given the address), `cpu::flush_tlb_non_global` (a CR3 reload with its own value), and two in the Loom models (writes through Loom's checked cell, which is what the models test). Each has its `SAFETY:` argument; `undocumented_unsafe_blocks` is denied.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code agent (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-10. Original code; no third-party source was read or copied (§3).
- **Specifications:** ADR-0004 H2; ADR-0005 C7 (unmap and protect work on whole mappings; S3-5b's rule above this layer); Intel SDM Vol. 3A §4.10 as the code cites it, not re-read. The AMD64 manual was not read.
- **Dependencies:** none new. Loom stays in xtask's scratch workspace.
- **Toolchain:** Rust 1.99.1 (stable, edition 2024), QEMU 11.1.3 (TCG) + OVMF.
- **Test evidence:** at `e73a021`, with Rust 1.99.1 and QEMU 11.1.3 (TCG) + OVMF, host load averages 6 to 70 from other sessions' work:
  - `cargo xtask check` passes: 1,121 host tests, 0 failed, 7 ignored; the unsafe gate; Loom, all 37 models passed and all 56 negative controls were caught (83 model runs). The 8 new models are in `framekernel/frame/sync/src/models.rs` and the 17 new controls in `developer-tools/xtask/src/loom.rs`.
  - `cargo xtask boot-matrix` passes on its first attempt, host load 5 to 7: Intel VT-d and AMD-Vi at 1, 2 and 4 processors, the sparse x2APIC machine under both CPU models, the bridge machine, the legacy-free machine and the 9 console machines. All 18 of its full boots end `boot verdict: 53 of 53 proofs passed`.
  - Boot controls: ADR-0013 C18 to C23, each a temporary edit to the framework that fails the boot at an `address spaces` line, read from the serial log; two more controls run in every boot. Boots lost to the clock and timer proofs on the loaded host were retried and are not counted.
  - Costs, as QEMU TCG figures with no budget (CLAUDE.md rule 21): a map and unmap of one page with a thread of the space on another processor, 5 to 23 us a round over the matrix's 16 boots with more than one processor (6 us in most), one interrupt each; 4 to 5 us with the thread on the same processor, no interrupt. The kernel's tables take 274 frames where they took 21: the 253 kernel-half tables that did not exist yet, about 1 MiB.
- **Not proven:** physical hardware; past the Loom models' bounds; the spurious fault after a permission upgrade, which QEMU's TLB does not produce; a processor that does not answer, which no boot can arrange (host tests only); any limit on a hostile loop, which is S3-5b's.
- **Review:** an independent review by one AI reviewer, 2026-11-10 (`docs/engineering/REVIEW_S3-5A_2026-11-10.md`). No human has reviewed this code.
- **The review's findings, fixed** on `claude/s3-5a-review-fixes` from `1d352c4`, one commit per change; the threat model lists them by finding too (`THREAT_MODEL_ADDRESS_SPACES.md`, "Review findings"):
  - *Finding 1, the record could disagree with CR3* (`de67a7c`): `Shootdown::switch_space` writes `leaving`, `loaded` and CR3 with interrupts off, and reads the processor (`this_cpu`) and the root it leaves (`TlbHardware::current_root`) inside, so the scheduler cannot switch the processor between the record and the CR3 write. Modelled: `a_switch_and_the_scheduler_on_one_processor`, whose `IrqCpu` holds a lock for its interrupt flag; control `a_switch_that_can_be_interrupted`.
  - *Finding 2, an activation outside the scheduler is undone on resume* (`e00402b`): `UserSpace::activate` and `vm::activate_kernel_space` take a `trap::Switch`, which only the trap entry makes, for the scheduling hooks. The proofs read through another space with `UserSpace::probe_read`, a visit (`Shootdown::visit`) with interrupts off that is recorded in `visiting` and loads the old CR3 again before it ends. Modelled: `shootdown_and_a_processor_visiting_the_space`; control `a_visit_that_is_not_recorded`.
  - *Finding 3, a stalled `protect` is forgotten* (`f8eb5d5`): `origin_sync::shootdown::Confirmation` marks the space after a stall, and the next `unmap` or `protect` first flushes every processor in it (`Request::NonGlobal`); only a completed flush clears the mark (`UserSpace::change_unconfirmed`). Host tests.
  - *Finding 4, the kernel-half control did not fault on a real processor* (`40c8299`): the probe page is mapped not global, each read drops its translation first (`invlpg`), and the proof prints and checks the G bit. Boot control C24 (ADR-0013). Not yet run under KVM, where the finding was seen.
  - *Finding 5, W^X per mapping only* (`7187c2f`): `origin_frame::aliases::Aliases` counts a shared frame's writable and executable mappings in one atomic word, across every space; a mapping is counted before its entry is written and given back only after the shootdown that removes it completes. `map_shared` (now `Result<(), ChangeError>`) and `protect` refuse with `ChangeError::WriteAndExecute`, `protect` for its whole range before it changes anything. Boot proof `shared_frames_keep_w_xor_x`, boot control C25, four host tests.
  - *Finding 6, `edit()` waits without bound:* not changed; the review's resolution covers findings 1–5 and 7.
  - *Finding 7, gaps in the models* (`20d0259`, `53b7b32`, `67948b5`, with the models of findings 1 and 2): a processor outside the space fails its model the moment it is interrupted (`TlbWorld::with_bystander`); the models' clock ticks once per reading, so an initiator gives up after `PATIENCE` (64) polls with "a processor the shootdown asked never answered", which no correct execution reaches; controls `holds_reads_leaving_first` and `initiator_reads_answers_relaxed`. No control is counted as caught by Loom's branch limit any more, except `rwlock_readers_exclude_each_other`, which predates S3-5a.
  - *Housekeeping* (`090d069`, `51c6823`): `RefCount::retain` returns `TooMany` once the count has passed `isize::MAX`, and `ObjectRef::clone` panics, which halts and never unwinds: Arc's abort, moved to the caller because `origin-sync` cannot panic. `UserSpace::without_probe_slot` is crate-private, used only inside `KernelProbe::read_without_its_slot`. On ADR-0004 H2's table, a recommendation went to the coordinator; the accepted ADR is not edited here.
  - *Soundness of the safe interfaces these change:* `UserSpace::activate(&Switch)` and `vm::activate_kernel_space(&Switch)`: a `Switch` is made only by the trap entry, inside the scheduler's switch point with interrupts off, and is not `Send`; what it loads is what the scheduler resumes. `UserSpace::probe_read`: the visit cannot be interrupted, is in the record for as long as the processor can reach the space, and puts the old root back; the space is complete and alive for the borrow. `KernelProbe::read_without_its_slot`: the space lacking slot 480 is visited for one read and dropped before the call returns. `UserSpace::map_shared`, `protect`: as before, and never a frame writable through one mapping and executable through another while a processor can still use either. `RefCount::retain`: the count stops its caller before it can wrap.
  - *`unsafe`:* one new `unsafe fn`, `cpu::load_cr3`, the bare CR3 write that `cpu::write_cr3` used to hold, so that `switch_space` and `visit` can run it inside their interrupts-off sections; and one new call to it, in `tlb::visit`. Each has its `SAFETY:` argument. The gate counts 321 sites in the framework, 318 before.
  - *Test evidence of the fixes:* at `c189a5d`, with Rust 1.99.1 and QEMU 11.1.3 (TCG) + OVMF, host load averages 3 to 8:
    - `cargo xtask check` passes: 1,129 host tests, 0 failed, 7 ignored; the unsafe gate; Loom, all 39 models passed and all 60 negative controls were caught (88 model runs). Each new or changed control is caught with its property's own message: `a_switch_that_can_be_interrupted` ("the record names a space this processor has left"), `a_visit_that_is_not_recorded`, `holds_reads_leaving_first` and `initiator_reads_answers_relaxed` (a stale translation, and a causality violation in the deferred free), `shootdown_waiting_initiator_does_not_serve` ("a processor the shootdown asked never answered") and `a_space_request_asks_everyone` ("a shootdown for one space reached a processor in another").
    - `cargo xtask boot-test` passes, 11 of 11 scenarios, its kernel boot `53 of 53 proofs passed`; `cargo xtask boot-matrix` passes on its first attempt, and all 18 of its full boots end `boot verdict: 53 of 53 proofs passed`, each with the probe page not global and every W^X check true.
    - Boot controls C24 and C25 (ADR-0013) each failed the boot at an `address spaces` line on its first boot.
    - The two intermediate commits of finding 7 (`20d0259`, `53b7b32`) were run with their own shootdown and deferred-free models and their two changed controls: each model passed, and each control was caught as that commit's `loom.rs` expects. Every commit of the branch passes clippy for the kernel target and the host and the host tests of the crates it touches, built on its own.
    - Costs, as QEMU TCG figures with no budget (CLAUDE.md rule 21): a map and unmap of one page with a thread of the space on another processor, 5 to 20 us a round over the matrix's 16 boots with more than one processor (6 to 8 us in most), one interrupt each and none on a processor outside the space; 4 to 5 us with one processor.

## The loader's build is reproducible bit for bit, and a gate keeps it so (TASKS item 31; CLAUDE.md §75; 2026-11-10)

- **What:** on `claude/clever-robinson-751c44`, cut from `docs/design-review-2026-11-10` at `2fbaea6`. Two release builds of the same loader source gave `origin-boot.efi` files that differed in 10 to 12 bytes (item 17's finding, in its entry's "What it did to the built code"). They now give the same bytes, and `cargo xtask check` fails if they stop.
  - **The cause, by experiment with the pinned toolchain** (`docs/research/2026-11-10-loader-reproducible-build.md`, written under §16). Two things differed. The linker writes the time of the link into the PE header. And for the UEFI target rustc passes `/DEBUG` whatever `-C strip` says, so the linker writes a PDB, and a CodeView record in the image whose identifier is a hash of that PDB; the PDB holds the path of every file linked, and one of them is in a directory rustc creates under a random name for each link. Relinking by hand from rustc's saved command line showed it: the same command twice gives the same image, and the same command with only that directory renamed does not. So an argument about the time alone leaves two builds different.
  - **The change:** two link arguments for `x86_64-unknown-uefi` in `.cargo/config.toml`. `/DEBUG:NONE` removes the PDB, the record, and with them the debug directory. `/TIMESTAMP:0` makes the header's stamp zero. No line of the loader's source changed.
  - **The second argument was `/Brepro` at first** (`b3b641e`), which makes the stamp a hash of the image and leaves one `IMAGE_DEBUG_TYPE_REPRO` entry in a debug directory. That was built, tested and booted at `32f1a94`. The owner then supplied UEFI 2.11, which `uefi.org` had refused to serve. Its section 2.1.1 says what firmware uses of an image: the PE32+ header's `Subsystem` and `Machine`, every section, the relocations and the entry point. A search of its text finds no mention of the header's time stamp or of a debug directory, and the PE/COFF revision it cites is version 8.1, not today's. With `/TIMESTAMP:0` (`42391cd`) the image holds no debug directory, so nothing in it rests on how a firmware treats a debug entry of a type it may not know, which could only be tried on real firmware (§74). The ledger's §5 has the reasons.
  - **Not a build script.** The contract named `boot/uefi/build.rs`, as the kernel has one. A build script for the loader, even one that prints nothing, changes the `-C metadata` hash Cargo gives the loader's crates, and the image then differs from the old one in 3,755 bytes with `.text` among them (same section sizes and the same count of each instruction: the same code in another order). With the arguments in the configuration file the hash does not change.
  - **The gate:** `developer-tools/xtask/src/reproducible.rs`. `check` runs it after the quick gates and before Loom; `cargo xtask reproducible-gate` runs it alone, in a turn on the machine. It builds four images from nothing in `target/xtask/reproducible/a`, waits two seconds, builds them from nothing in `target/xtask/reproducible/another-target-directory`, and compares each pair byte for byte: the loader with no feature (what a release builds), with `test-trust-store`, with `developer-mode`, and the kernel ELF. It prints each image's size and SHA-256. A failure gives the count of differing bytes, the first eight places with both builds' bytes, and says so if the PE header's time stamp is among them; both files are kept. An empty file is a difference. `build_loader` and `build_kernel` now call `build_loader_in` and `build_kernel_in`, which take a target directory; the commands they run for everything else are unchanged.
- **What it did to the built code:**
  - Loader (`test-trust-store`, 175,616 bytes before and after): 74 bytes differ from the image built at `2fbaea6`. They are the header's stamp (4), the header's entry for the debug directory (4), `.rdata`'s size (1), the debug directory's one entry (12) and the 57-byte CodeView record (53; four of its bytes were zero), all zero now but `.rdata`'s size. `.text` (154,319 bytes) is the same bytes, and the disassembly is the same text. `Machine` (`0x8664`), `Subsystem` (10, an EFI application) and the entry point are unchanged.
  - Kernel: not touched. SHA-256 `a0faf324…7f461` from each of the gate's builds, from a copy of the source in another directory, and in item 17's record for `2fbaea6`, which was built in another worktree.
- **Negative controls on the real tree,** each planted in `.cargo/config.toml`, run through `cargo xtask reproducible-gate` and undone by restoring that one file, with everything else committed first. Run for both forms of the change:
  - *Both arguments removed:* fails at the first image, "the loader as a release builds it (no feature) is not reproducible": 10 bytes in 3 places, the header's stamp at 0x80, the debug directory's at 0x29B84 and the identifier's eight bytes at 0x29BA0, with the line that names the time stamp. This is the tree as it was before the change.
  - *`/DEBUG:NONE` alone:* fails, 1 byte, the header's stamp.
  - *`/TIMESTAMP:0` alone:* fails, 8 bytes, the identifier. The two stamps are zero and agree.
  - *`/Brepro` alone,* run with the first form: fails, 20 bytes in 4 places: the hash that stands for the stamp, in three places, and the identifier.
  - *The kernel linked with `--build-id=uuid`:* the three loaders pass, then "the kernel ELF is not reproducible": 16 bytes at 0x280, the random identifier. So the kernel's comparison is live too.
  - After each set of four, `.cargo/config.toml` was as committed, and the gate passed.
- **Unit tests:** 11 new in `xtask` (82 in all): the same bytes are no difference; one changed byte found at four offsets with both values, told both ways round; a longer and a shorter file; an empty file against anything; differences near each other counted as one place and far apart as two; a long report cut short, saying how much it left out; a time stamp that differs named, and a byte on either side of it not called a time stamp; what is and is not a PE image; the list of images and the two directories.
- **Author / date:** Claude Code agent (local, M1 Max), 2026-11-10. Original code; `std` and the project's own `origin-crypto` (for the digests it prints). No linker, compiler or operating-system source was opened (§3).
- **Architecture decisions:** CLAUDE.md §75, §60 and §14, and rule 28. No ADR: this is not an ABI or format decision (§84). Choosing a zero stamp over `/Brepro` was Claude's, is recorded with its reasons in the ledger, and is one line to change back.
- **Specifications:** each read on 2026-11-10. UEFI 2.11 (title page dated Nov 21, 2024), sections 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 7.4.1, 18.4, 32.2.2, 32.2.3, 32.5.1, 32.5.3.3 and Appendix Q, from a copy the owner supplied (SHA-256 `a64b8e44…5400cee9`), which came through a third-party file store and was not compared with the publisher's file; it forbids copying, was read in memory, and none of its text is in the repository (§17). Microsoft's PE format specification (page dated 2026-09-10). The rustc and Cargo books as published for 1.99.1. What the toolchain itself does, by experiment (§9). Version 8.1 of the PE/COFF specification, which UEFI 2.11 cites, was not read.
- **Dependencies:** none new. The gate runs `cargo`, as every build step of `xtask` does.
- **Toolchain:** Rust 1.99.1 (`58cf8f9c3`, 2026-10-13), stable, edition 2024, on `aarch64-apple-darwin`; its `rust-lld` is LLD 23.1.1. QEMU 11.1.3 (TCG) + OVMF.
- **Test evidence (2026-11-10, on the code tip `42391cd`; the commits after it change only documents). One turn on the machine held all of it, host load average 4 to 5:**
  - `cargo xtask reproducible-gate` passes in 31 s. The digests, which a build elsewhere can be compared with: the loader with no feature, 172,544 bytes, `6137018f5331a082b477300503de796ce1a8ae2203d6916c13363fb36ddf868c`; with `test-trust-store`, 175,616 bytes, `f0b34d7883ed6ca60b03744471b1223b299370c38c698adcca99451052d5b823`; with `developer-mode`, 175,616 bytes, `944f41111b6a2af53f689dde195bcf0f595a2cbfc09c39770119a8059a8eec25`; the kernel ELF, 1,203,984 bytes, `a0faf324ba77e4f2ae669edb621b8f5573a1e00896f5be195d719b668547f461`.
  - The same four digests came from a copy of the source (`git archive`) built with plain `cargo` in a directory outside the checkout, and the `test-trust-store` one from `touch boot/uefi/src/main.rs` and a rebuild in the working target directory.
  - `cargo xtask check` passes in 4 min 49 s, the gate included: 1,205 host tests, 0 failed, 8 ignored; Loom, all 39 models passed and all 60 negative controls were caught.
  - `cargo xtask boot-test` passes on its first attempt, 11 of 11 scenarios in 93 s: the signed kernel boots with developer mode off and ends `boot verdict: 56 of 56 proofs passed`; the unsigned kernel boots only in developer mode; and the unsigned, wrong-key, tampered-statement, tampered-Ed25519, tampered-ML-DSA, tampered-content, substituted and bad-signature-in-developer-mode images are each refused. No proof, marker or bound changed: nothing under `boot/` or `framekernel/` is touched, and none of xtask's boot markers. The loader on the boot's EFI partition has the digest the gate printed for `test-trust-store`.
  - The first form, with `/Brepro`, at `32f1a94`: the gate passed in 28 s, `cargo xtask check` passed (1,205 host tests, 0 failed, 8 ignored; Loom 39 models, 60 controls) and `cargo xtask boot-test` passed on its first attempt (11 of 11 scenarios, 56 of 56 proofs). Its loader digests were `d07cb7fe…17048`, `31d81e4b…88e58` and `4cf80ce2…4cb45`.
  - Before the change, at `2fbaea6`: build, copy, `touch boot/uefi/src/main.rs`, build, `cmp -l` gave 10 differing bytes.
  - In a scratch merge of this branch (at `32f1a94`) with item 17's (`053ceff`) and item 19's (`claude/intelligent-dhawan-a7f6d4`), `xtask` was clippy-clean and its 140 tests passed, and item 17's `cfg-lint` and `unsafe-gate` passed. `boot-matrix` was not run: no kernel or loader code changed.
  - Each commit builds. The four that change code or configuration (`b3b641e`, `68493c1`, `32f1a94`, `42391cd`) were each built on their own with `-j 2`: rustfmt clean, `xtask` clippy-clean under `-D warnings`, its tests passing (70 at the first, 81 at the others, 1 ignored), and the loader building.
- **Found, not changed** (ledger §9; TASKS item 32):
  - Both images hold the path the toolchain is installed at, because `rust-toolchain.toml` installs `rust-src`: one such path in the loader and eight in the kernel. Another account or another host gives a path of another length, so two machines cannot give the same bytes yet. The gate cannot see it: both of its builds use one toolchain.
  - `RUSTFLAGS` in the environment replaces the configuration file's list: the two link arguments and `force-frame-pointers` are then all dropped, for the kernel too. The gate fails in that case and says what to look at.
  - A worktree under the main checkout also reads the main checkout's `.cargo/config.toml`. Once this change is on `main`, a worktree whose own file lost the arguments would still get them, and pass the gate. CI's checkout has nothing above it.
- **Not proven, and limits:**
  - One machine. No image built on another machine, account or host system was compared, and the gate has not yet run on Linux, where CI will run it.
  - Nothing ran on physical hardware (rule 30). Only OVMF has loaded this loader.
  - The copy of UEFI 2.11 was not compared with the publisher's file, and the text inside its figures was not searched.
  - The gate shows two builds agree, not that the image is right. It does not build the signed or packed kernel image; `onbf-pack` has its own test that packing twice gives the same bytes.
  - The loader's PDB is no longer written. Nothing read it.
  - No human has reviewed any of this.
